[Qur'an 12:1]

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra.﴾

The discussion of these and similar disjointed letters (al-muqatta'at) has already preceded at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

* * *

﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾
The discussion of "These are the verses of the Book" has passed in Surat Yunus. The Book is described here as "the Clear" (al-Mubin), whereas in the opening of Surat Yunus it was described as "the Wise" (al-Hakim), because mentioning the attribute of clarity (ibanah) is more fitting here, since the story contained in this surah is a detailed account clarifying the most important events of the period of Yusuf (peace be upon him) in Egypt. The story of Yusuf (peace be upon him) was not known to the Arabs before the revelation of the Qur'an, either in summary or in detail, unlike the stories of the prophets Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut and Shu'ayb (peace be upon them all), which were known to them in summary. Therefore the Qur'an came to clarify and elaborate them.

Page 201
Its revelation before the Prophet (ﷺ) mixed with the Jews in Madinah is a great miracle, a communication from God, exalted is He, informing him of the knowledge of the earlier peoples. By this, the Companions were made equal to the scholars of the Children of Israel in knowledge of the history of religions and prophets, and this is among the most important things that lawgivers know.

So "al-Mubin" is an active participle from abana, the transitive form. What is meant is complete clarity in both wording and meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 2:

﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, that you might understand.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) which indicates the reason for the clarity (ibana) in both its wording and its meaning. The fact that it is a Qur'an (qur'an, a recited text) indicates the clarity of its meanings, for it was made to be recited only because of the meanings in its structures that are beneficial to the reader.

That it is Arabic indicates that the clarity of its words conveys the intended meanings to those to whom it was first addressed, namely the Arabs, for they could not comprehend anything of the other nations around them, since their books were in languages other than Arabic.

The emphasis with "inna" (indeed) is directed at its predicate, which is the verb "anzalnahu" (We have sent it down), in response to those who denied that it was sent down from Allah.

The pronoun in "anzalnahu" refers to the Book in His saying: "the Clear Book" (al-kitab al-mubin).

"Qur'anan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun (ha') in "anzalnahu," meaning a book that is recited, that is, arranged in a style prepared to be read, not like the style of letters, sermons, or poetry, but rather the style of a book that benefits people with continuous benefit which they read.

"'Arabiyyan" is an adjective of "Qur'anan." Thus it is a book in Arabic, unlike the earlier books, for no book in the language of the Arabs had preceded it.

Page 202

The intended reason has been expressed by the clause "la'allakum ta'qilun," that is, the hope of attaining knowledge for you from its wording and its meaning, because you are Arabs; so its descent in your language, containing what is beneficial to you, is the cause of your understanding what it contains. He expressed knowledge by "intellect" (aql) to indicate that the evidence of the Qur'an for this knowledge has reached such clarity that whoever does not gain knowledge from it is placed in the rank of one without intellect, and that as long as they turn away from it, they are among those who are not intelligent.

The omission of the object of "ta'qilun" indicates that its sending down in this manner is the cause of attaining understanding of many things of knowledge, including its miraculous nature (i'jaz) and other matters.

The manner in which "la'alla" occurs in the speech of God the Exalted has been mentioned earlier. Its implied sense of hope, which reverts to the meaning of causation, was discussed in the commentary on His saying: "Then We pardoned you after that, so that you might be grateful" (2:52) in Surat al-Baqara, and in many verses after it, without any ambiguity remaining.

[Page 203]

This sentence stands in the place of a substitution of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*) from the sentence ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2], because the best of narratives is among the things that the sending down of the Qur'an includes. The narratives being from God is, in the same way, a substitution of inclusion that emphasizes its being sent down from God.

His saying ﴿by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ contains a link between the substituting sentence and the sentence being substituted.

The opening of the sentence with the pronoun of majesty (*damir al-'azamah*, the royal "We") serves to draw attention to the report, as the secretaries of the chancery (*kitab al-diwan*) say: "The Commander of the Believers orders such-and-such."

[Page 203 continues]

Placing the pronoun before the verbal predicate conveys exclusivity (*ikhtisas*), meaning: "It is We who narrate, not anyone else," in answer to the polytheists who attacked the Qur'an by saying ﴿Only a human teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl: 103], and their saying ﴿Tales of the ancients which he has had written down﴾ [al-Furqan: 5], and their saying: "He is taught by a man from the people of Yamamah whose name is al-Rahman." And the statement of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, mentioned earlier, is the preamble to the tafsir of this surah.

In this exclusivity there is an agreement between the substituting sentence and the sentence being substituted in affirming that the Qur'an is from God, which is conveyed by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2].

The meaning of *naqussu* is "we relate the past reports." It is derived from *qassa al-athar*, meaning to follow the places of footsteps in order to learn the end of the path taken by their owner. Its verbal noun is *al-qassu* with assimilation (*idghам*), and *al-qasas* without it, and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they went back, retracing their footsteps [qasasan]﴾ [al-Kahf: 64]. This is because recounting the reports of those who passed away resembles following their steps. Do you not see that they called deeds *sirah* (conduct), although its original sense is the manner of walking, and they said: "So-and-so walked the way (*sara sirata*) of so-and-so," meaning he did the same as his deed? They distinguished between this figurative usage and the tracing of footprints: they reserved the figurative meaning for the unassimilated form, and they gave the assimilated verbal noun precedence for the literal meaning, while the unassimilated verbal noun also remains, as in His saying: ﴿So they went back, retracing their footsteps [qasasan]﴾ [al-Kahf: 64].

So ﴿the best of narratives [ahsan al-qasas]﴾ here is either an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) specifying the type of its verb, or *al-qasas* may be used in the sense of the object (*maf'ul*) through the usage of the verbal noun to mean the object, like *al-khalq* meaning "the created thing." This usage of *al-qasas* in this sense is also common. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There was certainly in their narratives [qasasihim] a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111]. The form *fa'al* may also mean the object, as in *al-naba'* and *al-khabar* meaning "that which is reported" and "that which is informed," and similarly *al-hasab* and *al-naqd*.

This narrative was described as "the best of narratives" because some narratives are not free of a beauty that souls find delightful. The narratives of the Qur'an are better than the narratives of others in terms of the beauty of their composition, the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of their style, and what they contain of lessons and wisdom. Thus every narrative in the Qur'an is the best of narratives in its own category, and every story in the Qur'an is better than everything that a storyteller recounts outside the Qur'an. The intended meaning is not "the best of the Qur'an's narratives," such that the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, would be better than the rest of the Qur'an's narratives, as His saying ﴿by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ indicates.

The *ba'* in ﴿by what We have revealed to you﴾ indicates cause (*sababiyyah*) and is connected to *naqussu*. The narratives contained in the Qur'an are the best because they come from the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. He reveals what He knows to be most beneficial for the listeners in the most wondrous words and structures, and thereby there comes forth nourishment for the intellect and the spirit, delight for the soul, and savor, of a kind that the minds of human beings cannot bring about.

The demonstrative (*ism al-isharah*) serves to add distinction. The mention of the Qur'an has been repeated, explicitly, by pronoun, and by demonstrative, six times, and it has been given all the methods of definiteness: the definite article, the pronoun, proper-name status (*'alamiyyah*), demonstration, and annexation (*idafah*).

The clause ﴿and indeed you were, before it, among the unaware﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the *kaf* of address. The particle *in* is the light form (*mukhaffafah*) of the heavy *inna*, and its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*).

The clause ﴿you were before it among the unaware﴾ is the predicate of the omitted pronoun of the matter. The *lam* that enters the predicate of *kunta* is the *lam* of distinction (*lam al-farq*) between the light *in* and the negating *in*.

The *lam* was introduced into the predicate of *kana* because it is part of the clause that serves as the predicate of *in*.

The pronoun in *qablihi* refers to the Qur'an, and what is meant by "before it" is before its descent, as indicated by the context.

Heedlessness (*al-ghaflah*) is the absence of knowledge due to the mind not being directed toward the known. The meaning intended by heedlessness is clear. The reason for describing him as among the unaware, rather than describing him alone as unaware, is to indicate that he was favored with the Qur'an over everyone who did not benefit from the Qur'an, and so his companions and the Muslims entered into this favor, despite their differing ranks in knowledge.

The implication of *min qablihi* is intended to allude to the polytheists who turned away from the guidance of the Qur'an. The Prophet ﷺ said:

[Page 205]

"The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which God has sent me is like abundant rain that fell on a land. Part of it was fertile ground that absorbed the water and produced abundant grass and vegetation. Part of it was hard ground that held the water, so God benefited people with it: they drank, gave drink, and cultivated. It also fell on another part, which was flat barren plains that neither hold water nor produce grass. That is the likeness of one who has understanding in the religion of God and whom what God has sent me with benefits, so he knows and teaches. And the likeness of one who does not lift his head toward that and does not accept the guidance of God with which I was sent."

That is, the polytheists, whose likeness is that of one who does not lift his head to look.

﴿When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."﴾

"When" (idh) is a *badal ishtimal* (inclusive substitution) or a *badal ba'd* (partitive substitution) for ﴿the best of stories﴾ [Yusuf: 3], on the condition that "the best of stories" is taken in the sense of the object (*al-maf'ul*). This is because "the best of stories" comprises many stories, among them the story of the time when Joseph, peace be upon him, said to his father, ﴿I saw eleven stars﴾, and the events that followed that statement. If "the best of stories" [Yusuf: 3] is understood as a verbal noun (*masdar*), then the most appropriate reading is that *idh* is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted but indicated by the context, and the implied meaning is: "Remember."

"Yusuf" (Joseph) is a Hebrew name, whose mention was already discussed in the commentary on the words of God, ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ [al-An'am: 83], etc., in Surat al-An'am. He is Joseph son of Jacob son of Isaac, from his wife Rachel. He is one of the tribes (*al-asbat*) whose mention was already made in Surat al-Baqarah. Joseph was the most beloved of Jacob's sons to him, and the father's excessive love for him became the cause of his brothers' jealousy, so they plotted against him. They asked their father to let him go out with them. They took him out with them under the pretext of play and recreation, threw him into a well, and told their father that they had lost him, and that they had found his shirt stained with blood. They showed him the shirt after smearing it with blood. A caravan (*sayyarah*) of Arabs, the Isma'ilites, who were travelling on their way to Egypt, picked him up from the well, and they sold him as a slave in the market of the capital of Egypt, the Lower (*al-sufla*), which at that time was under the rule of a people of the Canaanites known as the Amalekites, or the Hyksos (*al-Hukṣus*). This happened in the time of the king Abu Fis, or Ibibi. It is likely that this occurred around the year 1729 BC.

Potiphar (*Futifar*), the chief of police of Pharaoh, who is called in the Qur'an "the 'Aziz", that is, the chief of the city, bought him. A plot was hatched against him by the wife of his master, because of which he was thrown into prison. Because of a dream seen by the king, which Joseph, peace be upon him, interpreted while he was in prison, the king brought him near and gave him a high station, and placed him over all the land of Egypt. This is the title of "the 'Aziz," and he named him Safnat-Fa'aneeh, and married him to Asenath (*Asnat*), the daughter of one of the priests. He was thirty years old at that time. During his rule, he brought his father and his relatives from the desert to the land of Egypt, and this was the cause of the settlement of the Children of Israel in the land of Egypt. He died in Egypt around the year 1635 BC, before the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him. He was embalmed in the Egyptian manner and placed in a coffin, and before his death he instructed that when they left Egypt they should carry his body with them. When the Children of Israel left Egypt, they carried Joseph's coffin, peace be upon him, with them and moved it along with them on their journey until they buried it in Shechem (*Shakim*) during the time of Joshua son of Nun.

[Page 207]

The *ta'* in *abati* is a *ta'* specific to the word for "father" and the word for "mother" in the vocative only, with the intention of an added pronoun referring to the speaker. Its meaning is thus the same as "*ya abi*" (O my father), though the Arabs hardly ever say "*ya abi*." It occurs in the greeting of Ibn 'Umar upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companion when he stood at their illuminated graves. The linguists (*a'immat al-lughah*) were perplexed in explaining why it is joined to the end of the word in the vocative. They preferred that its origin is the *ta'* of feminine gender, based on the evidence that they sometimes change it into *ha'* when pausing, and that it was made a substitute for the first-person *ya'* for an unconvincing reason. What appears to me is that its origin is *ha' al-sakt* (the silent *ha'*), which they brought in for pausing on the end of *ab*, because a letter had been dropped from the root of the word. Then, when it came to resemble the feminine *ha'* through frequent use, it was treated as the last letter of the word when they added the pronoun to the vocative, saying "*ya abati*," and then they dispensed with the *ya'* of the pronoun by the *kasrah* (vowel) because of frequent use. The survival of the *ya'* in some speech supports this, as in the words of the poet, whose identity we do not know:

*O my father, may you not cease to be among us, for we have hope in life as long as you are alive.*

This *ta'* may be pronounced with a *kasrah* or with a *fathah*. The majority of reciters read it with a *kasrah*, while Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it with a *fathah*.

The vocative in the verse, even though the addressee is present, is intended to draw attention to the news that will be conveyed to the addressee. Thus it places the addressee in the position of an absent person whose presence is desired. This is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for attentiveness, or a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for it.

*Al-kawkab* means "star," which was already discussed in the commentary on the words of God, ﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star﴾ [al-An'am: 76], in Surat al-An'am.

The clause ﴿I saw them﴾ is an emphatic restatement (*mu'akkidah*) of the clause ﴿I saw eleven stars﴾. It has been brought in accordance with the usage in narrating dream visions, that the verb "to see" is repeated as a verbal emphasis or as an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), as though the listener of the dream wishes the dreamer to tell him more about what he saw.

An example of this is what occurs in the *Muwatta'* (the book of Imam Malik) that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I was shown last night at the Ka'bah, and I saw a man, dark-complexioned..." and so on.

In al-Bukhari it is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw in a dream that I was migrating from Mecca to a land with palm trees, and I saw in it cows being slaughtered, and I saw... by God, it is good." Another word than the verb of seeing may be used in dreams, as in the long hadith: "There came to me last night two visitors, and they sent me forth, and they said to me, 'Go,' and I went with them, and we came upon a man lying down..." and so on, with the repetition of the words *inna* and *inna* many times in this hadith.

[Page 208]

The majority read *ahada 'ashara* (eleven) with a *fathah* on the 'ayn, from *'ashara*. Abu Ja'far read it with a *sukun* on the 'ayn.

He used the plural masculine pronoun for the stars, the sun, and the moon in his words ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾, because the attribution of this to rational beings is the general rule but not a consistent one, as God said of idols, ﴿And you see them looking at you, but they do not see﴾ [al-A'raf: 198], and He said, ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml: 18].

Some of the exegetes said: since the visible state of the stars, the sun, and the moon was the state of rational beings, which is the state of prostration, He placed them in the position of rational beings, and so applied to them the pronoun *hum* and the plural form.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing element in ﴿prostrating to me﴾ serves emphasis. By this, it expresses the meaning implied in Joseph's speech, in his language, indicating a condition in the stars of reverence toward him that calls for attention to be given to mentioning him. The fronting of the prepositional phrase in the Arabic language conveys this.

The beginning of the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, with the mention of his dream is an indication that God prepared him for prophethood, so He began with a true dream, as came in the hadith of 'A'ishah: "The first thing with which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was begun in revelation was the true dream, and he would not see a dream except that it came like the break of dawn." In this there is a preparation for the purpose of the story, which is to establish the virtue of Joseph, peace be upon him, in purity, soundness of soul, and patience. So He mentioned this dream at the beginning of the story as a preface and introduction to the intended story.

God made that dream a reminder to Joseph, peace be upon him, of the loftiness of his rank, so that he would recall it whenever distress befell him, and his soul would be reassured that his end would be good.

Joseph, peace be upon him, told his father of this dream because he knew, by inspiration or by prior teaching from his father, that dreams have an interpretation, and he knew that the stars, the sun, and the moon are a metonymy

[Page 209]

for noble existents, and that the prostration of noble creatures to him is a metonymy for the greatness of his station. Perhaps he knew that the stars are a metonymy for similar existents, and that the sun and the moon are a metonymy for the two origins of those existents, so he sensed in general terms that his dream indicated the elevation of his rank, and so he told his father of it.

They used to count dreams among the means of informing about the unseen, when they were free from confusion, when the temperament of the dreamer was not deviant or disturbed, and when the dreamer was accustomed to the occurrence of the interpretation of his dreams. This is something they inherited from the purity of the souls of their forefathers Abraham and Isaac, peace be upon them both, for they were the household of prophethood and purity of heart.

Since the dreams of the prophets are revelation, and Abraham, peace be upon him, saw in a dream that he was slaughtering his son, when he informed him, [his son] said: ﴿O my father, do what you are commanded﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. To this refers the saying of Joseph's father, peace be upon him: ﴿And He will complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Abraham and Isaac﴾ [Yusuf: 6]. Therefore it is inevitable that the visions of their sons are an unveiling and a angelic discourse.

In a hadith: "Nothing remains of the good tidings except the good dream, which a Muslim sees or which is seen for him."

Reliance on dreams is among the ancient matters of prophethood. It has come in the Torah that God addressed Abraham, peace be upon him, in a dream he saw while on his way in the land of Shalim, a royal and truthful city, and promised him that He would grant him abundant offspring and give him the land in which he was traveling (in chapter 15 of the Book of Genesis).

As for the Arabs, although nothing has come in their speech indicating their reliance on dreams, perhaps the verse of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr indicates their non-reliance on dreams:

*Indeed, wishes and dreams are delusion.*

[Page 210]

For "dreams" in this verse are the visions of sleep.

However, Ibn Ishaq mentioned the dream of 'Abd al-Muttalib, while he was standing in al-Hijr, that a comer came to him and commanded him to dig the well of Zamzam, and he described its location to him. The Jurhum had filled it in when they left Mecca. Ibn Ishaq also mentioned the dream of 'Atikah, daughter of 'Abd al-Muttalib, that: "A rider came on a camel and stopped at al-Abtah, then cried out: 'O Ghadar's people, go out to your place of death in three days!'" and the battle of Badr occurred three nights after it.

The dream visions have been counted among the principles of Illuminationist wisdom (*al-hikmah al-ishraqiyyah*), and they are part of its heritage from the wisdom of earlier religions, such as the Hanifiyyah. Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi, the sage, exaggerated in bringing them close to psychological principles in *Hayakil al-Nur* and *Hikmat al-Ishraq*, and Abu 'Ali Ibn Sina in *al-Isharat*, with what amounts to the following, and its essence: the rational soul, which is what is expressed by the spirit, is one of the immaterial substances whose abode is the higher world. It is thus capable of discovering existents, with varying degrees of this capacity. It is deposited into the body of the fetus when the stage of the lump of flesh is complete. The rational soul has traces of unveilings, and when they appear, some of them may be imprinted by the perceptions of the owner of the soul upon the tablet of his common sense. The imprinting may be prevented by two preoccupations: one external and sensory, and the other internal, intellectual or imaginative. The faculties of the soul compete with and oppose one another, and when some of them become strong, others become weak. Just as when anger is aroused, desire weakens, so likewise if the inner sense becomes free for work, it becomes occupied away from the outer sense. Sleep occupies the senses. When the preoccupations of the outer senses decrease, the soul may be freed from the preoccupation of its imaginings, and so it gains insight into hidden matters, and true dreams occur.

True dreaming is a state with which God honors some of His chosen servants whose souls are purified, so their souls become connected with allotments of the knowledge of God, and allotments of His will, power, and creative command. Through it, things hidden in time before their occurrence are unveiled, or things hidden in place before people's ordinary perception of them. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

[Page 211]

"The good dream from a righteous man is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood."

The determination of this ratio mentioned in the hadith has been explained in the commentaries on the hadith. And he said: "Nothing remains of prophethood except the good tidings, which are the good dreams of a righteous man, which he sees or which are seen for him."

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah Yusuf 12:4 (part 2 of 2):

The condition that the truthful dream comes to one who is righteous among people was stipulated because disciplining oneself in righteous deeds keeps the soul occupied away from evil deeds. Moreover, righteous deeds are elevations and perfections, so they aid the essence of the soul in connecting with its world, in which it was created and from which it was sent down. By contrast, evil deeds distance it from what it is accustomed to, dull it, and make it unstable.

Dreams have degrees.

Among them: you see images of actions whose likenesses come to be realized in existence, such as the Prophet's (ﷺ) dream that he was migrating from Makkah to a land of palm trees. He thought that land was al-Yamamah, but it turned out to be Madinah. There is no doubt that when he saw Madinah, he found it matching the image he had seen. Likewise, [there is] his dream of a woman in a silk cloth, and it was said to him, "Uncover her, for she is your wife," so he uncovered her and behold, it was 'A'ishah, and he knew that he would marry her. This type is rare, and the state of unveiling (kashf) in it is strong.

Among them: you see images that serve as symbols of realities that will occur or that have occurred in fact. These belong to the category of the soul's unveiling of meanings and intimations, and the imagination's shaping of those realities into perceptible forms that manifest those meanings. This is a kind of likening and representation, of the sort that the minds of orators and poets devise, except that this is devised by the mind when the brain is calm from distracting preoccupations, so it is more precise and truthful. This is the most common type of dreams. From it is the Prophet's (ﷺ) dream that he was drinking from a bowl of milk; he saw the fullness appearing in his fingernails, then he gave its surplus to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). He interpreted that as knowledge.

Likewise, [there is] his dream of a black woman with disheveled hair going out of Madinah to al-Juhfah, and he interpreted her as fever moving from Madinah to al-Juhfah. "'Abdullah ibn Salam saw that he was in a garden, and that in it there was a pillar, and that on the pillar there was a handle, and that he took hold of that handle and climbed to the top of the pillar. The Prophet (ﷺ) interpreted it as meaning that he would continue to hold fast to faith, which is the most trustworthy handhold, and that the garden is Paradise." Thus the dream's imagery coincides with the commonly known imagery in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the Taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], and in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What lies between my house and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise."

The interpretation of this dream will come at His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before"﴾ [Yusuf: 100].

[Page 212]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 5:

﴿He said, "O my little son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy."﴾

The sentence is detached from the one before it, following the manner of dialogue. It was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The vocative (nida') with a present addressee is used to draw the listener's attention, showing concern for the matter being addressed.

(Bunayya), with a kasra on the doubled ya', is the diminutive (tasghir) of ibn (son), with the first-person possessive ya' attached. Its underlying form is bunayawi or bunayayi, depending on the disagreement over whether the letter lam of ibn, whose retention is always dropped, is a waw or a ya'. In either case, the diminutive ya' was assimilated into it (idgham) after the waw was changed into a ya', because ya' and waw are close to each other or alike, and it became "bunayyi." Three ya's then came together, so one had to be removed. The ya' of the speaker was necessarily dropped, and the kasra that had been brought in for it was placed on the diminutive ya' as an indication of the deleted ya'. Dropping the ya' of the speaker from a construction of the vocative with a possessive is common, especially when keeping it would be burdensome, as here, since the meeting of three ya's is burdensome.

This diminutive is a kinaya (metonymy) for affection and compassion. The elder is treated as the younger, since it is the nature of the young to be loved and pitied. This also implies a kinaya for sincere counsel to him.

Al-qass (relating) means recounting a dream: one says qassa al-ru'ya when he recounts it and reports it. It derives from qasas, as you have already learned.

Al-ru'ya (the dream), with the feminine alif, is the seeing of images during sleep. They distinguished it from waking sight by the difference in the feminine markers. It follows the pattern of bushra and buqya.

Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew that the ten brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, were jealous of him because of his great excellence over them in character and in form. He knew that they interpret dreams, in general and in detail, and he knew that this dream announced an elevation that Yusuf, peace be upon him, would attain over his brothers, who were eleven. So he feared that if Yusuf, peace be upon him, related it to them, their jealousy would intensify to the point of envy, and they would interpret it according to its literal meaning, and the worst of the envier would arise in them when they envy. Then they would plot a scheme against him so that they might be safe from his superiority over them and his excellence among them.

Al-kayd (scheming) is concealing an action that harms the one plotted against. It was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-A'raf: 183] in Surat al-A'raf.

The lam in (laka) is for emphasizing the connection of the verb to its object, as in the saying: "I thanked you for the favour."

The tanwin on kaydan is for magnification and dread, an added warning against relating the dream to them.

Ya'qub, peace be upon him, intended by this the safety of his son from harms that would befall him, and he did not intend to nullify what the dream indicated, for it would occur after harms and hardships. He knew that his sons had not reached the depth of insight that leads to the realization that if the dream indicates a great good that he will attain, then it is a divine report, and it is not permissible for it to fail to match what will happen in the future. Rather, they might regard it as a warning through natural causes, whose causation ceases when some of them are disabled.

Ya'qub's saying this to his son was a warning, along with his confidence that the warning would not stir up in his soul any aversion towards his brothers, because he trusted in his perfect intellect, purity of inner nature, and noble character. One whose state is like this is generous, forgiving, overlooking faults, and aware of the effect of patience in attaining high rank. For this reason he said to his brothers: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears God and is patient, then indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ [Yusuf: 90], and he said: ﴿No reproach will be upon you today. May God forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [Yusuf: 92]. One of the two sons of Adam, peace be upon him, also said to his brother, who had said to him, "I will surely kill you out of envy": ﴿If you extend your hand against me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 28]. So it is not problematic how Ya'qub warned Yusuf, peace be upon them both, against the scheming of his brothers. For this reason he followed his statement with His words: ﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾, so that it would be known that he warned him only against the incitement of Satan in the souls of his brothers.

This is like the excuse of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the two men of the Ansar who met him at night while he was escorting his wife, the Mother of the Believers, to her house. When they saw him, they turned away. He said: "Slow down, she is Safiyya." They said: "Glory be to God, O Messenger of God!" and they regarded that as a great matter. He said to them: "Indeed, Satan flows through the son of Adam as the blood flows, and I feared that he would cast something into your souls."

So this is a verse of lesson, indicating Ya'qub's, peace be upon him, insight into the states of his sons and his judgment that he should restrain some of them from scheming against others.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Satan is to man﴾ and so on is in the position of a causal explanation for the prohibition against relating the dream to his brothers. The enmity of Satan towards the human species drives him to push them to harm one another.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not relate his dream to his brothers, which suits his perfection that moves him to obey his father's command. It occurs in the Isra'iliyyat (narrations from Israelite sources) that he related it to them, and so they envied him.

[Page 215]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 6:

﴿And thus your Lord will choose you, and teach you the interpretation of events, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Ya'qub, just as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq. Indeed your Lord is Knowing, Wise.﴾

This statement is connected to his (Ya'qub's) warning against relating the dream to his brothers. It informs him of his elevated rank and of the perfection that awaits him, so that he increases in contemplating the sublimity of noble character, his breast becomes broad enough to bear the harm of his brothers, and he forgives their jealousy and envy of him, so that his warning becomes purely for good, and the harm of stirring up hatred and the like is removed from him. This is a great prophetic wisdom and an effective spiritual remedy.

The reference in His words "and thus" is to what the dream indicated of the divine care for him; that is, "and like that choosing, your Lord will choose you in the future." The comparison here is a comparison of cause (tashbih ta'lil), because it is the comparison of one of two effects with the other on account of the unity of the cause. The position of the prepositional phrase is that of an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of "yajtabika" (will choose you), specifying the type and manner of the choosing.

Al-ijtiba' (choosing) is selection and preference. It was mentioned in His words, exalted is He, "wa-ijtabaynahum" in Surat al-An'am, meaning His selecting him from among his brothers, or from among many of His creation. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew this through the interpretation of the dream and its indication of a rise in rank in the future. When this is combined with the virtues he already possessed, it leads to God's choosing him, and that signals his prophethood. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew that Yusuf's elevation in his future was a divine elevation because he knew that God's blessings are proportionate; since what He began bestowing upon him of blessings was choosing and psychological perfection, it became necessary that what follows them be of their kind.

Then, that spiritual ascent, which is one of the divine inspirations, has as its ultimate aim to bring its possessor to prophethood or wisdom. Therefore Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew that God would teach Yusuf, peace be upon him, the interpretation of events, because the cause of a thing is derived from the cause of that thing. So the teaching of interpretation arises from the comparison contained in His words "and thus." Also, Yusuf's concern for his dream and his presenting it to his father indicated to his father that God had placed in Yusuf's soul care for the interpretation and explanation of dreams. This is a lesson in the state of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, with his son, for he informed him of what he perceived of God's care for him, so that he would increase in turning toward perfection, by His words: ﴿and complete His favor upon you﴾.

Al-ta'wil: returning a thing to its reality and its evidence. It was mentioned at His words, exalted is He: ﴿and none knows its interpretation except God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7].

Al-ahadith: it may be the plural of hadith in the sense of "a thing that has occurred (haditha)," so the interpretation of events is returning occurrences to their causes and reasons by fully grasping their realities; this is what is meant by wisdom, and it is achieved by reasoning from the kinds of existing things to the power and wisdom of God. It may also be the plural of hadith in the sense of a report that is narrated, so ta'wil is the interpretation of dreams. They were called ahadith because the dreamer relates them to those who see them. Some exegetes took it in this sense, and they relied on His words at the end of the story: ﴿And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before"﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. Perhaps both meanings are intended, on the basis of the validity of using a homonym in both its meanings, which is the more correct view; or the choice of this word may be a miraculous conciseness, since a lengthy speech uttered by Ya'qub, peace be upon him, in his own language is thereby related, expressing the interpretation of things by all those meanings.

Completing the favor upon him is giving him the greatest of blessings, which is the blessing of prophethood; or it is adding kingship to prophethood and messengerhood. Thus the intended meaning is the completion of the blessing of the otherworldly choosing with the blessing of worldly glory.

Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew this from the indication of the dream concerning the prostration of the stars and the two luminaries to him. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew the interpretation of those as his brothers and his parents, or the wife of his father, who was Yusuf's maternal aunt. He knew from their representation in the dream that when they prostrate to him, his brothers will have attained prophethood. By this he also knew that God would complete His favor upon his brothers and upon the wife of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, with truthfulness, since she was the wife of a prophet. Thus the intended meaning of "the family of Ya'qub" is his close kin, namely his sons and his wife. If the intended completion of the favor upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, is the giving of kingship, then the completion of it upon the family of Ya'qub is that He added to what He had given them of excellence the blessing of kinship to the king; so it is valid then that the intended meaning of "his family" is all his relatives.

The comparison in His words: ﴿just as He completed it upon your two fathers before﴾ is a reminder to him of earlier blessings, and it is not among what the dream indicated. If the intended completion of the favor is prophethood, then the comparison is complete; and if the intended completion of the favor is kingship, then the comparison is in the completion of the favor in general.

He made Ibrahim and Ishaq, peace be upon them both, his two fathers because they had begetting over him, so they are his highest forefathers by the context, like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib."

The sentence ﴿Indeed your Lord is Knowing, Wise﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) glorifying these blessings and affirming that they occur in accordance with His knowledge and wisdom. His knowledge is His knowledge of the souls fit for these virtues, because He created them to receive that; so His knowledge of them is prior, and His wisdom is placing the blessings in their appropriate places.

The opening of the sentence with "inna" is for emphasis of concern, not for confirmation, since Yusuf, peace be upon him, does not doubt God's knowledge and wisdom. The concern serves as a means to conveying the causal explanation. The branching (tafri') in this is an allusive praise of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and his worthiness of such virtues.

[Page 218]

﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers there are signs for those who ask.﴾

This is an initial sentence (jumla ibtida'iyya), and it marks the beginning of the story that is intended, since what precedes it serves as an introduction announcing the eminence of the story's subject. So it is not one of the events that befell Joseph, peace be upon him. For this reason the style of this sentence resembles the style of the narratives, such as His saying: ﴿When they said, "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are"﴾ [Yusuf: 8]. It is similar to His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿It has only been revealed to me that I am a clear warner﴾ [Sad: 70], and ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "I am going to create a human being from clay"﴾ [Sad: 71], through to the end of the story.

The sense of containment conveyed by (fi) is a figurative sense of containment, by likening the connection between the proof and what it proves to the connection between the contained and the container. That is, the affair of Joseph, peace be upon him, and his brothers was accompanied by great proofs of lessons and admonitions, and by the manifestation of the great craftsmanship and decree of God, may He be exalted.

The word "ayat" (signs) means proofs for matters whose knowledge requires the discovery of hidden realities.

The word "ayat" is literally used for the markers of a road, which are signs that people place in the deserts so that they remain visible and are not covered by sand, in order to guide travellers. Then it was applied to decisive proofs and evidences for precise knowledge. The plural "ayat" here is intended to indicate their multiplicity and the multiplicity of their kinds. In the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, there are proofs of the good consequences of patience and good intention, of victory, and also of the disappointment, defeat and downfall that befall envy and the harming of people.

Among its proofs is the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the fact that the Qur'an is a revelation from God, for this surah contains what none knows except the rabbis of the People of the Book (ahbar ahl al-kitab), and this without reading or writing. That is among the miracles.

[Page 219]

In the eloquence of its composition and the excellence of its style there is i'jaz (inimitability), which is evidence that this speech is the work of God, which He conveyed to His Messenger (ﷺ) as a miracle for him against his people, who were people of eloquence and rhetorical skill.

By "the askers" (al-sa'ilin) is meant those from whom questioning about the admonitions and wisdoms is expected, as in His saying: ﴿in four days, equal for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat: 10]. Such usage occurs in the speech of the Arabs to arouse eagerness and to urge the seeking of news and narratives. Tarafa said:

*Ask about us the one who knows us by our strength, on the day of shaving the forelocks.*

And al-Samaw'al, or Abd al-Malik al-Harithi, said:

*Ask, if you are ignorant of people about us and about them, for the knowledgeable and the ignorant are not equal.*

And 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl said:

*You shall be divorced if you do not ask which knight your husband became when he met Sada and Khath'am.*

And Anif ibn Zibban al-Nabhani said:

*When we met between the swords, between us, for a questioner whose question about us is keen.*

Most of its usage in their speech is directed to the feminine pronoun, because women are concerned with asking about the news that people speak of. When the Qur'an came, and its news, which it made eager to be known, was news of knowledge and wisdom, that usage was diverted from addressing the feminine plural pronoun and was addressed to the masculine pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will surely befall﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1], and His saying: ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1].

It has been said that by "the askers" is meant the Jews, since a group of them asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this. This does not hold, because the surah is Meccan, and the Jews had no close contact with the Muslims in Mecca.

[Page 220]

﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a band. Indeed our father is in plain error."﴾

*Idh* (when) is an adverbial of time (*zarf*) governed by *kāna* in His saying: ﴿Certainly there were signs in Joseph and his brothers for those who ask [Yusuf: 7]﴾. That time was one of the occasions of the signs, since in their saying at that moment there is a lesson among the lessons of morality that arise from the envy of brothers and relatives. There is also a lesson in the recklessness of misleading their father, in their contempt for his opinion out of conceit, and in their heedlessness of the proper grounds that make a father prefer some of his sons. These signs remain present in the narrative about that time.

This saying reported of them is a saying of conspiracy and mutual consultation.

The opening of the speech with the emphatic *lām* of the beginning (*lām al-ibtidāʾ*), which conveys emphasis, is for the purpose of affirming the report.

The intended meaning is the affirmation of what the report necessarily implies, since none of them doubted that Joseph, peace be upon him, and his brother were dearer to their father than the rest of them. However, they were not equal in their envy of the two and in their jealousy at their father's preference for them over the rest. So some of them wanted to persuade the others of this, so that they would unite in plotting against Joseph, peace be upon him, and his brother, as will come in His saying: ﴿though we are a band﴾, and His saying: ﴿A speaker among them said: "Do not kill Joseph" [Yusuf: 10]﴾. So the speaker of these words was some of his brothers, that is, a group of them, by the indication of their saying after ﴿Kill Joseph [Yusuf: 9]﴾ and their saying ﴿A speaker among them said: "Do not kill Joseph" [Yusuf: 10]﴾.

The brother of Joseph, peace be upon him, is meant to be Benjamin. They singled him out with the term brotherhood because he was his full brother: their mother was Rachel, daughter of Laban. The rest of his brothers were half-brothers through the father. The mother of some of them was Leah, daughter of Laban, and the mother of some of them was Bilhah, the maidservant of Leah, whom Leah gave to her husband Jacob, peace be upon him.

*Ahabb* is an elative form (*ism tafḍīl*, comparative/superlative noun). The elative takes the one preferred over with *min* (from), and takes the one in whose sight the preference holds with *ilā* (to).

[Page 221]

Their claim that Joseph and his brother were dearer to Jacob, peace be upon him, than they were may be a false claim, which the belief in it roused in their souls intense jealousy at the superiority of Joseph, peace be upon him, and his brother over them in perfections. Perhaps they heard their father praising Joseph, peace be upon him, and his brother for deeds that proceeded from them, or they saw him following their guidance, or they saw from him compassion toward the two because of their youth and the death of their mother. So they imagined from this that he loved them more intensely than he loved them, a false imagination. It may also be that their claim corresponded to reality, and that the increase of his love for the two was a matter he could not control, because it is an inner feeling (*wijdān*). However, he did not favour them over the others in dealings and outward affairs. Their sons would then have known the extent of their father's love for the two from insight and signs, not from preference in treatment. Thus Jacob, peace be upon him, would not be blamed for anything that leads to hatred among brothers.

The clause ﴿though we are a band﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relating to *ahabb*, that is: "while we are more numerous." The purpose of the circumstantial clause is to express wonder at the preference of the two in love while the hope of benefit from his other sons is stronger than his hope from those two. This rests on what is common among the people of the desert, namely pride in numbers. So they assumed that the faculties of Jacob, peace be upon him, were equal to the faculties of the common people, and minds rarely grasp the heights above them. They did not know that what the people of perfection look at as grounds for preference is other than what those below them look at.

The clause ﴿Indeed our father is in plain error﴾ serves as a justification for the wonder and as a consequence of it. The pronoun in ﴿though we are a band﴾ refers to all the brothers except Joseph and his brother.

It is also possible that the clause ﴿though we are a band﴾ is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with the clause ﴿Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father﴾. The intended meaning is then a necessary implication of the report, namely the encouragement of some of them toward the other, to remove any hesitation about the act that will incite them to it in their saying ﴿Kill Joseph [Yusuf: 9]﴾. That is: "We are not unable to plot against Joseph and his brother, for we are a band, and a band finds it easy to do a great deed that a small number cannot accomplish." This is like His saying: ﴿They said: "If the wolf eats him while we are a band, then we would indeed be losers" [Yusuf: 14]﴾. In this case the clause ﴿Indeed our father﴾ serves as a justification for the incitement and as a consequence of it.

[Page 222]

*Al-ʿuṣba* (the band) is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like the names of groups, and it is also said *al-ʿiṣāba*. Most philologists said that *al-ʿuṣba* is applied to a group of ten to forty. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is from three to ten, and some lexicographers held this view, noting that in the codex of Hafsa there is His saying, may He be exalted: "Indeed those who brought the slander are a band of four among you."

The sons of Jacob, peace be upon him, were twelve, and they were the *asbāt* (the tribes). Their discussion has already been treated at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do you say that Abraham [Al-Baqarah: 140]﴾ and the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-ḍalāl* (error) is missing the path of what is right. What is meant is that he erred in managing livelihood, not that he erred in religion or belief. Error in the affairs of this world does not contradict acknowledging that the one who errs is a prophet.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 9:

﴿Kill Joseph or cast him out to some land, so that your father's face may be free for you, and after him you will be a righteous people.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustaʼnafa) in the mode of explanatory resumption (istiʼnaf bayani), because the preceding speech raises a question in the minds of the listeners about the purpose of the speakers in what they said. Thus this is the aim of the speakers. They placed the preceding speech as an introduction (muqaddima) so that the souls of the listeners would be affected, and when the desired matter is then delivered to them, they are quick to comply with it.

This is a kind of the art of oratory (sina'at al-khitaba): the orator opens his speech by preparing the souls of the listeners to be affected by the intended aim, for the state of the souls being affected dispenses with the orator the way that many sentences of explaining causes and benefits would. As al-Hariri said in the eleventh maqama: "When they had buried the dead and the phrase 'if only' had passed, an old man appeared on a mound, leaning on a staff, and said: 'For the like of this, let the workers work.'" And he went on at length in sermons.

The imperative (al-amr) is used here for guidance (al-irshad). They intended to commit an act that would separate Joseph and his father, peace be upon them both, a separation from which they would not seek nearness, by either killing him or transporting him to another land, where he would perish or be devoured.

This verse is an example of the lessons of evil morals, namely ridding oneself of the competition of one who is virtuous by his virtue, from one who is below him in it or equal to him, by destroying the possessor of virtue. It is the greatest crime, because it involves envy, harm to others, and violating what God commanded to be preserved. They were people of religion and from a household of prophethood, and God later amended their condition, praised them, and named them the Asbat (tribes).

The accusative of (ardan) (a land) is either by implying in "uṭrahūhu" the meaning of "awdiʻūhu" (deposit him), or by removing the preposition, or by treating it as analogous to the adverbial object (maf'ul fihi), because ardan is a noun of place; since it is not limited and is further made vague by being indefinite, it is treated like the names of directions. This is the weakest of the views. It is known that what is meant is a land unknown to his father.

The (yakhlu) is in the jussive mood as the answer to the imperative, meaning: if you do that, the face of your father will be free for you.

Khuluww means literally emptiness. It is used here metaphorically for not turning toward those whom they do not want him to turn toward, as if the face were emptied of things that had been present in it.

The lam in His saying "lakum" (for you) is the lam of cause, meaning: the face of your father will be free because of you, in the sense that it will be free of others besides you, so it will be solely yours.

This meaning is a figurative allusion (kinayat talwih) to the purity of his love for them without any partner.

He conjoined "and you will be after him" (wa takunu min ba'dihi), i.e., after Joseph, peace be upon him, to "yakhlu," so that it would be part of the answer to the imperative. Thus the intended meaning is a state arising from doing what was commanded, so it is determined that the righteousness meant here is worldly righteousness, i.e., the goodness of their circumstances in their life with their father, and not religious righteousness.

They did not plan anything to destroy Joseph's brother, peace be upon him, out of compassion for him because of his youth.

The insertion of the word (qawman) between kana and its predicate indicates that the goodness of condition is an established attribute in them, as if it were one of the constituents of their peoplehood. This has been discussed previously at His saying, Exalted is He: "Surely there are signs for a people who understand" [al-Baqara: 164] in Surat al-Baqara, and at His saying, Exalted is He: "But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe" [Yunus: 101] in Surat Yunus.

This matter proceeded from its speaker and its listeners among them before they attained prophethood or guardianship, because it involves committing the grave sin of killing or harming and transgression, and the grave sin of disobedience to parents.

﴿Said a speaker among them: "Do not kill Joseph, but cast him into the depths of the well; some passing caravan will pick him up, if you are going to act."﴾

The clause ﴿قالَ قائِلٌ﴾ (a speaker said) follows the manner of dialogues and exchanges of speech, as was explained earlier in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

This speaker was one of the brothers, which is why he is described as "from among them."

The speaker is referred to by an indefinite noun and a descriptive phrase rather than by a proper name, because knowing his individual identity serves no purpose; what matters is that he was one of their group. This also avoids the verbal burden of a proper name that there is no need to bear. It has been said that he was (Yahudha, Judah), and it has been said he was (Shim'un, Simeon), and it has been said he was (Ruben, Reuben). In the Book of Genesis of the Torah, it is (Reuben) who restrained them from killing him, and (Judah) who pointed the caravan to him, as in chapter 37. It is the custom of the Qur'an to mention only the name of the person relevant to the story, not the names of all those involved, as in His statement: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said...﴾ [Ghafir: 28].

Al-ilqa' (casting) means throwing.

Al-ghayabat is the plural of ghayabah, which is whatever is hidden from sight. One says ghayabat al-jubb (the darkness of the well) and ghayabat al-qabr (the darkness of the grave), and what is meant is the bottom of the well.

Al-jubb is the well that is dug and not lined with stone.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read ﴿غَياباتِ﴾ in the plural. Its meaning is the directions of that darkness, or the plural is used for emphasis on the reality of the noun, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿or like darknesses in a deep sea﴾ [al-Nur: 40]. The rest of the readers read ﴿فِي غَيابَةِ الجُبِّ﴾ in the singular.

The definite article in al-jubb is the definite article of mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni), meaning "in the darkness of a certain well among wells," like the phrase "enter the market." In meaning it is like an indefinite noun.

Perhaps they had known of wells situated at suitable distances along their travel routes, to which they would turn during their stages of travel to water their mounts and drink. They had deliberately chosen routes that passed by them. I think these wells were places where flood water flowed, and they were not very deep, since they knew that casting him into the well would not shatter his bones, and that there was no water in it that would drown him.

﴿يَلْتَقِطُهُ﴾ (will pick him up) is the answer to the imperative in ﴿وألْقُوهُ﴾ (and cast him). The implied sense is: if you cast him, a caravan will pick him up. The purpose of the causal relation implied by the answer to the imperative is to show that what this speaker suggested, namely casting Joseph, peace be upon him, into the darkness of a well, was better than what the others suggested, namely killing him or leaving him in a deadly wilderness. This is because it achieves removing Joseph, peace be upon him, far from his father, a removal after which reunion between them is not expected, without inflicting the harm of death upon Joseph, peace be upon him. For the caravan's picking him up preserves him better and better fulfills their intended aim, which is his removal. If a caravan picks him up, they will take him with them or sell him, and so he will be removed further and further.

Al-iltiqat (picking up) is taking something from the ground or the road, and it is used figuratively for taking up something lost (mud'a).

Al-sayyarah is the group characterized by the state of traveling and the frequency of it. Its feminine form is because it is interpreted as a group that travels, such as a company of farmers or sailors.

The definite article in al-sayyarah is the definite article of mental reference, because they knew that the road was never free of caravans between Syria and Egypt for trade and the transport of goods.

The clause ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ فاعِلِينَ﴾ (if you are going to act) is a conditional whose answer has been omitted, indicated by ﴿وألْقُوهُ﴾ (and cast him). That is: if you are going to act to remove him from his father, then cast him into the darkness of the wells, and do not kill him.

In it there is an implicit suggestion to delay further in what they had resolved, perhaps they would see that turning back from it was better than carrying it out. For this reason the conditional particle (in) (if) was used in its condition, as a hint that one should not be definite about it. Thus this speaker was the best of the brothers in judgment and the closest to piety. They knew that caravans go to all the wells for water, because the wells were dug at intervals matching the stages of the journey.

In this opinion there is a lesson in moderation regarding retaliation, and in being content with what achieves the purpose without excess.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 11–12:

[Page 227]
﴿They said, "O our father, what is [wrong] with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph, while we are indeed sincere toward him?" Send him with us tomorrow so he may enjoy and play, and indeed we will be his guardians.﴾

This is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because the progression of the narrative calls for the listener to ask what happened after the brother's advice to them, and whether they returned from what they had plotted and resolved upon, or held firm to what their brother had suggested.

The opening of the speech with their father, by saying "O our father," indicates that this was their habitual manner of addressing their father as sons.

Perhaps Ya'qub (peace be upon him) did not permit Yusuf (peace be upon him) to go out with his brothers for pasturing or racing, out of fear that some harm might befall him from their plotting or from others. He did not explicitly tell them that he did not trust them with him, but his situation in preventing him from going out was like the situation of one who does not trust them with him, so they treated him as one who does not trust them. They used the interrogative form employed for denial, upon the negation of trust.

In the Torah, Ya'qub (peace be upon him) sent him to his brothers, and they had gone out to pasture. If this is not a distortion, then perhaps Ya'qub (peace be upon him), after he had refused to let Yusuf (peace be upon him) go out with them, permitted him to do so, or after he heard their blame of him, he permitted him.

The construction "ma laka la taf'alu" has been discussed at his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So what is [wrong] with you, how do you judge?﴾ [Yunus: 35] in Surat Yunus; and see his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, what is [wrong] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38] in Surat Bara'ah; and his saying: ﴿So what is [wrong] with you regarding the hypocrites, [that you are] two groups?﴾ [al-Nisa': 88] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The readers agreed on the reading (﴿la ta'manna﴾) with a doubled, assimilated nun, from the nun of "amina" and the nun of the first person plural, and it is written in the Mushaf with a single nun. They differed

[Page 228]
regarding the manner of pronouncing this nun: between full idgham (assimilation), idgham with ishmam (partial rounding), and ikhfa' without idgham. This last mode is weaker, and the more preferred of the other two is idgham with ishmam; both are methods accepted for all, and they are not two schools of thought.

The particle (ʿala), with which the negated verb of trust is construed, indicates figurative elevation, in the sense of the trust being established over what follows (ʿala).

Advice (nusḥ) is an action or speech in which there is benefit for the one advised, and its verb is construed mostly with (li) and sometimes directly. It was discussed at his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord and I advise you﴾ [al-A'raf: 62] in Surat al-A'raf.

The clause ﴿And indeed we are sincere toward him﴾ is parenthetical between the clause ﴿What is [wrong] with you that you do not entrust us﴾ and the clause (send him). The meaning here is that they are doing what is beneficial to Yusuf (peace be upon him).

The clause "send him" is a resumptive explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because the preceding denial arouses Ya'qub's (peace be upon him) anticipation to know what they want from Yusuf (peace be upon him).

(Yartaʿi) was read by Nafi', Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub with the ya' of the third person and kasra on the ʿayn. Ibn Kathir read it with the nun of the speaking plural and kasra on the ʿayn. According to the reading of these four, it is the imperfect of irtaʿa, which is ifti'al from ra'y (pasturing), for emphasis in it.

It is literally used for the eating of livestock and beasts, and was borrowed in their speech for abundant eating, because when people go out to meadows and countryside for play and racing, their appetite grows strong, and they eat voraciously; therefore their eating was likened to the eating of cattle. They mentioned this only because it would please their father that they be joyful.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a nun and sukun on the ʿayn. ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with the ya' of the third person and sukun on the ʿayn. According to the reading of these six, it is the imperfect of rataʿa, when one remains in abundance and plenty of food. The verification is that

[Page 229]
this is borrowed from "ratayat al-dabbah," when the animal eats in the pasture until it is satiated. Thus the meaning according to both interpretations is one.

Play (al-la'ib): an action or speech not intended for what such things are normally intended for, such as running, leaping, racing, and training, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"So the maidens continued to pelt one another with its fat"

It intends by it relaxation and the removal of boredom. It is permissible in all the laws when it does not become a habit. Therefore there is no basis for the questioning by the author of al-Kashshaf about Ya'qub's (peace be upon him) permitting them to play.

Those who read "narta'" with the nun of plurality also read "wa-nal'ab" with the nun.

The clause ﴿And indeed we are his guardians﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), like ﴿And indeed we are sincere toward him﴾. The emphasis in both is for affirmation, presenting their father as one who doubts that they would guard and advise him, just as they treated him as one who does not trust them with him, in that he was not permitting him to go out with them for pasturing and the like.

The placing of "lahu" in ﴿lahu lanasihun﴾ and ﴿lahu lahafizun﴾ may be for the sake of rhyme (fasila) and attention to Yusuf's (peace be upon him) matter on the surface, and it may be for pretended restriction (al-qasr al-idda'i): they made themselves, because of their excessive care for him, like one who guards no one else and advises no one else.

In this statement which they agreed upon before their father there is a lesson about the collusion of people with a single aim in devising schemes to achieve a base purpose. And how they began with the interrogation about his not trusting them with their brother, and displaying that they were advisors to him, and confirmed that with the nominal sentence and the emphatic particle; then they showed that they were only eager for their brother's benefit and that they were guarding him, and they also emphasized that.

**Page 230**

﴿He said, "Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that the wolf will devour him while you are heedless of him."﴾ ﴿They said, "If the wolf devours him while we are a group, then we would indeed be losers."﴾

The clause introduced by (قال) (qala, "he said") is a disjoined clause, following the manner of dialogue.

He showed them the reason for his refusal to let Yusuf (peace be upon him) go out with them to the pasture: that it would grieve him because of being parted from him for days, and that he feared wolves for him, since Yusuf (peace be upon him) was then a young boy who had been raised in comfort and was not accustomed to confronting wild beasts. Wolves are bold toward whoever they perceive to be weak in defending himself. Al-Rabi' ibn Dab' al-Fazari said, complaining of the weakness of old age:

*The wolf I fear if I pass by it alone,*
*and I fear the winds and the rain.*

Al-Farazdaq said, mentioning a wolf:

*I said to it when it bared its teeth laughing,*
*and my sword was not in my hand at that place:*

*Live, for if you pledge to me you will not betray me,*
*we will be like two companions, O wolf.*

The wolves of the Syrian desert (badiyat al-Sham) were more fierce in their wickedness than the rest of the wolves, and perhaps they were like the wolves of the land of the Russians. The Arabs say that when a wolf is attacked and defends itself until it bites a human and draws his blood, it becomes savage when it sees blood and turns fiercely upon the human. He said:

*You were like an evil wolf when it saw blood*
*in its companion one day, and turned toward the blood.*

A pack of wolves may gather, and then they are more dangerous to a single person, or to a child, than to a group of people.

**Page 231**

The definiteness in (الذئب) (al-dhi'b, "the wolf") is the definiteness of reality and nature, and it is called the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). Here it is intended to refer to an unspecified member of the wolf species, or to a group of them, and the judgment is not directed at the genus itself, as indicated by the fact that eating is one of the states of individuals, not of the genus. Rather, what is meant is any individual of this genus without specification. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿like the example of a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5], meaning an unspecified individual of donkeys. The indication that the individual rather than the genus is meant is the attribution of carrying books to it, since the genus does not carry. From this is the saying, "Enter the market (al-suq)" when you want an unspecified individual market. Your saying "enter" is an indicator of what has been mentioned. This definiteness resembles the indefinite in meaning, except that it is intended to refer to an individual of the genus. Close to this definiteness by the article (al-) is the definiteness by a genus-name (ʿalam al-jins), and the difference between this article and the indefinite is like the difference between a genus-name and the indefinite noun.

So the meaning is: "I fear that the wolf will devour him," that is, that it will kill him and eat of him, because you are far from him, due to what he knows of their excessive playing and their preoccupation with frivolity and racing, so the wolves will become bold toward Yusuf (peace be upon him).

The wolf (al-dhi'b) is an animal of the canine family; it is a wild, untamed dog. Among its traits are cunning and aversion (to humans). It preys upon sheep. When it fights a human, wounds him, and sees blood on him, it becomes savage with him, and perhaps tears him apart.

Ya'qub (peace be upon him) mentioned that their taking him away tomorrow would bring about a future grief for him, in order to turn them away from insisting on taking him out, because it is the way of a righteous son to avoid what grieves his father.

**Page 232**

The emphasis of the clause by a particle of emphasis (harf al-ta'kid) is to cut off their insistence, by affirming that his grief at separation is established, treating them as those who deny it, since he saw their insistence. The emphasis extends to the clause ﴿and I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾.

They refused except to respond, saying: ﴿If the wolf devours him while we are a group, then we would indeed be losers.﴾

The lam in (لئن أكله) (la-in akalahu) is a preparatory lam for an oath (muwatti'a li-l-qasam). They intended to emphasize the response by (la-), by (in), by the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), and by (idhan), the answering particle, to affirm the occurrence of their loss on the assumption that the condition occurs. The intended meaning is a metonymy (kinaya) for their not being negligent regarding him and for their guarding him, since a man does not accept being described as a loser.

By "loss" (al-khusran) is meant the failure of the hoped-for benefit from men. They borrowed for it the failure of a merchant's profit from his trade, which is a blameworthy failure. That is, "we would then indeed be deprived of the qualities of manliness: of strength, capacity, and alertness." Their being a group prevents them from colluding upon what would cause loss to all of them. The meaning of "group" (ʿusba) has been explained just above. In this there is a lesson about the extent of displaying righteousness together with concealing harm and destruction.

Al-Jumhur read the hamza of (الذئب) with full pronunciation (tahqiq), according to the original form. Warsh, from Nafi', al-Susi, from Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i read it with the hamza lightened into a ya' (تخفيف الهمزة ياءً). In some tafsir works, the lightening of the hamza is attributed to Khalaf and Abu Ja'far, but this is not known in the books of qira'at. In al-Baydawi it is stated that Abu 'Amr pronounced the hamza clearly when pausing, and that Hamza pronounced it clearly in continuous recitation.
