[p. 233]

The narration of their taking him away and their resolve to throw him into the well follows on from the account of the dialogue between Ya'qub (peace be upon him) and his sons, concerning their attempt to take Yusuf (peace be upon him) out to the open desert. This implies omitted sentences in which they pressed Ya'qub (peace be upon him) until they persuaded him, and so he permitted Yusuf (peace be upon him) to go out with them. This is an instance of brevity (ijaz).

The meaning is: when Ya'qub (peace be upon him) agreed to what they requested, they took him away and reached the place where the well was.

The verb "ajma'a" (to resolve) takes its object directly. Its meaning is: to determine upon an action. Thus his saying, "an yaj'aluhu" (that they should put him), is the object of "wa-ajma'u" (and they resolved).

The response (jawab) of "lamma" (when) is omitted, indicated by "an yaj'aluhu fi ghayabat al-jubb" (that they should put him in the depths of the well). The implied sense is: "they put him in the well." Similar instances are numerous in the Qur'an, and this belongs to the brevity peculiar to the Qur'an, being a reduction in wording because the meaning is clear.

The clause "wa-awhayna ilayhi" (and We revealed to him) is conjoined to the clause "wa-ajma'u an yaj'aluhu fi ghayabat al-jubb," because this revelation is one of the important lessons of the story.

It has also been said that the "wa" is superfluous and that the clause "awhayna" is the response of "lamma." A similar view has been stated regarding the line of Imru' al-Qays:

"When we passed the courtyard of the tribe and he turned aside..." ... the verse.

The same has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when they had both submitted, and he had put him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103] ﴿and We called to him, "O Ibrahim"﴾ [al-Saffat: 104], and so on. In all of this there is room for consideration.

[p. 234]

The pronoun in "ilayhi" (to him) refers, according to the view of most exegetes (mufassirun), who limit themselves to this, to Yusuf (peace be upon him). Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned that it has been said the pronoun refers to Ya'qub (peace be upon him).

The clause "la-tunabbi'annahum bi-amrihim hadha" (you will surely inform them of this affair of theirs) explains the clause "awhayna." It is emphasised with the lam and the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) to confirm its content, whether what is intended is information about the future or a command in the present. On the first view, this revelation may be an inspiration (ilham) that God cast into Yusuf's soul at the time of their plotting against him. It may also be a revelation through an angel, in which case it is an early sign (irhas) for Yusuf (peace be upon him) before prophethood, a mercy from God to relieve his distress. He was informed of what indicates that God would deliver him from this calamity, and that the final outcome would be his over those who plotted against him. It is also a notice that He would console him in the loneliness of the well with revelation and good tidings, and that in the future he would inform his brothers of what they had done to him, as the energetic nun indicates when it is attached to a declarative sentence. This entails his deliverance and his being empowered over his brothers, since such information could only be given while he had power over them and was safe from their evil.

The meaning of "bi-amrihim" (of their affair) is: of their great act of wrongdoing.

The clause "wa-hum la yash'urun" (while they do not perceive) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: you will inform them of what they did to you while they do not perceive that you are their brother, but rather they will be in a state in which they consider you one who knows the unseen and foretells it. This is information about what occurred years later, which is related in this surah in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?"﴾ [Yusuf: 89], and the verses that follow.

On the view that the pronoun "ilayhi" refers to Ya'qub (peace be upon him), the revelation is God's casting of that into him through an angel. The "wa" is then more evidently a conjunction. It is then conjoined to the clause "lamma dhahabu bihi" (when they took him away) through to its end, and "wa-awhayna ilayhi" (and We revealed to him) comes before it. "La-tunabbi'annahum" is then an imperative: "We revealed to him: inform them of this affair of theirs," meaning: make them aware of what they plotted against Yusuf (peace be upon him),

[p. 235]

as a hint by way of allusion. This is in His saying: ﴿I fear that the wolf may eat him while you are heedless of him﴾ [Yusuf: 13].

On this interpretation, the clause "wa-hum la yash'urun" is a circumstantial clause relating to the plural pronoun of the absent persons: "and they do not perceive that We revealed this to him."

The well into which Yusuf (peace be upon him) was thrown is stated in the Torah to be in the land of Dothan. Dothan was a fortified city which became ruins. What is meant is that there was desert around it, a pasture and grazing ground. The description of the well implies that it was on the caravan route. Those who described the well agree that it lay between Banyas and Tiberias, twelve miles from Tiberias on the side towards Damascus, near a village called Sanjal or Sanjil. Qudama said: it is the postal route between Ba'labakk and Tiberias.

Later scholars described it, by a precise determination drawn from ancient historical descriptions, as the great road between Syria and Egypt. It passed through Jordan beneath the Lake of Tiberias and went by Dothan, and caravans of the Arabs carrying perfumes to the East used it. On this road there are many wells at Dothan. The Well of Yusuf is known between Tiberias and Safad, and a dome was built over it in the era of the Ayyubid dynasty, according to conjecture, and it still stands today.

[Page 236]

Its connection: this is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿So when they took him away﴾ [Yusuf: 15], as a conjunction of a part of the story.

**Translation of the verses:** ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, we went off racing one another and left Yusuf by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful."﴾ ﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood.﴾ [Yusuf: 16–18]

**Al-ʿishāʾ** (the time of nightfall, when the remaining twilight from the rays of the sun after its setting has disappeared) is the time of the disappearance of the twilight that remains after sunset.

**Al-bukāʾ** (weeping) is the flowing of tears from the eyes out of sorrow, grief, and oppression. It was discussed earlier in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So let them laugh a little and weep much﴾ [al-Tawbah: 82]. Here it is applied to feigned weeping, which is pretending (al-tabākkī). They only feigned weeping to deceive their father, lest he suspect that they had killed Yusuf, peace be upon him. Perhaps they had the ability to weep without the cause for it being present. Among people there are marvels of deception and cunning. Among people are those whose nerves are affected by imagining something and imitating it, so that they experience what people experience in reality.

Some who make false claims of injustice do this, but the shrewdness of a judge is not deceived by such tricks, and he does not base a ruling on them. Rather, a ruling is based on clear evidence (al-bayyinah).

A woman came to Shurayh (the judge) disputing over something, and she was in the wrong. She began to weep, and Shurayh showed that he was not reassured by her claim. It was said to him: "Do you not see her weeping?" He said: "The brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, came to their father in the evening weeping, and they were wrongdoers and liars. It is not fitting for anyone to judge except by the truth."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: Our scholars have said: this indicates that a person's weeping does not prove the truth of his statement, since it may be feigned. Some creatures are unable to do this, and some are able to.

I say: among the proverbs is "the tears of the wicked are in his hands," and this is a lesson within this lesson.

**Al-istibāq** (racing) is an iftiʿāl form from al-sabq, and here it means mutual racing. In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) he said: the iftiʿāl and tafāʿul forms share meaning, like al-intiḍāl and al-tanāḍul (both meaning competing in archery), and al-irtimāʾ and al-tarāmī (both meaning shooting). That is, it has the meaning of the mufāʿalah form. For this reason, al-sibāq is also said, just as al-niḍāl and al-rimāʾ are said.

The intended meaning is racing on foot, and that is from the playfulness and games of youth.

**Al-matāʿ** (belongings) is that from which one benefits, that is, one enjoys it. It was discussed earlier in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿If you were heedless of your weapons and your belongings﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 102], in Surat al-Nisāʾ. What is meant here is their baggage: clothing, utensils, and provisions.

[Page 237]

The meaning of ﴿the wolf devoured him﴾ is that it killed him and ate from him. The verb "to eat" is connected to the name of the thing, and what is meant is part of it. It is said: "The lion ate him" if it ate from him. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and what the beast of prey has eaten﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 3], as a conjunction to the things forbidden from being eaten from, that is, by killing them.

From the words of ʿUmar, when Abu Lu'lu'ah stabbed him: "The dog has eaten me," that is, it bit me.

What is meant by "the wolf" is a group of wolves, as you have understood just now at His statement: ﴿and I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13]. In such a way that the wolves left nothing of him, and for this reason they did not say "and we buried him."

His statement: ﴿But you will not believe us﴾ is a predicate used in a secondary benefit, namely that the speaker knows the content of the predicate. It is an allusion that they are truthful in what they claimed, because they know that their father would not believe them about it, so they were not hoping for him to believe them.

The verb of belief (īmān) is transitive with the preposition lām to the one believed, with the dāl vowelled with a fatḥah, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So Lot believed him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 26]. Its explanation was given earlier at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿None believed in Musa except some of his people's offspring﴾ [Yunus: 83], in Surat Yunus.

The clause ﴿even though we are truthful﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), so the wāw is the wāw of circumstance. (Law) here is concessive (ittiṣāliyyah), and it indicates that what follows it is the state furthest from the realization of the content of what precedes it in that state. The estimate is: "And you will not believe us, even if we were truthful in reality," that is, we know that your belief in us is absent in both states, so we do not hope to deceive you.

It is not necessary to estimate a deleted condition that is the opposite of the stated condition, because that is an estimate merely to draw attention to making the wāw a circumstantial wāw with the concessive "law" and "in." That estimate does not hold in every place. Do you not see the saying of al-Maʿarri:

*"Though I am the last of the times,*
*I bring what the ancients were not able to bring."*

How can the estimate "Though I am, if I were, the first in time" not hold? Rather, even "though I am the last in time" holds. So the condition of concessive law and concessive in has no implication of contrast, because the condition with them is not for restriction.

[Page 238]

The concessive law was mentioned earlier at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything and were not guided?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170], in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then none of them will be accepted, even if he offers the earth full of gold﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 91], in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

The clause ﴿And they brought his shirt﴾ [Yusuf: 18] is in the position of a circumstantial clause. Since the blood was smeared on the shirt, and they had come accompanied by the shirt, they had brought the blood on the shirt.

Describing the blood as "false" (kadhib) is a description by a verbal noun, and the verbal noun here has the meaning of a passive participle, like "creation" meaning "what is created." That is, its being the blood of Yusuf, peace be upon him, is falsely claimed, since it is the blood of a kid goat. So it is blood in truth, but it is not the blood that was claimed. There is no doubt that they did not leave any aspect of simulating the blood and the state of the shirt like the shirt of someone eaten by a wolf, with marks of tearing and rending, which the state of a wolf's attack does not lack. And they were too clever to overlook this, being a band in which such a thing would not escape the notice of the group. So what some commentators have said, that Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, said to his sons: "I have never seen a wolf gentler than this one, which ate my son and did not tear his shirt," is one of the embellishments of stories.

His statement: ﴿on his shirt﴾ [Yusuf: 18] is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from "blood," and it was placed before the element it modifies.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 18:

﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter. So patience is most fitting. And Allah is the one whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾

The particle *bal* (rather) is a particle of retraction (*idrab*), meaning that it cancels their claim that the wolf ate him. Thus he has openly declared their lie to them.

*Taswil* means facilitating something and beautifying it to the self, so that it desires to attain it.

The vagueness in the word *amran* (a matter) allows for several possibilities of what they might have done to Yusuf, peace be upon him: killing, selling, or exiling him, since he did not know the specific thing they had done. The indefiniteness of *amran* serves to magnify the matter (*li-l-tahwil*).

From this follows the declaration of patience: ﴿So patience is most fitting﴾. It stands in place of "be patient with a beautiful patience." It was shifted from the accusative to the nominative to indicate steadfastness and permanence, as was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace"﴾ [Hud: 69] in Surat Hud. This may be an interjection in the midst of his address to his sons, or the implied sense may be: "Be patient with a beautiful patience," addressed to himself. It is also possible that *sabrun jamil* is the predicate of an omitted subject indicated by the context, meaning: "So my affair is patience," or it is a subject whose predicate is similarly omitted. The meaning as a declaration is more forceful. Patience was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The description *jamil* (beautiful) may be a descriptive qualifier that reveals (*kashif*), since all patience is good apart from impatient distress (*jaza'*), as Ibrahim ibn Kunayf al-Nabhani said:

*Be patient, for patience with the free is more beautiful, and one does not rely on the vicissitudes of time.*

That is: more beautiful than distress.

It is also possible that it is a restrictive descriptor (*mukhassis*). The beautiful patience has been explained as that which is not mixed with distress.

*Jamal* is the goodness of a thing in the qualities of the excellences of its kind. Thus the beauty of patience is its best state, which is that nothing accompanies it that diminishes the properties of its essence.

In the authentic hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a woman weeping at a grave. He said to her, 'Fear Allah and be patient.' She said, 'Leave me alone, for you have not been afflicted with my calamity,' and she did not recognize him. When he had departed, a man passed by her and said to her, 'That was the Prophet (ﷺ).' So she came to the door of the Prophet (ﷺ)
[Page 240]
and said, 'I did not recognize you, O Messenger of Allah.' He said, 'Patience is only at the first shock,'" meaning, patience is complete only at the first shock.

His saying, ﴿And Allah is the one whose help is sought against what you describe﴾, is conjoined to the clause ﴿So patience is most fitting﴾. It may therefore carry the two meanings mentioned: either the declaration of seeking help, or the report that he is seeking help from Allah to bear patience in this matter. Or he intended seeking help from Allah on behalf of Yusuf, peace be upon him, for deliverance from what has befallen him.

The expression of what befell Yusuf, peace be upon him, as ﴿what you describe﴾ is supremely eloquent, because he was certain that they were lying in their description, and certain that they had inflicted harm upon Yusuf, peace be upon him. Since the specific calamity was not determined for him, he expressed it in a general and directed manner, because they believed that what they described was his death by the wolf's eating him, whereas Ya'qub, peace be upon him, meant that what they described was the actual calamity, which they had described with a false description. This is close to His saying, ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat: 180].

Ya'qub, peace be upon him, committed the matter to Allah and did not strive to uncover the fate of Yusuf, peace be upon him, because he knew that this was beyond his reach due to his old age, and because he had no supporter to rely on against those sons. They had become the ones working to keep him apart from Yusuf, peace be upon him, so he despaired of being able to uncover the truth about Yusuf, peace be upon him, without them. Do you not see that when he found an opening from them, he said to them, ﴿Go and search for Yusuf and his brother﴾ [Yusuf: 87].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 19:

[Page 241]
﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, "O joy! This is a boy!" And they concealed him as merchandise, but Allah was Knowing of what they did.﴾

This is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping﴾ [Yusuf: 16], the conjunction of one narrative upon another narrative. This is a return to what occurred concerning Yusuf, peace be upon him. The meaning is: and the caravan came to the well.

The "caravan" (al-sayyara) [Yusuf: 10] has been mentioned just above.

The wārid (water-drawer) is the one who comes to the water to draw it for the people.

The idlāʾ (letting down) is the sending of the bucket into the well to draw up water.

The dalw (bucket) is a large container made of stitched leather, having a spout at its bottom, which is folded over the outside of the container by being tied with a rope that accompanies the rope from which the bucket is suspended. The dalw is feminine.

The sentence "He said, 'O joy!'" is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf bayānī), because the mention of the letting down of the bucket prepares the hearer to ask what happened at that moment, so its answer is "He said, 'O joy!'"

Al-bushrā (good news): it was mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus: 64] in Surat Yunus.

The address to good news is a metaphor, because good news is not addressed; rather, it is likened to an absent rational being who is needed, so it is called, as if it were said to it: "This is the time of your presence." From this come "O my regret!" and "O wonder!" So it is a metaphorical personification (makniyya), and the particle of address is an imaginative depiction (takhyīl) or a subordinate metaphor (tabaʿiyya).

The meaning: he rejoiced and was delighted at finding a boy.

The majority read "yā bushrāya" with the bushrā attached to the first-person pronoun. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read it without the attachment.

[Page 242]
The demonstrative (ism al-ishāra) refers to the very person of Yusuf, peace be upon him. The water-drawer addressed the rest of the caravan, and they had not seen the person of Yusuf, peace be upon him, when the water-drawer brought him up from the well; for if they had seen him, there would have been no benefit in informing them that he was a boy, since seeing suffices instead of informing. Thus it is also established that they had not seen the figure of Yusuf, peace be upon him, when he emerged from the well. Therefore, it is apparent that the demonstrative in such a context is not intended to indicate a specific visible entity, but is intended to alert the hearer that something has occurred over which one rejoices, unexpectedly, just as the hunter says to his companions, "This is a gazelle!" and as the diver says, "This is a shell!" or "A pearl!" and as the well-digger says, "This is water!" Al-Nābigha said, describing a hunter, his dogs and his horse:

"His rider, the jinn-like one, reclining, says: 'This! But the flesh of the sheep is forbidden.'"

The divers, when they found a pearl, would shout. Al-Nābigha said:

"Or a pearl from its oyster, whose diver... rejoices; when he sees it, he cries out and prostrates."

The meaning: I found a boy in the well, so he is a foundling (luqata), and he will be a slave to whoever picked him up. This is the cause of his delight in saying: "O joy! This is a boy!"

The ghulām (boy) is one between ten and twenty years old. Yusuf's age at that time was seventeen years.

These caravanners were, as in the Torah, from the Ishmaelites, that is, the sons of Ishmael son of Abraham. It was said that they were from the people of Madyan, and their coming to the well was to draw water from it; the brothers of Yusuf did not notice them, since they had moved away from the well.

The meaning of "asarrūhu" is "they concealed him." The pronoun refers unquestionably to the caravan, i.e., they concealed Yusuf, peace be upon him, meaning the news of his finding was kept hidden, fearing that he might be a child of some of the nearby tribes who had fallen into the well; if his people learned of his news, they would seek him and take him back from them, since they had discerned from him the marks of children of households. It was customary that they would make known who had been near that well and announce it, as is the custom in making known a foundling. Therefore his saying "and they concealed him" [means] that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had informed them of his story, yet they disregarded that out of greed in hope of selling him. This is due to the lack of religion among them, or to their not acting upon religion.

"Bidā'atan" is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl muqaddara) from the pronoun in "asarrūhu," i.e., they made him merchandise. Bidāʿa: trade goods and commodities, i.e., they resolved to sell him.

The sentence "But Allah was Knowing of what they did" is parenthetical (muʿtaridha), i.e., Allah knows what they do of enslaving one who has no right to be enslaved, and one whose right it was that they should ask about his people and convey him to them, since they knew his news, or it was their right to ask him, since he was able to inform them of his news.

In the caravan's finding of the well in which Yusuf, peace be upon him, was, there is a sign of Allah's gentleness toward him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 20:

﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams (silver coins), and they were among those who had no desire for him.﴾

The meaning of "shaaruhu" is "they sold him." It is said "shara" just as it is said "baa'a" (to sell), and it is said "ishtara" just as it is said "ibtaa'a" (to buy). Similar to these pairs are "rahana" and "irtahana" (to pledge, to take as a pledge), "'awada" and "i'tada" (to exchange), and "kara" and "iktara" (to rent).

The principle in this and similar forms is that the basic verb (fa'ala) denotes the action itself, while the form with the infix (iftaala) denotes the undergoing or acceptance of the action.

Whoever explained "shaaruhu" as "ishtaraw-hu" (they bought him) erred, an error caused by a poor understanding of His saying: ﴿and they were among those who had no desire for him﴾. As for what some lexicographers claimed, that "shara" and "ishtara" are synonyms in both their meanings, it is my strong opinion that this was a mistake, since there is no evidence indicating it.

Page 244
The word "bakhs" originally is the verbal noun of "bakhasahu," meaning when one diminishes something from its true value. Here it has the sense of the object diminished, as "khalq" has the sense of "makhluq" (the created). The verb "bakhs" has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not diminish anything from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282] in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿Dara'ima⁠﴾ (dirhams) is a substitute (badal) for "thaman" (price), and it is the plural of "dirham," which is the minted coin. It is an arabicised word from Persian, as stated in al-Jawhari's Sihah.

Those who compiled what is arabicised in the Qur'an, such as al-Suyuti in al-Itqan, overlooked it.

﴿Ma'dudatin⁠﴾ (counted) is a metaphor (kinaya) for its being few, because a small amount is easy to count; when it becomes large, its quantity is estimated by weight or measure. In the metaphorical sense of abundance, it is said: "it is not counted."

All the plural pronouns refer to the caravan (al-sayyara), according to the most correct interpretations.

Zuhd (abstention, indifference) is little desire for obtaining a thing that one would normally desire, or little desire for its compensation, as here; that is, the caravan people were not keen to raise the price of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Perhaps the reason for this was their little knowledge of prices.

The expression of their indifference to him with the form ﴿among those who had no desire⁠﴾ is more emphatic than if it had said "and they were indifferent to him," because placing them among a group of indifferent people indicates that they went in their indifference to such things according to the ways of their simple peers, who do not appreciate the value of precious things.

"Fihi" is related to "al-zahidin," and "al" is a particle for defining the genus, not a relative pronoun, contrary to most grammarians who make "al" attached to derived nouns a relative pronoun when no specific reference is established; they relied on weak reasons, and al-Akhfash and al-Mazini disagreed with them.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing word serves to highlight the importance of the thing being disdained, and to draw attention to the weakness of their discernment and insight, while also observing the rhyme (fasila).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 21:

[Page 245]
﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his residence honorable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son."﴾

﴿The one who bought him﴾ means the one who paid the price and thus owned him, even if he did not personally conduct the purchase. The verb "bought" (ishtara) indicates only the payment of an exchange, such that attributing the purchase to one who gives the price and receives the goods, when he is not himself the owner of the price and the goods, is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi). For this reason, notaries write in such cases that his purchase was on behalf of so-and-so.

The one who bought Yusuf (peace be upon him) was a man named (Futifar), the chief of the police (shurta) of the king of Egypt, and he was the governor of the city of Egypt. He is given the title al-'Aziz in this surah, as will come.

The city of Egypt is (Memphis), also said to be (Manf), and it was the capital of Lower Egypt, which was ruled by tribes of the Canaanites known among the Copts as the (Hyksos), meaning the shepherds. Upper Egypt, known today as al-Sa'id, was under the rule of the Coptic pharaohs. Its city was (Thebes) or (Thiba), which is today in ruins, and its site is called al-Uqsur, plural of qasr (palace), because there are remnants of ancient palaces there, i.e., the temples. The government of Upper Egypt at that time was weak due to the domination of the Canaanites over most of the country and its best lands.

His wife is called in the books of the Arabs (Zulaykha), with a fatha on the zay, a kasra on the lam, and the final letter shortened; the Jews named her Ra'il. And "﴿from Egypt﴾" is an adjective of "﴿the one who bought him﴾".

"﴿To his wife﴾" is connected to "said", or to "bought", or both verbs govern it, so that he bought him in order to give him to her, to adopt him as a son. This implies that they had no child.

"His wife" means his spouse, for the wife may be called "woman" (imra'a) and the meaning of wife is intended. This was mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And his wife was standing, and she laughed﴾ [Hud: 71].

[Page 246]
Al-mathwa: its literal meaning is the place where a person dwells, i.e., returns to. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Fire is your abode﴾ [al-An'am: 128], in Surat al-An'am. Here it is a metonymy for the state of residence with them, because a person returns to the dwelling of his residence.

So the meaning is: make his stay with you honorable, i.e., complete in its kind. He intended that kindness to him be a cause for bringing about their love for him and his counsel to them, so that he benefits them, or that they adopt him as a son, so that he is dutiful to them, and that is closer in nearness. Perhaps he had despaired of his wife bearing children. He said this because of his good insight into the features of Yusuf (peace be upon him), which indicated perfection. And how could he not be a man of discernment, when the king made him chief of his police? Kings were cautious and did not entrust their affairs to other than the competent.

* * *

﴿And thus We established Yusuf in the land, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant in His affair, but most of the people do not know.﴾

If we take the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) according to the analogy of many of its like in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And thus We made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], in Surat al-Baqarah, then the reference is to the establishment derived from ﴿We established Yusuf﴾, as an indication that this establishment reached the utmost of what is sought of its kind, such that if one wished to liken it to a more complete establishment, it could only be likened to itself, in the manner of the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And foolishness is like its name" (as-safahatu ka-ismiha)

So the kaf is in the position of an accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). The estimate is: We established Yusuf with an establishment like that establishment.

If we take it according to what the wording may bear, then it refers to the aforementioned result, which is what the finding of him by the caravan indicates, namely that it was a deliverance for him of wondrous occurrence, by the concurrence of the absence of haste in pulling him out of the well, meaning: We established Yusuf (peace be upon him) with an establishment of Our making like that deliverance by which We saved him. Then the kaf is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) from a verbal noun derived from "We established". Its parallel is ﴿Thus We made the deeds of every nation fair-seeming to them﴾ [al-An'am: 108], in Surat al-An'am.

The establishment in the land here is intended to mean its beginning and the estimate of the first part of it. So Yusuf (peace be upon him), by his coming into the place of care from the Aziz of Egypt, had already laid out for him the future of his establishment in the land in the fullest manner, which was indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, later: ﴿Thus We established Yusuf in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed﴾ [Yusuf: 56]. What is mentioned there is like the return of the last part to the first, of what is here, and it is its completion.

He connected "And thus" with a cause for a meaning derived from the speech, which is the giving; that cause is ﴿and that We might teach him the interpretation of events﴾, because Allah, when He had decreed in His prior knowledge that He would make Yusuf (peace be upon him) knowledgeable of the interpretation of dreams and would make him a prophet, delivered him from destruction and established him in the land, as a preparation of the means for the purpose of Allah.

The meaning of "the interpretation of events" was mentioned just above, at the mention of his father's saying to him: ﴿and He will teach you the interpretation of events﴾ [Yusuf: 6], i.e., the interpretation of dreams.

The clause ﴿And Allah is predominant in His affair﴾ is a parenthetical insertion at the end of the speech, and a concluding remark (tadhyil), because its meaning is general and includes Allah's overcoming of the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) by nullifying their scheme. The pronoun in "His affair" refers to the name of Majesty (Allah).

The particle "ala" after the root of overcoming and the like enters upon the thing in which dispute is expected, as in their saying: "We overcame them over the water."

"The affair of Allah" is what He has decreed and willed. Whoever strives toward an action that opposes what Allah has willed, his condition is like that of one who disputes in order to bring about the matter he wants and to prevent the occurrence of Allah's purpose, Exalted is He, and nothing occurs except what Allah, Exalted is He, has willed. So the state of Allah, Exalted is He, is like that of the victor over his opponent. The meaning: Allah is the completer of what He has decreed. Therefore,

[Page 248]
He followed it with the transition (istidrak) in His saying: ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾, as a qualification of what this ruling requires, that it is a fact established whose nature is that it should not be unknown, because there are evidences of it in the events of occurrences; but most people do not know that, despite its being manifest.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 22:

﴿When he reached his full strength, We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

This is an account of the choosing of Yusuf (peace be upon him) for prophethood. It is mentioned here, in the context of the beginning of his settling in Egypt, because of its connection to the mention of God's favour upon him in granting him authority in the land and teaching him the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith).

Al-Ashudd (full strength) means power. It has been explained as his reaching the age between thirty-five and forty years.

Al-hukm (judgment) and al-hikmah (wisdom) are synonymous, and it means: knowledge of the realities of things and acting upon what is good and avoiding its opposite. Here it is intended to mean prophethood, as in His saying, exalted is He, in mention of Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them both): ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya': 79]. By knowledge ('ilm) is meant a knowledge additional to prophethood.

The indefinite form of 'ilman (knowledge) is either for specifying a kind or for magnifying it. What is meant is the knowledge of interpreting dreams, as will come in His saying, exalted is He, quoting him: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾ [Yusuf: 37].

Fakhr al-Din said: judgment (hukm) is practical wisdom, because it is a judging over the guidance of the soul. And knowledge ('ilm) is theoretical wisdom.

What is said regarding ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ is like what is said regarding its counterpart, and it was previously discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

In the mention of the good-doers (al-muhsinin) there is an indication that his good-doing was the cause of his being rewarded with that blessing.

Page 249

In what God, exalted is He, arranged there is a clear statement of one of the signs that were in Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brothers.

**[Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr, *al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr*, on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29, part 1]**

﴿The woman in whose house he was sought him to yield himself to her, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "God forbid! He is my Lord; he has given me the best residence. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper."﴾ ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ ﴿And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her master at the door. She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿He said, "It was she who sought me to yield myself to her." And a witness from her own family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars.﴾ ﴿But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said, "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ ﴿"Yūsuf, turn away from this, and [you, woman], ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners."﴾

This is the attaching of one narrative to another (ʿaṭf qiṣṣah ʿalā qiṣṣah), so it does not necessarily follow that this narrative occurred in time after the one preceding it. This incident occurred before Yūsuf was given prophethood, since the bestowal of prophethood generally occurs at the age of forty. The more evident view is that he was granted prophethood and messengerhood after his family entered Egypt and after the death of his father. The verses have addressed the establishment of Yūsuf's steadfastness (peace be upon him) in chastity, fidelity, and nobility of character.

[Page 250]

Thus *murāwadah* (seeking to persuade or seduce), which requires repeated attempts, is expressed in the form of *mufāʿalah* (the verbal form implying reciprocity), and *mufāʿalah* is used to indicate repetition. It has been said that the *mufāʿalah* here is notional (*taqdīriyyah*), in that the action from one side and the resistance from the other side are considered as an action countered by a similar action. The word *murāwadah* derives from *rāda yarūdu*, meaning to come and go. The state of one who repeatedly tries to get someone to do something is compared to the state of one who goes back and forth in returning to the thing one has turned away from; thus *rāwada* is used in the sense of *ḥāwala* (to attempt).

*ʿAn* here indicates separation (*mujāwazah*), meaning that she sought him, distancing him from himself, that is, that he should make himself hers. Apparently this construction is one of the Qur'an's original expressions. The word "self" (*nafs*) here is a metonymy for the purpose of intercourse, as Ibn ʿAṭiyyah stated: thus "self" refers to his chastity and her enabling herself to have what she wanted from him, as though she were seeking to have him surrender his will and his judgment over himself.

As for its construction with *ʿalā* ("upon"), that indicates the thing whose attainment is sought. In the saying of Abū Hurayrah, it occurred that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was urging his uncle Abū Ṭālib toward Islam." And in the hadith of the Night Journey, Mūsā said to him: "I had tried (*rāwadtu*) the Children of Israel for less than that, and they abandoned it."

The expression referring to the wife of the ʿAzīz by way of the relative clause, in His saying ﴿the one in whose house he was﴾, is intended for what the relative clause implies of affirming Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) infallibility, because his being in her house is of a nature that would make him submit to her desire.

*Baytihā* ("her house") is the house of her residence in which she spends the night. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ is that at that time he was in the house where she was. It is also possible that the intended "house" is the whole dwelling, which is the palace of the ʿAzīz. From this comes the saying "*rabbat al-bayt*" (the mistress of the house), meaning the wife of the head of the household. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ would then be that he was among the dependents of that dwelling.

Closing the doors (*ghalq al-abwāb*) means placing each door so as to block the opening through which one enters.

The doubling in *ghallaqat* serves to express the intensity and strength of the action, meaning that they were closed firmly and securely.

[Page 251]

*Al-abwāb* is the plural of *bāb* (door), and it was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Enter upon them through the door﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 23].

*Hayta* is a verb-form noun (*ism fiʿl*) meaning "hurry" or "make haste." It is said that its origin is from the Hauranian language, which is Nabataean. It is also said that it is from the Hebrew language.

The *lām* in *laka* serves to clarify the intended addressee of the address, as in their saying "*suqyan laka*" (watering to you) and "*shukran laka*" (thanks to you). Its original form is *hayta-ka*. It appears that she asked of him something that was not unusual in their palaces, namely that a woman enjoy her servant as a man enjoys his female slave. For this reason she did not first approach him with an enticement, but began by offering herself to him. The matter will be further clarified when we reach His saying: ﴿She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife…"﴾.

There are several readings of *Hayta*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Dhakwān (on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir), and Abū Jaʿfar read it with a *kasrah* on the *hāʾ* and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hīta*). Ibn Kathīr read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ* (*Haytu*). The rest read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hayta*). The *fatḥah* and *ḍammah* are indeclinable vowels (*ḥarakatā bināʾ*).

*Maʿādh* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that is annexed to the Name of Majesty (Allāh) in the manner in which a verbal noun is annexed to its object. Its original form is "*aʿūdhu ʿawdhan billāh*," meaning "I seek refuge in God," that is, I take refuge in Him from what you are attempting. Its explanation will come when we reach His saying: ﴿He said, "God forbid that we take…"﴾ [Yūsuf: 79] in this sūrah.

*Inna* here conveys the reason for what ﴿God forbid!﴾ conveys of refusal and seeking refuge in God from it, which implies that God commanded that seeking of refuge.

The pronoun in *innahu* ("indeed he") may refer to the Name of Majesty, in which case *rabbī* means "my Creator." It may also refer to something known from the context, namely her husband, who would not be content for anyone else to touch her; he is known from customary understanding, and in that case *rabbī* means "my master" and "my owner."

This is speech that has been eloquently directed in a manner by which the words of Yūsuf (peace be upon him) are reported; either because Yūsuf (peace be upon him) used such a construction in the language of the Copts, or because he gave two excuses for his refusal, and the Qur'an reports them with brevity and allusion.

[Page 252]

Whichever is the case, the statement is an explanation of his refusal and an allusion to her for betraying her pledge.

In this statement there is a great lesson in chastity and piety, and the infallibility of the prophets before prophethood from the major sins.

The mention of the description of the Lord under both possibilities indicates the obligation of obeying Him and being thankful for the blessing of creation with respect to God, and for the blessing of upbringing with respect to his noble master.

He confirmed this by describing it with the clause ﴿He has given me the best residence﴾, meaning: He made my final state good, since He rescued me from destruction, or He honored my care. The explanation of *al-mathwā* (residence) has been given just above.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾ is a second reason for the refusal. The pronoun that is made the subject of *inna* is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), which conveys the importance of the clause made its predicate, because it is a comprehensive admonition. It also indicates that answering her solicitation is wrongdoing, because in it there is the wronging of both of them: himself, by committing a sin of a kind on which the religions agree that it is a major sin; and his master, who trusted him with his household and trusted her with herself, since he took her as a wife and kept her chaste.

*Al-hamm* is resolve to act. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿and they plotted what they could not attain﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74] in Sūrat Barāʾah. The resolve of hers is emphasized with *qad* and the oath-*lām* to convey that she resolved firmly and in earnest.

The clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ begins a fresh, independent statement. The intended meaning is that she was serious in what she sought from him, not testing him. The purpose of mentioning her desire for him is to prepare for the mention of the absence of his desire for her, in order to explain the difference between their two states in religion, since he was protected from sin.

The clause ﴿and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ is coordinated with the whole clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾. It is not coordinated with the clause *hammat* ("she desired"), which is the answer to the oath implied by the *lām*.

[Page 253]

Because the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ is followed by the clause introduced by *lawlā* ("had it not been"), which is exclusively about Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) own state and not about the state of the ʿAzīz's wife, it is evident that there is no connection between the two clauses. Hence the second clause is independent, since the condition of *lawlā* pertains to the state of the subject in it. The sense is: "And had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her." The answer was placed before its condition for emphasis. He did not attach the answer to the *lām* that frequently accompanies the answer to *lawlā*, because it is not obligatory, and because, since it was placed before *lawlā*, it was disliked to attach it to the *lām* before the mention of the conditional particle. Therefore it is good to pause at His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ so that the meaning of a new beginning with the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ appears clearly. By this it becomes evident that no desire for the ʿAzīz's wife ever touched Yūsuf (peace be upon him), because God protected him from desiring sin by what He showed him of the proof.

Abū Ḥātim said: "I used to read the strange words of the Qur'an to Abū ʿUbaydah, and when I came to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾ and so on, Abū ʿUbaydah said: 'This is in the order of anteriority and posteriority (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*), that is, the placing of the answer before the condition and the postponing of the condition; as if he said: "And she certainly desired him, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her."'"

al-Ṭabarī criticized this interpretation, on the grounds that the answer of *lawlā* does not precede it. What repels this criticism is that when Abū ʿUbaydah said that, we know that he did not see a prohibition on placing the answer of *lawlā* first. Moreover, he may make what is mentioned before *lawlā* an indication of the answer, with the answer being omitted due to what precedes *lawlā* indicating it. There is no escape from this under any reading, since *lawlā* and its condition restrict his saying "and he would have desired her" under all interpretations, so whatever answer is supposed is supposed under all interpretations.

A group said: Yūsuf desired to yield to her in what she invited him to, then he drew back and refrained from it when he saw the proof of his Lord. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Ibn Abī Mulaykah, and Tha'lab. The explanation of this is that he turned away from what he desired by God's protection or His infallibility; and desiring an evil deed while refraining from carrying it out is not a major sin, so it does not contradict the infallibility of the prophets from major sins before prophethood, according to those who hold that they were infallible from them before prophethood, which is the view of the majority.

[Page 254]

There is a difference of opinion on this, and for this reason Ibn ʿAbbās permitted this concerning Yūsuf. A group said: Yūsuf desired and began to prepare for it, then he saw a proof that turned him away from it, so he desisted. This is the view of al-Suddī, and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās. It returns to what we have explained in the previous view.

The author of *al-Kashshāf* erred in attaching these reports to those he calls *al-Ḥashwiyyah* and *al-Mujabbirah*, by which he means the Ashʿarites. He averted his gaze from the names of those to whom these interpretations are attributed, "He threw his own disease at me and slipped away." He also did not marvel at the consensus of all on the attempt of Yūsuf's brothers (peace be upon him) to kill him, and killing is more grave.

The seeing (*al-ruʾyah*) here is cognitive (*ʿilmiyyah*), because the proof (*burhān*) is among the meanings that are not seen by the eye.

*Al-burhān* is the argument. This proof is included in it: its turning him away from desire for her. Had it not been for that, the state of human nature would not have been free from desiring to comply with her in that situation, because of the abundance of motives for desire arising from her beauty, her eagerness for him, the delight of such men in obeying her, nearness to her, and the impulses of youth that make it appealing. Thus God's proof was the barrier between him and desire for her, and nothing else.

The commentators differed about what this proof is. Some of them indicate that it is a theoretical argument that made this act abhorrent to him. It was said: it is divine revelation. It was said: divine protection. It was said: visions that appeared to him.

The indication in His saying ﴿Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾ refers to something understood from what precedes it, which is implied by His saying ﴿he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, namely the seeing of the proof. That is: We showed him that seeing in this manner so that We might turn away from him evil.

*Al-ṣarf* is the transfer of a thing from one place to another. Here it is used metaphorically for protection from a thing's arriving at the place where it would normally arrive. The turning away is used to express infallibility from something that is about to befall him.

[Page 255]

The expression of infallibility by "turning away" indicates that the causes of the occurrence of evil and immorality were present, but God turned them away from him.

*Al-sūʾ* is the ugly thing, and it is the betrayal of one who entrusted him. *Al-faḥshāʾ* is the disobedience, and it is adultery. *Al-sūʾ* and *al-faḥshāʾ* were mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] in Sūrat al-Baqarah. The meaning of "He turned both away from him" is that He turned away his involvement with them.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿Indeed he is among Our sincere servants﴾ gives the reason for the wisdom of diverting him from evil and indecency, a diversion that went beyond the normal course of things, so that God's choosing of him would not be diminished in this severe test to the self.

Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar and Khalaf read *al-mukhlaṣīn* with a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, meaning those whom God has made sincere and chosen. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read it with a *kasrah* on the *lām*, meaning those who make their religion sincerely for God. The sense of the causal clause is one under both readings.

*Al-istibāq* (racing one another) is a *iftiʿāl* form from *al-sabq* (precedence). It was mentioned just before, and here it indicates that each of them was forcing himself to race, that is, each was trying to be the first to the door.

*Al-bāb* (the door) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. Its original form was *wa-istabaqā ilā al-bāb* ("and they raced to the door"), like ﴿Mūsā chose from his people seventy men﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 155], meaning "from his people." Or the verb *istabaqā* is taken to include the meaning of *ibtadarā* (hastened).

The definite article in *al-bāb* is the definite article of the category, since there were several closed doors. Yūsuf, peace be upon him, fled from her solicitation toward the door, wishing to open it and go out, while she wished to get ahead of him to the door to prevent him from opening it.

The clause ﴿and she tore his shirt﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Qadda* means *qaṭaʿa* (cut), that is, she cut from it a rent. This happened before the racing, without doubt, because if the tearing of the shirt had occurred during the racing, there would have been no evidence in it for the truthfulness of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, that she had solicited him. The tearing during the racing indicates no more than that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, had raced ahead of her, hastening to the door. This shows that she had seized him by his shirt when he turned away from her, wishing [p. 256] to force him into what she had solicited. He pulled himself free, and the shirt was torn by the force of the pull. The cutting of the shirt was from behind, because he was turning away from her, fleeing and averting himself, so she seized him by it to turn him back from his aversion.

The concision of the verse has excellently gathered all these meanings under the phrase ﴿they raced to the door and she tore his shirt﴾.

It happened that they found her master, that is, her husband, al-ʿAzīz, at the outer door, wishing to enter the house through the outer door. The use of "master" (*sayyid*) for the husband: it has been said that the Qurʾān related the custom of the Copts at that time, that they called the husband "sayyid." The apparent meaning is that this was not in use in the custom of the Arabs, so the expression here is one of the fine historical details, like His saying later ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ [Yūsuf: 76]. Perhaps marriage in Egypt in that era was mostly by way of ownership.

It is known from the discourse that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, opened the doors that Zulaykhā had locked, one door after another, until he reached the outer one. All of that happened during their racing, and this is concision.

*Al-ilfāʾ* (finding) is the obtaining of a thing in a particular state without seeking to obtain it. Most often it is sudden, or it occurs through ignorance of its first occurrence, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Rather we will follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170].

The clause ﴿She said: "What is the recompense..."﴾ and so on is a resumptive clause of explanation (*mustaʾnafah bayānīyah*), because the listener asks: what happened at the moment of her master's surprise while they were in that state?

She rushed to speak to him, persisting in slander, in such a way that she did not stammer. She made him imagine that she was in the right, and she poured the speech into a universal mould so that it would take the form of a law, and it would be a principle whose intended object is not known, so the addressee has no choice but to acknowledge it for her. Perhaps she feared that al-ʿAzīz's love for Yūsuf, peace be upon him, would prevent him from punishing him, so she poured her speech into a universal mould. She wanted by this that her husband should not perceive that she was in love with someone other than her master, and that she should frighten Yūsuf, peace be upon him, with her scheming, so that he would not refuse her again.

She set Yūsuf, peace be upon him, between two kinds of punishment, which are: prison, that is, confinement. Confinement was an ancient punishment in that era, and it continued until the time of Mūsā, peace be upon him, for Pharaoh said to Mūsā, peace be upon him, ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 29].

As for punishment (*ʿadhāb*), it is of various kinds, and it is an older punishment in the terminology of mankind. Among it are beating and inflicting pain by fire and by cutting off limbs. The mention of prison will come in this sūrah repeatedly.

The clause ﴿He said: "It was she who solicited me against myself"﴾ is part of the speech of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, and it is separated (*faṣl*) because it comes in the manner of a reply to her speech. The variation of the expression between ﴿that he be imprisoned, or a painful punishment﴾, without saying "except prison or a punishment," is because the word *al-sijn* is applied to the place in which the prisoner is put, and it is applied to the verbal noun of *sajana*. So His saying ﴿that he be imprisoned﴾ is clearer in showing the governing of the meaning of the verb over him.

Placing the subject before its predicate, which is a verb, gives restriction (*qaṣr*), and this is a restriction by reversal (*qaṣr qalb*), as a rebuttal to her.

With al-ʿAzīz was a man from among his wife's people, and he is the one who gave testimony, and he was perceptive, knowing the aspects of evidence.

His saying was called testimony (*shahādah*) because it tends toward the manifestation of the truth in establishing the transgression of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, against his mistress, or refuting it. This is judgment by clear circumstantial evidence (*al-qarīnah al-bayyinah*), because if she had held his garment in order to seize him and punish him, that would have occurred when he was facing her and approaching her. Then if he wished to slip away from her, his shirt would have been torn at the front, and conversely if his being held was while he was fleeing and turning away. There is no doubt that the reasoning by the manner of tearing the shirt arose from the mention of the wife of al-ʿAzīz of the occurrence of the tearing of the shirt, as she was trying to make it a proof that she had seized him in order to punish him. Had it not been for that, it would not have occurred to the witness that a tearing had happened, for otherwise from where would the witness have known the tearing of the shirt? The apparent meaning is that the witness was thinking of her truthfulness, so he wished to set up a proof of her truthfulness, but the opposite of that happened, as an honour for Yūsuf, peace be upon him.

[p. 258] The clause ﴿If his shirt has been torn from the front﴾ explains the verb *shahida* (testified).

The addition of ﴿and he is of the liars﴾ after ﴿she is truthful﴾, and the addition of ﴿and he is of the truthful﴾ after ﴿she is lying﴾, is an emphasis for increasing the establishment of the truth, as is the case with rulings.

The particles of condition indicate no more than the linking and causal relation between the content of their protasis and the content of their apodosis, without restriction to the future or to the past. So the meaning of ﴿If his shirt was torn from the front, she has spoken truly﴾ and what follows it is: if that happened in the past, then her truthfulness happened in the past.

The one who saw his shirt torn from behind and said, "Indeed it is of your scheming," is without doubt al-ʿAzīz. It had become clear to him that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, was innocent of assaulting the woman, so he was content with blaming his wife, saying that her accusation against him was of the scheming of women. So the plural feminine pronoun is an address to her, and it included those of her class by treating them as the townswomen (*ḥawāḍir*).

*Al-kayd* (scheming) is doing a thing in a form other than what is intended, in order to reach an intended end. It has been discussed before at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed My scheme is firm﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 183], in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

Then he commanded Yūsuf, peace be upon him, to turn away from what she had charged him with, that is, not to hold her to account for it, and to refrain from returning to discuss it. And he commanded his wife to seek forgiveness for her sin, that is, for her accusation of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, of boldness and assault against her.

The exegetes said: al-ʿAzīz was little given to jealousy. It was said: he was forbearing and wise. Perhaps he was infatuated with her, or the semblance of ownership lessened the blame on a woman for soliciting her slave. This is what is indicated by the state of her solicitation of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, when she rushed him with her words "Come, you," as has been discussed just before.

[p. 259] *Al-khāṭiʾ* is the doer of a sin (*khaṭīʾah*), which is a crime. He placed her among the group of those who erred, lightening the blame on her. The form of the masculine plural is by predominance (*taghlīb*).

The clause ﴿Yūsuf, turn away from this﴾ is part of the speech of al-ʿAzīz, since he is the possessor of the judgment.

The clause ﴿and seek forgiveness for your sin﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Yūsuf, turn away﴾ in the speech of al-ʿAzīz, as a conjunction of command upon command where the one commanded differs. The feminine second-person *kāf* is definitely an address to the wife of al-ʿAzīz. So al-ʿAzīz, after addressing her that what she had devised was of the scheming of women, directed the address to Yūsuf, peace be upon him, by calling him, then returned the address to the woman.

This manner of address is called *al-iqbāl* (turning toward), and it may be called *al-iltifāt* (turning) in the linguistic sense when it is the rhetorical *iltifāt*, and it is rare in eloquent speech. From it is the saying of al-Jarmī, of the Ṭayy, one of the poets of the *Ḥamāsah*:

I suppose you are my appointee at Bunniyy Jufayf and Hālah; indeed I forbid you, O Hālah.

Al-Marzūqī said in his commentary on the *Ḥamāsah*: The Arabs gather several people in address and report, then turn or direct their attention from among them to one, because he is the greatest of them, or the best of them in hearing, and the most particular of them in the matter.

**[Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr, *al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr*, on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29, part 1]**

﴿The woman in whose house he was sought him to yield himself to her, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "God forbid! He is my Lord; he has given me the best residence. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper."﴾ ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ ﴿And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her master at the door. She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿He said, "It was she who sought me to yield myself to her." And a witness from her own family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars.﴾ ﴿But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said, "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ ﴿"Yūsuf, turn away from this, and [you, woman], ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners."﴾

This is the attaching of one narrative to another (ʿaṭf qiṣṣah ʿalā qiṣṣah), so it does not necessarily follow that this narrative occurred in time after the one preceding it. This incident occurred before Yūsuf was given prophethood, since the bestowal of prophethood generally occurs at the age of forty. The more evident view is that he was granted prophethood and messengerhood after his family entered Egypt and after the death of his father. The verses have addressed the establishment of Yūsuf's steadfastness (peace be upon him) in chastity, fidelity, and nobility of character.

[Page 250]

Thus *murāwadah* (seeking to persuade or seduce), which requires repeated attempts, is expressed in the form of *mufāʿalah* (the verbal form implying reciprocity), and *mufāʿalah* is used to indicate repetition. It has been said that the *mufāʿalah* here is notional (*taqdīriyyah*), in that the action from one side and the resistance from the other side are considered as an action countered by a similar action. The word *murāwadah* derives from *rāda yarūdu*, meaning to come and go. The state of one who repeatedly tries to get someone to do something is compared to the state of one who goes back and forth in returning to the thing one has turned away from; thus *rāwada* is used in the sense of *ḥāwala* (to attempt).

*ʿAn* here indicates separation (*mujāwazah*), meaning that she sought him, distancing him from himself, that is, that he should make himself hers. Apparently this construction is one of the Qur'an's original expressions. The word "self" (*nafs*) here is a metonymy for the purpose of intercourse, as Ibn ʿAṭiyyah stated: thus "self" refers to his chastity and her enabling herself to have what she wanted from him, as though she were seeking to have him surrender his will and his judgment over himself.

As for its construction with *ʿalā* ("upon"), that indicates the thing whose attainment is sought. In the saying of Abū Hurayrah, it occurred that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was urging his uncle Abū Ṭālib toward Islam." And in the hadith of the Night Journey, Mūsā said to him: "I had tried (*rāwadtu*) the Children of Israel for less than that, and they abandoned it."

The expression referring to the wife of the ʿAzīz by way of the relative clause, in His saying ﴿the one in whose house he was﴾, is intended for what the relative clause implies of affirming Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) infallibility, because his being in her house is of a nature that would make him submit to her desire.

*Baytihā* ("her house") is the house of her residence in which she spends the night. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ is that at that time he was in the house where she was. It is also possible that the intended "house" is the whole dwelling, which is the palace of the ʿAzīz. From this comes the saying "*rabbat al-bayt*" (the mistress of the house), meaning the wife of the head of the household. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ would then be that he was among the dependents of that dwelling.

Closing the doors (*ghalq al-abwāb*) means placing each door so as to block the opening through which one enters.

The doubling in *ghallaqat* serves to express the intensity and strength of the action, meaning that they were closed firmly and securely.

[Page 251]

*Al-abwāb* is the plural of *bāb* (door), and it was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Enter upon them through the door﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 23].

*Hayta* is a verb-form noun (*ism fiʿl*) meaning "hurry" or "make haste." It is said that its origin is from the Hauranian language, which is Nabataean. It is also said that it is from the Hebrew language.

The *lām* in *laka* serves to clarify the intended addressee of the address, as in their saying "*suqyan laka*" (watering to you) and "*shukran laka*" (thanks to you). Its original form is *hayta-ka*. It appears that she asked of him something that was not unusual in their palaces, namely that a woman enjoy her servant as a man enjoys his female slave. For this reason she did not first approach him with an enticement, but began by offering herself to him. The matter will be further clarified when we reach His saying: ﴿She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife…"﴾.

There are several readings of *Hayta*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Dhakwān (on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir), and Abū Jaʿfar read it with a *kasrah* on the *hāʾ* and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hīta*). Ibn Kathīr read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ* (*Haytu*). The rest read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hayta*). The *fatḥah* and *ḍammah* are indeclinable vowels (*ḥarakatā bināʾ*).

*Maʿādh* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that is annexed to the Name of Majesty (Allāh) in the manner in which a verbal noun is annexed to its object. Its original form is "*aʿūdhu ʿawdhan billāh*," meaning "I seek refuge in God," that is, I take refuge in Him from what you are attempting. Its explanation will come when we reach His saying: ﴿He said, "God forbid that we take…"﴾ [Yūsuf: 79] in this sūrah.

*Inna* here conveys the reason for what ﴿God forbid!﴾ conveys of refusal and seeking refuge in God from it, which implies that God commanded that seeking of refuge.

The pronoun in *innahu* ("indeed he") may refer to the Name of Majesty, in which case *rabbī* means "my Creator." It may also refer to something known from the context, namely her husband, who would not be content for anyone else to touch her; he is known from customary understanding, and in that case *rabbī* means "my master" and "my owner."

This is speech that has been eloquently directed in a manner by which the words of Yūsuf (peace be upon him) are reported; either because Yūsuf (peace be upon him) used such a construction in the language of the Copts, or because he gave two excuses for his refusal, and the Qur'an reports them with brevity and allusion.

[Page 252]

Whichever is the case, the statement is an explanation of his refusal and an allusion to her for betraying her pledge.

In this statement there is a great lesson in chastity and piety, and the infallibility of the prophets before prophethood from the major sins.

The mention of the description of the Lord under both possibilities indicates the obligation of obeying Him and being thankful for the blessing of creation with respect to God, and for the blessing of upbringing with respect to his noble master.

He confirmed this by describing it with the clause ﴿He has given me the best residence﴾, meaning: He made my final state good, since He rescued me from destruction, or He honored my care. The explanation of *al-mathwā* (residence) has been given just above.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾ is a second reason for the refusal. The pronoun that is made the subject of *inna* is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), which conveys the importance of the clause made its predicate, because it is a comprehensive admonition. It also indicates that answering her solicitation is wrongdoing, because in it there is the wronging of both of them: himself, by committing a sin of a kind on which the religions agree that it is a major sin; and his master, who trusted him with his household and trusted her with herself, since he took her as a wife and kept her chaste.

*Al-hamm* is resolve to act. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿and they plotted what they could not attain﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74] in Sūrat Barāʾah. The resolve of hers is emphasized with *qad* and the oath-*lām* to convey that she resolved firmly and in earnest.

The clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ begins a fresh, independent statement. The intended meaning is that she was serious in what she sought from him, not testing him. The purpose of mentioning her desire for him is to prepare for the mention of the absence of his desire for her, in order to explain the difference between their two states in religion, since he was protected from sin.

The clause ﴿and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ is coordinated with the whole clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾. It is not coordinated with the clause *hammat* ("she desired"), which is the answer to the oath implied by the *lām*.

[Page 253]

Because the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ is followed by the clause introduced by *lawlā* ("had it not been"), which is exclusively about Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) own state and not about the state of the ʿAzīz's wife, it is evident that there is no connection between the two clauses. Hence the second clause is independent, since the condition of *lawlā* pertains to the state of the subject in it. The sense is: "And had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her." The answer was placed before its condition for emphasis. He did not attach the answer to the *lām* that frequently accompanies the answer to *lawlā*, because it is not obligatory, and because, since it was placed before *lawlā*, it was disliked to attach it to the *lām* before the mention of the conditional particle. Therefore it is good to pause at His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ so that the meaning of a new beginning with the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ appears clearly. By this it becomes evident that no desire for the ʿAzīz's wife ever touched Yūsuf (peace be upon him), because God protected him from desiring sin by what He showed him of the proof.

Abū Ḥātim said: "I used to read the strange words of the Qur'an to Abū ʿUbaydah, and when I came to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾ and so on, Abū ʿUbaydah said: 'This is in the order of anteriority and posteriority (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*), that is, the placing of the answer before the condition and the postponing of the condition; as if he said: "And she certainly desired him, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her."'"

al-Ṭabarī criticized this interpretation, on the grounds that the answer of *lawlā* does not precede it. What repels this criticism is that when Abū ʿUbaydah said that, we know that he did not see a prohibition on placing the answer of *lawlā* first. Moreover, he may make what is mentioned before *lawlā* an indication of the answer, with the answer being omitted due to what precedes *lawlā* indicating it. There is no escape from this under any reading, since *lawlā* and its condition restrict his saying "and he would have desired her" under all interpretations, so whatever answer is supposed is supposed under all interpretations.

A group said: Yūsuf desired to yield to her in what she invited him to, then he drew back and refrained from it when he saw the proof of his Lord. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Ibn Abī Mulaykah, and Tha'lab. The explanation of this is that he turned away from what he desired by God's protection or His infallibility; and desiring an evil deed while refraining from carrying it out is not a major sin, so it does not contradict the infallibility of the prophets from major sins before prophethood, according to those who hold that they were infallible from them before prophethood, which is the view of the majority.

[Page 254]

There is a difference of opinion on this, and for this reason Ibn ʿAbbās permitted this concerning Yūsuf. A group said: Yūsuf desired and began to prepare for it, then he saw a proof that turned him away from it, so he desisted. This is the view of al-Suddī, and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās. It returns to what we have explained in the previous view.

The author of *al-Kashshāf* erred in attaching these reports to those he calls *al-Ḥashwiyyah* and *al-Mujabbirah*, by which he means the Ashʿarites. He averted his gaze from the names of those to whom these interpretations are attributed, "He threw his own disease at me and slipped away." He also did not marvel at the consensus of all on the attempt of Yūsuf's brothers (peace be upon him) to kill him, and killing is more grave.

The seeing (*al-ruʾyah*) here is cognitive (*ʿilmiyyah*), because the proof (*burhān*) is among the meanings that are not seen by the eye.

*Al-burhān* is the argument. This proof is included in it: its turning him away from desire for her. Had it not been for that, the state of human nature would not have been free from desiring to comply with her in that situation, because of the abundance of motives for desire arising from her beauty, her eagerness for him, the delight of such men in obeying her, nearness to her, and the impulses of youth that make it appealing. Thus God's proof was the barrier between him and desire for her, and nothing else.

The commentators differed about what this proof is. Some of them indicate that it is a theoretical argument that made this act abhorrent to him. It was said: it is divine revelation. It was said: divine protection. It was said: visions that appeared to him.

The indication in His saying ﴿Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾ refers to something understood from what precedes it, which is implied by His saying ﴿he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, namely the seeing of the proof. That is: We showed him that seeing in this manner so that We might turn away from him evil.

*Al-ṣarf* is the transfer of a thing from one place to another. Here it is used metaphorically for protection from a thing's arriving at the place where it would normally arrive. The turning away is used to express infallibility from something that is about to befall him.

[Page 255]

The expression of infallibility by "turning away" indicates that the causes of the occurrence of evil and immorality were present, but God turned them away from him.

*Al-sūʾ* is the ugly thing, and it is the betrayal of one who entrusted him. *Al-faḥshāʾ* is the disobedience, and it is adultery. *Al-sūʾ* and *al-faḥshāʾ* were mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] in Sūrat al-Baqarah. The meaning of "He turned both away from him" is that He turned away his involvement with them.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿Indeed he is among Our sincere servants﴾ gives the reason for the wisdom of diverting him from evil and indecency, a diversion that went beyond the normal course of things, so that God's choosing of him would not be diminished in this severe test to the self.

Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar and Khalaf read *al-mukhlaṣīn* with a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, meaning those whom God has made sincere and chosen. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read it with a *kasrah* on the *lām*, meaning those who make their religion sincerely for God. The sense of the causal clause is one under both readings.

*Al-istibāq* (racing one another) is a *iftiʿāl* form from *al-sabq* (precedence). It was mentioned just before, and here it indicates that each of them was forcing himself to race, that is, each was trying to be the first to the door.

*Al-bāb* (the door) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. Its original form was *wa-istabaqā ilā al-bāb* ("and they raced to the door"), like ﴿Mūsā chose from his people seventy men﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 155], meaning "from his people." Or the verb *istabaqā* is taken to include the meaning of *ibtadarā* (hastened).
