The definite article in *al-bāb* is the definite article of the category, since there were several closed doors. Yūsuf, peace be upon him, fled from her solicitation toward the door, wishing to open it and go out, while she wished to get ahead of him to the door to prevent him from opening it.

The clause ﴿and she tore his shirt﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Qadda* means *qaṭaʿa* (cut), that is, she cut from it a rent. This happened before the racing, without doubt, because if the tearing of the shirt had occurred during the racing, there would have been no evidence in it for the truthfulness of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, that she had solicited him. The tearing during the racing indicates no more than that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, had raced ahead of her, hastening to the door. This shows that she had seized him by his shirt when he turned away from her, wishing [p. 256] to force him into what she had solicited. He pulled himself free, and the shirt was torn by the force of the pull. The cutting of the shirt was from behind, because he was turning away from her, fleeing and averting himself, so she seized him by it to turn him back from his aversion.

The concision of the verse has excellently gathered all these meanings under the phrase ﴿they raced to the door and she tore his shirt﴾.

It happened that they found her master, that is, her husband, al-ʿAzīz, at the outer door, wishing to enter the house through the outer door. The use of "master" (*sayyid*) for the husband: it has been said that the Qurʾān related the custom of the Copts at that time, that they called the husband "sayyid." The apparent meaning is that this was not in use in the custom of the Arabs, so the expression here is one of the fine historical details, like His saying later ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ [Yūsuf: 76]. Perhaps marriage in Egypt in that era was mostly by way of ownership.

It is known from the discourse that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, opened the doors that Zulaykhā had locked, one door after another, until he reached the outer one. All of that happened during their racing, and this is concision.

*Al-ilfāʾ* (finding) is the obtaining of a thing in a particular state without seeking to obtain it. Most often it is sudden, or it occurs through ignorance of its first occurrence, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Rather we will follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170].

The clause ﴿She said: "What is the recompense..."﴾ and so on is a resumptive clause of explanation (*mustaʾnafah bayānīyah*), because the listener asks: what happened at the moment of her master's surprise while they were in that state?

She rushed to speak to him, persisting in slander, in such a way that she did not stammer. She made him imagine that she was in the right, and she poured the speech into a universal mould so that it would take the form of a law, and it would be a principle whose intended object is not known, so the addressee has no choice but to acknowledge it for her. Perhaps she feared that al-ʿAzīz's love for Yūsuf, peace be upon him, would prevent him from punishing him, so she poured her speech into a universal mould. She wanted by this that her husband should not perceive that she was in love with someone other than her master, and that she should frighten Yūsuf, peace be upon him, with her scheming, so that he would not refuse her again.

She set Yūsuf, peace be upon him, between two kinds of punishment, which are: prison, that is, confinement. Confinement was an ancient punishment in that era, and it continued until the time of Mūsā, peace be upon him, for Pharaoh said to Mūsā, peace be upon him, ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 29].

As for punishment (*ʿadhāb*), it is of various kinds, and it is an older punishment in the terminology of mankind. Among it are beating and inflicting pain by fire and by cutting off limbs. The mention of prison will come in this sūrah repeatedly.

The clause ﴿He said: "It was she who solicited me against myself"﴾ is part of the speech of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, and it is separated (*faṣl*) because it comes in the manner of a reply to her speech. The variation of the expression between ﴿that he be imprisoned, or a painful punishment﴾, without saying "except prison or a punishment," is because the word *al-sijn* is applied to the place in which the prisoner is put, and it is applied to the verbal noun of *sajana*. So His saying ﴿that he be imprisoned﴾ is clearer in showing the governing of the meaning of the verb over him.

Placing the subject before its predicate, which is a verb, gives restriction (*qaṣr*), and this is a restriction by reversal (*qaṣr qalb*), as a rebuttal to her.

With al-ʿAzīz was a man from among his wife's people, and he is the one who gave testimony, and he was perceptive, knowing the aspects of evidence.

His saying was called testimony (*shahādah*) because it tends toward the manifestation of the truth in establishing the transgression of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, against his mistress, or refuting it. This is judgment by clear circumstantial evidence (*al-qarīnah al-bayyinah*), because if she had held his garment in order to seize him and punish him, that would have occurred when he was facing her and approaching her. Then if he wished to slip away from her, his shirt would have been torn at the front, and conversely if his being held was while he was fleeing and turning away. There is no doubt that the reasoning by the manner of tearing the shirt arose from the mention of the wife of al-ʿAzīz of the occurrence of the tearing of the shirt, as she was trying to make it a proof that she had seized him in order to punish him. Had it not been for that, it would not have occurred to the witness that a tearing had happened, for otherwise from where would the witness have known the tearing of the shirt? The apparent meaning is that the witness was thinking of her truthfulness, so he wished to set up a proof of her truthfulness, but the opposite of that happened, as an honour for Yūsuf, peace be upon him.

[p. 258] The clause ﴿If his shirt has been torn from the front﴾ explains the verb *shahida* (testified).

The addition of ﴿and he is of the liars﴾ after ﴿she is truthful﴾, and the addition of ﴿and he is of the truthful﴾ after ﴿she is lying﴾, is an emphasis for increasing the establishment of the truth, as is the case with rulings.

The particles of condition indicate no more than the linking and causal relation between the content of their protasis and the content of their apodosis, without restriction to the future or to the past. So the meaning of ﴿If his shirt was torn from the front, she has spoken truly﴾ and what follows it is: if that happened in the past, then her truthfulness happened in the past.

The one who saw his shirt torn from behind and said, "Indeed it is of your scheming," is without doubt al-ʿAzīz. It had become clear to him that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, was innocent of assaulting the woman, so he was content with blaming his wife, saying that her accusation against him was of the scheming of women. So the plural feminine pronoun is an address to her, and it included those of her class by treating them as the townswomen (*ḥawāḍir*).

*Al-kayd* (scheming) is doing a thing in a form other than what is intended, in order to reach an intended end. It has been discussed before at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed My scheme is firm﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 183], in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

Then he commanded Yūsuf, peace be upon him, to turn away from what she had charged him with, that is, not to hold her to account for it, and to refrain from returning to discuss it. And he commanded his wife to seek forgiveness for her sin, that is, for her accusation of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, of boldness and assault against her.

The exegetes said: al-ʿAzīz was little given to jealousy. It was said: he was forbearing and wise. Perhaps he was infatuated with her, or the semblance of ownership lessened the blame on a woman for soliciting her slave. This is what is indicated by the state of her solicitation of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, when she rushed him with her words "Come, you," as has been discussed just before.

[p. 259] *Al-khāṭiʾ* is the doer of a sin (*khaṭīʾah*), which is a crime. He placed her among the group of those who erred, lightening the blame on her. The form of the masculine plural is by predominance (*taghlīb*).

The clause ﴿Yūsuf, turn away from this﴾ is part of the speech of al-ʿAzīz, since he is the possessor of the judgment.

The clause ﴿and seek forgiveness for your sin﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Yūsuf, turn away﴾ in the speech of al-ʿAzīz, as a conjunction of command upon command where the one commanded differs. The feminine second-person *kāf* is definitely an address to the wife of al-ʿAzīz. So al-ʿAzīz, after addressing her that what she had devised was of the scheming of women, directed the address to Yūsuf, peace be upon him, by calling him, then returned the address to the woman.

This manner of address is called *al-iqbāl* (turning toward), and it may be called *al-iltifāt* (turning) in the linguistic sense when it is the rhetorical *iltifāt*, and it is rare in eloquent speech. From it is the saying of al-Jarmī, of the Ṭayy, one of the poets of the *Ḥamāsah*:

I suppose you are my appointee at Bunniyy Jufayf and Hālah; indeed I forbid you, O Hālah.

Al-Marzūqī said in his commentary on the *Ḥamāsah*: The Arabs gather several people in address and report, then turn or direct their attention from among them to one, because he is the greatest of them, or the best of them in hearing, and the most particular of them in the matter.

**[Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr, *al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr*, on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29, part 1]**

﴿The woman in whose house he was sought him to yield himself to her, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "God forbid! He is my Lord; he has given me the best residence. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper."﴾ ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ ﴿And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her master at the door. She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿He said, "It was she who sought me to yield myself to her." And a witness from her own family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars.﴾ ﴿But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said, "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ ﴿"Yūsuf, turn away from this, and [you, woman], ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners."﴾

This is the attaching of one narrative to another (ʿaṭf qiṣṣah ʿalā qiṣṣah), so it does not necessarily follow that this narrative occurred in time after the one preceding it. This incident occurred before Yūsuf was given prophethood, since the bestowal of prophethood generally occurs at the age of forty. The more evident view is that he was granted prophethood and messengerhood after his family entered Egypt and after the death of his father. The verses have addressed the establishment of Yūsuf's steadfastness (peace be upon him) in chastity, fidelity, and nobility of character.

[Page 250]

Thus *murāwadah* (seeking to persuade or seduce), which requires repeated attempts, is expressed in the form of *mufāʿalah* (the verbal form implying reciprocity), and *mufāʿalah* is used to indicate repetition. It has been said that the *mufāʿalah* here is notional (*taqdīriyyah*), in that the action from one side and the resistance from the other side are considered as an action countered by a similar action. The word *murāwadah* derives from *rāda yarūdu*, meaning to come and go. The state of one who repeatedly tries to get someone to do something is compared to the state of one who goes back and forth in returning to the thing one has turned away from; thus *rāwada* is used in the sense of *ḥāwala* (to attempt).

*ʿAn* here indicates separation (*mujāwazah*), meaning that she sought him, distancing him from himself, that is, that he should make himself hers. Apparently this construction is one of the Qur'an's original expressions. The word "self" (*nafs*) here is a metonymy for the purpose of intercourse, as Ibn ʿAṭiyyah stated: thus "self" refers to his chastity and her enabling herself to have what she wanted from him, as though she were seeking to have him surrender his will and his judgment over himself.

As for its construction with *ʿalā* ("upon"), that indicates the thing whose attainment is sought. In the saying of Abū Hurayrah, it occurred that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was urging his uncle Abū Ṭālib toward Islam." And in the hadith of the Night Journey, Mūsā said to him: "I had tried (*rāwadtu*) the Children of Israel for less than that, and they abandoned it."

The expression referring to the wife of the ʿAzīz by way of the relative clause, in His saying ﴿the one in whose house he was﴾, is intended for what the relative clause implies of affirming Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) infallibility, because his being in her house is of a nature that would make him submit to her desire.

*Baytihā* ("her house") is the house of her residence in which she spends the night. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ is that at that time he was in the house where she was. It is also possible that the intended "house" is the whole dwelling, which is the palace of the ʿAzīz. From this comes the saying "*rabbat al-bayt*" (the mistress of the house), meaning the wife of the head of the household. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ would then be that he was among the dependents of that dwelling.

Closing the doors (*ghalq al-abwāb*) means placing each door so as to block the opening through which one enters.

The doubling in *ghallaqat* serves to express the intensity and strength of the action, meaning that they were closed firmly and securely.

[Page 251]

*Al-abwāb* is the plural of *bāb* (door), and it was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Enter upon them through the door﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 23].

*Hayta* is a verb-form noun (*ism fiʿl*) meaning "hurry" or "make haste." It is said that its origin is from the Hauranian language, which is Nabataean. It is also said that it is from the Hebrew language.

The *lām* in *laka* serves to clarify the intended addressee of the address, as in their saying "*suqyan laka*" (watering to you) and "*shukran laka*" (thanks to you). Its original form is *hayta-ka*. It appears that she asked of him something that was not unusual in their palaces, namely that a woman enjoy her servant as a man enjoys his female slave. For this reason she did not first approach him with an enticement, but began by offering herself to him. The matter will be further clarified when we reach His saying: ﴿She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife…"﴾.

There are several readings of *Hayta*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Dhakwān (on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir), and Abū Jaʿfar read it with a *kasrah* on the *hāʾ* and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hīta*). Ibn Kathīr read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ* (*Haytu*). The rest read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hayta*). The *fatḥah* and *ḍammah* are indeclinable vowels (*ḥarakatā bināʾ*).

*Maʿādh* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that is annexed to the Name of Majesty (Allāh) in the manner in which a verbal noun is annexed to its object. Its original form is "*aʿūdhu ʿawdhan billāh*," meaning "I seek refuge in God," that is, I take refuge in Him from what you are attempting. Its explanation will come when we reach His saying: ﴿He said, "God forbid that we take…"﴾ [Yūsuf: 79] in this sūrah.

*Inna* here conveys the reason for what ﴿God forbid!﴾ conveys of refusal and seeking refuge in God from it, which implies that God commanded that seeking of refuge.

The pronoun in *innahu* ("indeed he") may refer to the Name of Majesty, in which case *rabbī* means "my Creator." It may also refer to something known from the context, namely her husband, who would not be content for anyone else to touch her; he is known from customary understanding, and in that case *rabbī* means "my master" and "my owner."

This is speech that has been eloquently directed in a manner by which the words of Yūsuf (peace be upon him) are reported; either because Yūsuf (peace be upon him) used such a construction in the language of the Copts, or because he gave two excuses for his refusal, and the Qur'an reports them with brevity and allusion.

[Page 252]

Whichever is the case, the statement is an explanation of his refusal and an allusion to her for betraying her pledge.

In this statement there is a great lesson in chastity and piety, and the infallibility of the prophets before prophethood from the major sins.

The mention of the description of the Lord under both possibilities indicates the obligation of obeying Him and being thankful for the blessing of creation with respect to God, and for the blessing of upbringing with respect to his noble master.

He confirmed this by describing it with the clause ﴿He has given me the best residence﴾, meaning: He made my final state good, since He rescued me from destruction, or He honored my care. The explanation of *al-mathwā* (residence) has been given just above.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾ is a second reason for the refusal. The pronoun that is made the subject of *inna* is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), which conveys the importance of the clause made its predicate, because it is a comprehensive admonition. It also indicates that answering her solicitation is wrongdoing, because in it there is the wronging of both of them: himself, by committing a sin of a kind on which the religions agree that it is a major sin; and his master, who trusted him with his household and trusted her with herself, since he took her as a wife and kept her chaste.

*Al-hamm* is resolve to act. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿and they plotted what they could not attain﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74] in Sūrat Barāʾah. The resolve of hers is emphasized with *qad* and the oath-*lām* to convey that she resolved firmly and in earnest.

The clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ begins a fresh, independent statement. The intended meaning is that she was serious in what she sought from him, not testing him. The purpose of mentioning her desire for him is to prepare for the mention of the absence of his desire for her, in order to explain the difference between their two states in religion, since he was protected from sin.

The clause ﴿and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ is coordinated with the whole clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾. It is not coordinated with the clause *hammat* ("she desired"), which is the answer to the oath implied by the *lām*.

[Page 253]

Because the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ is followed by the clause introduced by *lawlā* ("had it not been"), which is exclusively about Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) own state and not about the state of the ʿAzīz's wife, it is evident that there is no connection between the two clauses. Hence the second clause is independent, since the condition of *lawlā* pertains to the state of the subject in it. The sense is: "And had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her." The answer was placed before its condition for emphasis. He did not attach the answer to the *lām* that frequently accompanies the answer to *lawlā*, because it is not obligatory, and because, since it was placed before *lawlā*, it was disliked to attach it to the *lām* before the mention of the conditional particle. Therefore it is good to pause at His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ so that the meaning of a new beginning with the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ appears clearly. By this it becomes evident that no desire for the ʿAzīz's wife ever touched Yūsuf (peace be upon him), because God protected him from desiring sin by what He showed him of the proof.

Abū Ḥātim said: "I used to read the strange words of the Qur'an to Abū ʿUbaydah, and when I came to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾ and so on, Abū ʿUbaydah said: 'This is in the order of anteriority and posteriority (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*), that is, the placing of the answer before the condition and the postponing of the condition; as if he said: "And she certainly desired him, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her."'"

al-Ṭabarī criticized this interpretation, on the grounds that the answer of *lawlā* does not precede it. What repels this criticism is that when Abū ʿUbaydah said that, we know that he did not see a prohibition on placing the answer of *lawlā* first. Moreover, he may make what is mentioned before *lawlā* an indication of the answer, with the answer being omitted due to what precedes *lawlā* indicating it. There is no escape from this under any reading, since *lawlā* and its condition restrict his saying "and he would have desired her" under all interpretations, so whatever answer is supposed is supposed under all interpretations.

A group said: Yūsuf desired to yield to her in what she invited him to, then he drew back and refrained from it when he saw the proof of his Lord. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Ibn Abī Mulaykah, and Tha'lab. The explanation of this is that he turned away from what he desired by God's protection or His infallibility; and desiring an evil deed while refraining from carrying it out is not a major sin, so it does not contradict the infallibility of the prophets from major sins before prophethood, according to those who hold that they were infallible from them before prophethood, which is the view of the majority.

[Page 254]

There is a difference of opinion on this, and for this reason Ibn ʿAbbās permitted this concerning Yūsuf. A group said: Yūsuf desired and began to prepare for it, then he saw a proof that turned him away from it, so he desisted. This is the view of al-Suddī, and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās. It returns to what we have explained in the previous view.

The author of *al-Kashshāf* erred in attaching these reports to those he calls *al-Ḥashwiyyah* and *al-Mujabbirah*, by which he means the Ashʿarites. He averted his gaze from the names of those to whom these interpretations are attributed, "He threw his own disease at me and slipped away." He also did not marvel at the consensus of all on the attempt of Yūsuf's brothers (peace be upon him) to kill him, and killing is more grave.

The seeing (*al-ruʾyah*) here is cognitive (*ʿilmiyyah*), because the proof (*burhān*) is among the meanings that are not seen by the eye.

*Al-burhān* is the argument. This proof is included in it: its turning him away from desire for her. Had it not been for that, the state of human nature would not have been free from desiring to comply with her in that situation, because of the abundance of motives for desire arising from her beauty, her eagerness for him, the delight of such men in obeying her, nearness to her, and the impulses of youth that make it appealing. Thus God's proof was the barrier between him and desire for her, and nothing else.

The commentators differed about what this proof is. Some of them indicate that it is a theoretical argument that made this act abhorrent to him. It was said: it is divine revelation. It was said: divine protection. It was said: visions that appeared to him.

The indication in His saying ﴿Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾ refers to something understood from what precedes it, which is implied by His saying ﴿he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, namely the seeing of the proof. That is: We showed him that seeing in this manner so that We might turn away from him evil.

*Al-ṣarf* is the transfer of a thing from one place to another. Here it is used metaphorically for protection from a thing's arriving at the place where it would normally arrive. The turning away is used to express infallibility from something that is about to befall him.

[Page 255]

The expression of infallibility by "turning away" indicates that the causes of the occurrence of evil and immorality were present, but God turned them away from him.

*Al-sūʾ* is the ugly thing, and it is the betrayal of one who entrusted him. *Al-faḥshāʾ* is the disobedience, and it is adultery. *Al-sūʾ* and *al-faḥshāʾ* were mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] in Sūrat al-Baqarah. The meaning of "He turned both away from him" is that He turned away his involvement with them.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿Indeed he is among Our sincere servants﴾ gives the reason for the wisdom of diverting him from evil and indecency, a diversion that went beyond the normal course of things, so that God's choosing of him would not be diminished in this severe test to the self.

Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar and Khalaf read *al-mukhlaṣīn* with a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, meaning those whom God has made sincere and chosen. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read it with a *kasrah* on the *lām*, meaning those who make their religion sincerely for God. The sense of the causal clause is one under both readings.

*Al-istibāq* (racing one another) is a *iftiʿāl* form from *al-sabq* (precedence). It was mentioned just before, and here it indicates that each of them was forcing himself to race, that is, each was trying to be the first to the door.

*Al-bāb* (the door) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. Its original form was *wa-istabaqā ilā al-bāb* ("and they raced to the door"), like ﴿Mūsā chose from his people seventy men﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 155], meaning "from his people." Or the verb *istabaqā* is taken to include the meaning of *ibtadarā* (hastened).

The definite article in *al-bāb* is the definite article of the category, since there were several closed doors. Yūsuf, peace be upon him, fled from her solicitation toward the door, wishing to open it and go out, while she wished to get ahead of him to the door to prevent him from opening it.

The clause ﴿and she tore his shirt﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Qadda* means *qaṭaʿa* (cut), that is, she cut from it a rent. This happened before the racing, without doubt, because if the tearing of the shirt had occurred during the racing, there would have been no evidence in it for the truthfulness of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, that she had solicited him. The tearing during the racing indicates no more than that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, had raced ahead of her, hastening to the door. This shows that she had seized him by his shirt when he turned away from her, wishing [p. 256] to force him into what she had solicited. He pulled himself free, and the shirt was torn by the force of the pull. The cutting of the shirt was from behind, because he was turning away from her, fleeing and averting himself, so she seized him by it to turn him back from his aversion.

The concision of the verse has excellently gathered all these meanings under the phrase ﴿they raced to the door and she tore his shirt﴾.

It happened that they found her master, that is, her husband, al-ʿAzīz, at the outer door, wishing to enter the house through the outer door. The use of "master" (*sayyid*) for the husband: it has been said that the Qurʾān related the custom of the Copts at that time, that they called the husband "sayyid." The apparent meaning is that this was not in use in the custom of the Arabs, so the expression here is one of the fine historical details, like His saying later ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ [Yūsuf: 76]. Perhaps marriage in Egypt in that era was mostly by way of ownership.

It is known from the discourse that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, opened the doors that Zulaykhā had locked, one door after another, until he reached the outer one. All of that happened during their racing, and this is concision.

*Al-ilfāʾ* (finding) is the obtaining of a thing in a particular state without seeking to obtain it. Most often it is sudden, or it occurs through ignorance of its first occurrence, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Rather we will follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170].

The clause ﴿She said: "What is the recompense..."﴾ and so on is a resumptive clause of explanation (*mustaʾnafah bayānīyah*), because the listener asks: what happened at the moment of her master's surprise while they were in that state?

She rushed to speak to him, persisting in slander, in such a way that she did not stammer. She made him imagine that she was in the right, and she poured the speech into a universal mould so that it would take the form of a law, and it would be a principle whose intended object is not known, so the addressee has no choice but to acknowledge it for her. Perhaps she feared that al-ʿAzīz's love for Yūsuf, peace be upon him, would prevent him from punishing him, so she poured her speech into a universal mould. She wanted by this that her husband should not perceive that she was in love with someone other than her master, and that she should frighten Yūsuf, peace be upon him, with her scheming, so that he would not refuse her again.

She set Yūsuf, peace be upon him, between two kinds of punishment, which are: prison, that is, confinement. Confinement was an ancient punishment in that era, and it continued until the time of Mūsā, peace be upon him, for Pharaoh said to Mūsā, peace be upon him, ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 29].

As for punishment (*ʿadhāb*), it is of various kinds, and it is an older punishment in the terminology of mankind. Among it are beating and inflicting pain by fire and by cutting off limbs. The mention of prison will come in this sūrah repeatedly.

The clause ﴿He said: "It was she who solicited me against myself"﴾ is part of the speech of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, and it is separated (*faṣl*) because it comes in the manner of a reply to her speech. The variation of the expression between ﴿that he be imprisoned, or a painful punishment﴾, without saying "except prison or a punishment," is because the word *al-sijn* is applied to the place in which the prisoner is put, and it is applied to the verbal noun of *sajana*. So His saying ﴿that he be imprisoned﴾ is clearer in showing the governing of the meaning of the verb over him.

Placing the subject before its predicate, which is a verb, gives restriction (*qaṣr*), and this is a restriction by reversal (*qaṣr qalb*), as a rebuttal to her.

With al-ʿAzīz was a man from among his wife's people, and he is the one who gave testimony, and he was perceptive, knowing the aspects of evidence.

His saying was called testimony (*shahādah*) because it tends toward the manifestation of the truth in establishing the transgression of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, against his mistress, or refuting it. This is judgment by clear circumstantial evidence (*al-qarīnah al-bayyinah*), because if she had held his garment in order to seize him and punish him, that would have occurred when he was facing her and approaching her. Then if he wished to slip away from her, his shirt would have been torn at the front, and conversely if his being held was while he was fleeing and turning away. There is no doubt that the reasoning by the manner of tearing the shirt arose from the mention of the wife of al-ʿAzīz of the occurrence of the tearing of the shirt, as she was trying to make it a proof that she had seized him in order to punish him. Had it not been for that, it would not have occurred to the witness that a tearing had happened, for otherwise from where would the witness have known the tearing of the shirt? The apparent meaning is that the witness was thinking of her truthfulness, so he wished to set up a proof of her truthfulness, but the opposite of that happened, as an honour for Yūsuf, peace be upon him.

[p. 258] The clause ﴿If his shirt has been torn from the front﴾ explains the verb *shahida* (testified).

The addition of ﴿and he is of the liars﴾ after ﴿she is truthful﴾, and the addition of ﴿and he is of the truthful﴾ after ﴿she is lying﴾, is an emphasis for increasing the establishment of the truth, as is the case with rulings.

The particles of condition indicate no more than the linking and causal relation between the content of their protasis and the content of their apodosis, without restriction to the future or to the past. So the meaning of ﴿If his shirt was torn from the front, she has spoken truly﴾ and what follows it is: if that happened in the past, then her truthfulness happened in the past.

The one who saw his shirt torn from behind and said, "Indeed it is of your scheming," is without doubt al-ʿAzīz. It had become clear to him that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, was innocent of assaulting the woman, so he was content with blaming his wife, saying that her accusation against him was of the scheming of women. So the plural feminine pronoun is an address to her, and it included those of her class by treating them as the townswomen (*ḥawāḍir*).

*Al-kayd* (scheming) is doing a thing in a form other than what is intended, in order to reach an intended end. It has been discussed before at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed My scheme is firm﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 183], in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

Then he commanded Yūsuf, peace be upon him, to turn away from what she had charged him with, that is, not to hold her to account for it, and to refrain from returning to discuss it. And he commanded his wife to seek forgiveness for her sin, that is, for her accusation of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, of boldness and assault against her.

The exegetes said: al-ʿAzīz was little given to jealousy. It was said: he was forbearing and wise. Perhaps he was infatuated with her, or the semblance of ownership lessened the blame on a woman for soliciting her slave. This is what is indicated by the state of her solicitation of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, when she rushed him with her words "Come, you," as has been discussed just before.

[p. 259] *Al-khāṭiʾ* is the doer of a sin (*khaṭīʾah*), which is a crime. He placed her among the group of those who erred, lightening the blame on her. The form of the masculine plural is by predominance (*taghlīb*).

The clause ﴿Yūsuf, turn away from this﴾ is part of the speech of al-ʿAzīz, since he is the possessor of the judgment.

The clause ﴿and seek forgiveness for your sin﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Yūsuf, turn away﴾ in the speech of al-ʿAzīz, as a conjunction of command upon command where the one commanded differs. The feminine second-person *kāf* is definitely an address to the wife of al-ʿAzīz. So al-ʿAzīz, after addressing her that what she had devised was of the scheming of women, directed the address to Yūsuf, peace be upon him, by calling him, then returned the address to the woman.

This manner of address is called *al-iqbāl* (turning toward), and it may be called *al-iltifāt* (turning) in the linguistic sense when it is the rhetorical *iltifāt*, and it is rare in eloquent speech. From it is the saying of al-Jarmī, of the Ṭayy, one of the poets of the *Ḥamāsah*:

I suppose you are my appointee at Bunniyy Jufayf and Hālah; indeed I forbid you, O Hālah.

Al-Marzūqī said in his commentary on the *Ḥamāsah*: The Arabs gather several people in address and report, then turn or direct their attention from among them to one, because he is the greatest of them, or the best of them in hearing, and the most particular of them in the matter.

**[Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr, *al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr*, on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29, part 1]**

﴿The woman in whose house he was sought him to yield himself to her, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "God forbid! He is my Lord; he has given me the best residence. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper."﴾ ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ ﴿And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her master at the door. She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿He said, "It was she who sought me to yield myself to her." And a witness from her own family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars.﴾ ﴿But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said, "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ ﴿"Yūsuf, turn away from this, and [you, woman], ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners."﴾

This is the attaching of one narrative to another (ʿaṭf qiṣṣah ʿalā qiṣṣah), so it does not necessarily follow that this narrative occurred in time after the one preceding it. This incident occurred before Yūsuf was given prophethood, since the bestowal of prophethood generally occurs at the age of forty. The more evident view is that he was granted prophethood and messengerhood after his family entered Egypt and after the death of his father. The verses have addressed the establishment of Yūsuf's steadfastness (peace be upon him) in chastity, fidelity, and nobility of character.

[Page 250]

Thus *murāwadah* (seeking to persuade or seduce), which requires repeated attempts, is expressed in the form of *mufāʿalah* (the verbal form implying reciprocity), and *mufāʿalah* is used to indicate repetition. It has been said that the *mufāʿalah* here is notional (*taqdīriyyah*), in that the action from one side and the resistance from the other side are considered as an action countered by a similar action. The word *murāwadah* derives from *rāda yarūdu*, meaning to come and go. The state of one who repeatedly tries to get someone to do something is compared to the state of one who goes back and forth in returning to the thing one has turned away from; thus *rāwada* is used in the sense of *ḥāwala* (to attempt).

*ʿAn* here indicates separation (*mujāwazah*), meaning that she sought him, distancing him from himself, that is, that he should make himself hers. Apparently this construction is one of the Qur'an's original expressions. The word "self" (*nafs*) here is a metonymy for the purpose of intercourse, as Ibn ʿAṭiyyah stated: thus "self" refers to his chastity and her enabling herself to have what she wanted from him, as though she were seeking to have him surrender his will and his judgment over himself.

As for its construction with *ʿalā* ("upon"), that indicates the thing whose attainment is sought. In the saying of Abū Hurayrah, it occurred that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was urging his uncle Abū Ṭālib toward Islam." And in the hadith of the Night Journey, Mūsā said to him: "I had tried (*rāwadtu*) the Children of Israel for less than that, and they abandoned it."

The expression referring to the wife of the ʿAzīz by way of the relative clause, in His saying ﴿the one in whose house he was﴾, is intended for what the relative clause implies of affirming Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) infallibility, because his being in her house is of a nature that would make him submit to her desire.

*Baytihā* ("her house") is the house of her residence in which she spends the night. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ is that at that time he was in the house where she was. It is also possible that the intended "house" is the whole dwelling, which is the palace of the ʿAzīz. From this comes the saying "*rabbat al-bayt*" (the mistress of the house), meaning the wife of the head of the household. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ would then be that he was among the dependents of that dwelling.

Closing the doors (*ghalq al-abwāb*) means placing each door so as to block the opening through which one enters.

The doubling in *ghallaqat* serves to express the intensity and strength of the action, meaning that they were closed firmly and securely.

[Page 251]

*Al-abwāb* is the plural of *bāb* (door), and it was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Enter upon them through the door﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 23].

*Hayta* is a verb-form noun (*ism fiʿl*) meaning "hurry" or "make haste." It is said that its origin is from the Hauranian language, which is Nabataean. It is also said that it is from the Hebrew language.

The *lām* in *laka* serves to clarify the intended addressee of the address, as in their saying "*suqyan laka*" (watering to you) and "*shukran laka*" (thanks to you). Its original form is *hayta-ka*. It appears that she asked of him something that was not unusual in their palaces, namely that a woman enjoy her servant as a man enjoys his female slave. For this reason she did not first approach him with an enticement, but began by offering herself to him. The matter will be further clarified when we reach His saying: ﴿She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife…"﴾.

There are several readings of *Hayta*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Dhakwān (on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir), and Abū Jaʿfar read it with a *kasrah* on the *hāʾ* and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hīta*). Ibn Kathīr read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ* (*Haytu*). The rest read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hayta*). The *fatḥah* and *ḍammah* are indeclinable vowels (*ḥarakatā bināʾ*).

*Maʿādh* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that is annexed to the Name of Majesty (Allāh) in the manner in which a verbal noun is annexed to its object. Its original form is "*aʿūdhu ʿawdhan billāh*," meaning "I seek refuge in God," that is, I take refuge in Him from what you are attempting. Its explanation will come when we reach His saying: ﴿He said, "God forbid that we take…"﴾ [Yūsuf: 79] in this sūrah.

*Inna* here conveys the reason for what ﴿God forbid!﴾ conveys of refusal and seeking refuge in God from it, which implies that God commanded that seeking of refuge.

The pronoun in *innahu* ("indeed he") may refer to the Name of Majesty, in which case *rabbī* means "my Creator." It may also refer to something known from the context, namely her husband, who would not be content for anyone else to touch her; he is known from customary understanding, and in that case *rabbī* means "my master" and "my owner."

This is speech that has been eloquently directed in a manner by which the words of Yūsuf (peace be upon him) are reported; either because Yūsuf (peace be upon him) used such a construction in the language of the Copts, or because he gave two excuses for his refusal, and the Qur'an reports them with brevity and allusion.

[Page 252]

Whichever is the case, the statement is an explanation of his refusal and an allusion to her for betraying her pledge.

In this statement there is a great lesson in chastity and piety, and the infallibility of the prophets before prophethood from the major sins.

The mention of the description of the Lord under both possibilities indicates the obligation of obeying Him and being thankful for the blessing of creation with respect to God, and for the blessing of upbringing with respect to his noble master.

He confirmed this by describing it with the clause ﴿He has given me the best residence﴾, meaning: He made my final state good, since He rescued me from destruction, or He honored my care. The explanation of *al-mathwā* (residence) has been given just above.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾ is a second reason for the refusal. The pronoun that is made the subject of *inna* is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), which conveys the importance of the clause made its predicate, because it is a comprehensive admonition. It also indicates that answering her solicitation is wrongdoing, because in it there is the wronging of both of them: himself, by committing a sin of a kind on which the religions agree that it is a major sin; and his master, who trusted him with his household and trusted her with herself, since he took her as a wife and kept her chaste.

*Al-hamm* is resolve to act. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿and they plotted what they could not attain﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74] in Sūrat Barāʾah. The resolve of hers is emphasized with *qad* and the oath-*lām* to convey that she resolved firmly and in earnest.

The clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ begins a fresh, independent statement. The intended meaning is that she was serious in what she sought from him, not testing him. The purpose of mentioning her desire for him is to prepare for the mention of the absence of his desire for her, in order to explain the difference between their two states in religion, since he was protected from sin.

The clause ﴿and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ is coordinated with the whole clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾. It is not coordinated with the clause *hammat* ("she desired"), which is the answer to the oath implied by the *lām*.

[Page 253]

Because the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ is followed by the clause introduced by *lawlā* ("had it not been"), which is exclusively about Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) own state and not about the state of the ʿAzīz's wife, it is evident that there is no connection between the two clauses. Hence the second clause is independent, since the condition of *lawlā* pertains to the state of the subject in it. The sense is: "And had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her." The answer was placed before its condition for emphasis. He did not attach the answer to the *lām* that frequently accompanies the answer to *lawlā*, because it is not obligatory, and because, since it was placed before *lawlā*, it was disliked to attach it to the *lām* before the mention of the conditional particle. Therefore it is good to pause at His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ so that the meaning of a new beginning with the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ appears clearly. By this it becomes evident that no desire for the ʿAzīz's wife ever touched Yūsuf (peace be upon him), because God protected him from desiring sin by what He showed him of the proof.

Abū Ḥātim said: "I used to read the strange words of the Qur'an to Abū ʿUbaydah, and when I came to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾ and so on, Abū ʿUbaydah said: 'This is in the order of anteriority and posteriority (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*), that is, the placing of the answer before the condition and the postponing of the condition; as if he said: "And she certainly desired him, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her."'"

al-Ṭabarī criticized this interpretation, on the grounds that the answer of *lawlā* does not precede it. What repels this criticism is that when Abū ʿUbaydah said that, we know that he did not see a prohibition on placing the answer of *lawlā* first. Moreover, he may make what is mentioned before *lawlā* an indication of the answer, with the answer being omitted due to what precedes *lawlā* indicating it. There is no escape from this under any reading, since *lawlā* and its condition restrict his saying "and he would have desired her" under all interpretations, so whatever answer is supposed is supposed under all interpretations.

A group said: Yūsuf desired to yield to her in what she invited him to, then he drew back and refrained from it when he saw the proof of his Lord. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Ibn Abī Mulaykah, and Tha'lab. The explanation of this is that he turned away from what he desired by God's protection or His infallibility; and desiring an evil deed while refraining from carrying it out is not a major sin, so it does not contradict the infallibility of the prophets from major sins before prophethood, according to those who hold that they were infallible from them before prophethood, which is the view of the majority.

[Page 254]

There is a difference of opinion on this, and for this reason Ibn ʿAbbās permitted this concerning Yūsuf. A group said: Yūsuf desired and began to prepare for it, then he saw a proof that turned him away from it, so he desisted. This is the view of al-Suddī, and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās. It returns to what we have explained in the previous view.

The author of *al-Kashshāf* erred in attaching these reports to those he calls *al-Ḥashwiyyah* and *al-Mujabbirah*, by which he means the Ashʿarites. He averted his gaze from the names of those to whom these interpretations are attributed, "He threw his own disease at me and slipped away." He also did not marvel at the consensus of all on the attempt of Yūsuf's brothers (peace be upon him) to kill him, and killing is more grave.

The seeing (*al-ruʾyah*) here is cognitive (*ʿilmiyyah*), because the proof (*burhān*) is among the meanings that are not seen by the eye.

*Al-burhān* is the argument. This proof is included in it: its turning him away from desire for her. Had it not been for that, the state of human nature would not have been free from desiring to comply with her in that situation, because of the abundance of motives for desire arising from her beauty, her eagerness for him, the delight of such men in obeying her, nearness to her, and the impulses of youth that make it appealing. Thus God's proof was the barrier between him and desire for her, and nothing else.

The commentators differed about what this proof is. Some of them indicate that it is a theoretical argument that made this act abhorrent to him. It was said: it is divine revelation. It was said: divine protection. It was said: visions that appeared to him.

The indication in His saying ﴿Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾ refers to something understood from what precedes it, which is implied by His saying ﴿he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, namely the seeing of the proof. That is: We showed him that seeing in this manner so that We might turn away from him evil.

*Al-ṣarf* is the transfer of a thing from one place to another. Here it is used metaphorically for protection from a thing's arriving at the place where it would normally arrive. The turning away is used to express infallibility from something that is about to befall him.

[Page 255]

The expression of infallibility by "turning away" indicates that the causes of the occurrence of evil and immorality were present, but God turned them away from him.

*Al-sūʾ* is the ugly thing, and it is the betrayal of one who entrusted him. *Al-faḥshāʾ* is the disobedience, and it is adultery. *Al-sūʾ* and *al-faḥshāʾ* were mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] in Sūrat al-Baqarah. The meaning of "He turned both away from him" is that He turned away his involvement with them.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿Indeed he is among Our sincere servants﴾ gives the reason for the wisdom of diverting him from evil and indecency, a diversion that went beyond the normal course of things, so that God's choosing of him would not be diminished in this severe test to the self.

Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar and Khalaf read *al-mukhlaṣīn* with a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, meaning those whom God has made sincere and chosen. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read it with a *kasrah* on the *lām*, meaning those who make their religion sincerely for God. The sense of the causal clause is one under both readings.

*Al-istibāq* (racing one another) is a *iftiʿāl* form from *al-sabq* (precedence). It was mentioned just before, and here it indicates that each of them was forcing himself to race, that is, each was trying to be the first to the door.

*Al-bāb* (the door) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. Its original form was *wa-istabaqā ilā al-bāb* ("and they raced to the door"), like ﴿Mūsā chose from his people seventy men﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 155], meaning "from his people." Or the verb *istabaqā* is taken to include the meaning of *ibtadarā* (hastened).

The definite article in *al-bāb* is the definite article of the category, since there were several closed doors. Yūsuf, peace be upon him, fled from her solicitation toward the door, wishing to open it and go out, while she wished to get ahead of him to the door to prevent him from opening it.

The clause ﴿and she tore his shirt﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). *Qadda* means *qaṭaʿa* (cut), that is, she cut from it a rent. This happened before the racing, without doubt, because if the tearing of the shirt had occurred during the racing, there would have been no evidence in it for the truthfulness of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, that she had solicited him. The tearing during the racing indicates no more than that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, had raced ahead of her, hastening to the door. This shows that she had seized him by his shirt when he turned away from her, wishing [p. 256] to force him into what she had solicited. He pulled himself free, and the shirt was torn by the force of the pull. The cutting of the shirt was from behind, because he was turning away from her, fleeing and averting himself, so she seized him by it to turn him back from his aversion.

The concision of the verse has excellently gathered all these meanings under the phrase ﴿they raced to the door and she tore his shirt﴾.

It happened that they found her master, that is, her husband, al-ʿAzīz, at the outer door, wishing to enter the house through the outer door. The use of "master" (*sayyid*) for the husband: it has been said that the Qurʾān related the custom of the Copts at that time, that they called the husband "sayyid." The apparent meaning is that this was not in use in the custom of the Arabs, so the expression here is one of the fine historical details, like His saying later ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ [Yūsuf: 76]. Perhaps marriage in Egypt in that era was mostly by way of ownership.

It is known from the discourse that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, opened the doors that Zulaykhā had locked, one door after another, until he reached the outer one. All of that happened during their racing, and this is concision.

*Al-ilfāʾ* (finding) is the obtaining of a thing in a particular state without seeking to obtain it. Most often it is sudden, or it occurs through ignorance of its first occurrence, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Rather we will follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170].

The clause ﴿She said: "What is the recompense..."﴾ and so on is a resumptive clause of explanation (*mustaʾnafah bayānīyah*), because the listener asks: what happened at the moment of her master's surprise while they were in that state?

She rushed to speak to him, persisting in slander, in such a way that she did not stammer. She made him imagine that she was in the right, and she poured the speech into a universal mould so that it would take the form of a law, and it would be a principle whose intended object is not known, so the addressee has no choice but to acknowledge it for her. Perhaps she feared that al-ʿAzīz's love for Yūsuf, peace be upon him, would prevent him from punishing him, so she poured her speech into a universal mould. She wanted by this that her husband should not perceive that she was in love with someone other than her master, and that she should frighten Yūsuf, peace be upon him, with her scheming, so that he would not refuse her again.

She set Yūsuf, peace be upon him, between two kinds of punishment, which are: prison, that is, confinement. Confinement was an ancient punishment in that era, and it continued until the time of Mūsā, peace be upon him, for Pharaoh said to Mūsā, peace be upon him, ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 29].

As for punishment (*ʿadhāb*), it is of various kinds, and it is an older punishment in the terminology of mankind. Among it are beating and inflicting pain by fire and by cutting off limbs. The mention of prison will come in this sūrah repeatedly.

The clause ﴿He said: "It was she who solicited me against myself"﴾ is part of the speech of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, and it is separated (*faṣl*) because it comes in the manner of a reply to her speech. The variation of the expression between ﴿that he be imprisoned, or a painful punishment﴾, without saying "except prison or a punishment," is because the word *al-sijn* is applied to the place in which the prisoner is put, and it is applied to the verbal noun of *sajana*. So His saying ﴿that he be imprisoned﴾ is clearer in showing the governing of the meaning of the verb over him.

Placing the subject before its predicate, which is a verb, gives restriction (*qaṣr*), and this is a restriction by reversal (*qaṣr qalb*), as a rebuttal to her.

With al-ʿAzīz was a man from among his wife's people, and he is the one who gave testimony, and he was perceptive, knowing the aspects of evidence.

His saying was called testimony (*shahādah*) because it tends toward the manifestation of the truth in establishing the transgression of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, against his mistress, or refuting it. This is judgment by clear circumstantial evidence (*al-qarīnah al-bayyinah*), because if she had held his garment in order to seize him and punish him, that would have occurred when he was facing her and approaching her. Then if he wished to slip away from her, his shirt would have been torn at the front, and conversely if his being held was while he was fleeing and turning away. There is no doubt that the reasoning by the manner of tearing the shirt arose from the mention of the wife of al-ʿAzīz of the occurrence of the tearing of the shirt, as she was trying to make it a proof that she had seized him in order to punish him. Had it not been for that, it would not have occurred to the witness that a tearing had happened, for otherwise from where would the witness have known the tearing of the shirt? The apparent meaning is that the witness was thinking of her truthfulness, so he wished to set up a proof of her truthfulness, but the opposite of that happened, as an honour for Yūsuf, peace be upon him.

[p. 258] The clause ﴿If his shirt has been torn from the front﴾ explains the verb *shahida* (testified).

The addition of ﴿and he is of the liars﴾ after ﴿she is truthful﴾, and the addition of ﴿and he is of the truthful﴾ after ﴿she is lying﴾, is an emphasis for increasing the establishment of the truth, as is the case with rulings.

The particles of condition indicate no more than the linking and causal relation between the content of their protasis and the content of their apodosis, without restriction to the future or to the past. So the meaning of ﴿If his shirt was torn from the front, she has spoken truly﴾ and what follows it is: if that happened in the past, then her truthfulness happened in the past.

The one who saw his shirt torn from behind and said, "Indeed it is of your scheming," is without doubt al-ʿAzīz. It had become clear to him that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, was innocent of assaulting the woman, so he was content with blaming his wife, saying that her accusation against him was of the scheming of women. So the plural feminine pronoun is an address to her, and it included those of her class by treating them as the townswomen (*ḥawāḍir*).

*Al-kayd* (scheming) is doing a thing in a form other than what is intended, in order to reach an intended end. It has been discussed before at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed My scheme is firm﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 183], in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

Then he commanded Yūsuf, peace be upon him, to turn away from what she had charged him with, that is, not to hold her to account for it, and to refrain from returning to discuss it. And he commanded his wife to seek forgiveness for her sin, that is, for her accusation of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, of boldness and assault against her.

The exegetes said: al-ʿAzīz was little given to jealousy. It was said: he was forbearing and wise. Perhaps he was infatuated with her, or the semblance of ownership lessened the blame on a woman for soliciting her slave. This is what is indicated by the state of her solicitation of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, when she rushed him with her words "Come, you," as has been discussed just before.

[p. 259] *Al-khāṭiʾ* is the doer of a sin (*khaṭīʾah*), which is a crime. He placed her among the group of those who erred, lightening the blame on her. The form of the masculine plural is by predominance (*taghlīb*).

The clause ﴿Yūsuf, turn away from this﴾ is part of the speech of al-ʿAzīz, since he is the possessor of the judgment.

The clause ﴿and seek forgiveness for your sin﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Yūsuf, turn away﴾ in the speech of al-ʿAzīz, as a conjunction of command upon command where the one commanded differs. The feminine second-person *kāf* is definitely an address to the wife of al-ʿAzīz. So al-ʿAzīz, after addressing her that what she had devised was of the scheming of women, directed the address to Yūsuf, peace be upon him, by calling him, then returned the address to the woman.

This manner of address is called *al-iqbāl* (turning toward), and it may be called *al-iltifāt* (turning) in the linguistic sense when it is the rhetorical *iltifāt*, and it is rare in eloquent speech. From it is the saying of al-Jarmī, of the Ṭayy, one of the poets of the *Ḥamāsah*:

I suppose you are my appointee at Bunniyy Jufayf and Hālah; indeed I forbid you, O Hālah.

Al-Marzūqī said in his commentary on the *Ḥamāsah*: The Arabs gather several people in address and report, then turn or direct their attention from among them to one, because he is the greatest of them, or the best of them in hearing, and the most particular of them in the matter.

**[Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr, *al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr*, on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29, part 1]**

﴿The woman in whose house he was sought him to yield himself to her, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "God forbid! He is my Lord; he has given me the best residence. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper."﴾ ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ ﴿And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her master at the door. She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿He said, "It was she who sought me to yield myself to her." And a witness from her own family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars.﴾ ﴿But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said, "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ ﴿"Yūsuf, turn away from this, and [you, woman], ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners."﴾

This is the attaching of one narrative to another (ʿaṭf qiṣṣah ʿalā qiṣṣah), so it does not necessarily follow that this narrative occurred in time after the one preceding it. This incident occurred before Yūsuf was given prophethood, since the bestowal of prophethood generally occurs at the age of forty. The more evident view is that he was granted prophethood and messengerhood after his family entered Egypt and after the death of his father. The verses have addressed the establishment of Yūsuf's steadfastness (peace be upon him) in chastity, fidelity, and nobility of character.

[Page 250]

Thus *murāwadah* (seeking to persuade or seduce), which requires repeated attempts, is expressed in the form of *mufāʿalah* (the verbal form implying reciprocity), and *mufāʿalah* is used to indicate repetition. It has been said that the *mufāʿalah* here is notional (*taqdīriyyah*), in that the action from one side and the resistance from the other side are considered as an action countered by a similar action. The word *murāwadah* derives from *rāda yarūdu*, meaning to come and go. The state of one who repeatedly tries to get someone to do something is compared to the state of one who goes back and forth in returning to the thing one has turned away from; thus *rāwada* is used in the sense of *ḥāwala* (to attempt).

*ʿAn* here indicates separation (*mujāwazah*), meaning that she sought him, distancing him from himself, that is, that he should make himself hers. Apparently this construction is one of the Qur'an's original expressions. The word "self" (*nafs*) here is a metonymy for the purpose of intercourse, as Ibn ʿAṭiyyah stated: thus "self" refers to his chastity and her enabling herself to have what she wanted from him, as though she were seeking to have him surrender his will and his judgment over himself.

As for its construction with *ʿalā* ("upon"), that indicates the thing whose attainment is sought. In the saying of Abū Hurayrah, it occurred that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was urging his uncle Abū Ṭālib toward Islam." And in the hadith of the Night Journey, Mūsā said to him: "I had tried (*rāwadtu*) the Children of Israel for less than that, and they abandoned it."

The expression referring to the wife of the ʿAzīz by way of the relative clause, in His saying ﴿the one in whose house he was﴾, is intended for what the relative clause implies of affirming Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) infallibility, because his being in her house is of a nature that would make him submit to her desire.

*Baytihā* ("her house") is the house of her residence in which she spends the night. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ is that at that time he was in the house where she was. It is also possible that the intended "house" is the whole dwelling, which is the palace of the ʿAzīz. From this comes the saying "*rabbat al-bayt*" (the mistress of the house), meaning the wife of the head of the household. The meaning of ﴿he was in her house﴾ would then be that he was among the dependents of that dwelling.

Closing the doors (*ghalq al-abwāb*) means placing each door so as to block the opening through which one enters.

The doubling in *ghallaqat* serves to express the intensity and strength of the action, meaning that they were closed firmly and securely.

[Page 251]

*Al-abwāb* is the plural of *bāb* (door), and it was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Enter upon them through the door﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 23].

*Hayta* is a verb-form noun (*ism fiʿl*) meaning "hurry" or "make haste." It is said that its origin is from the Hauranian language, which is Nabataean. It is also said that it is from the Hebrew language.

The *lām* in *laka* serves to clarify the intended addressee of the address, as in their saying "*suqyan laka*" (watering to you) and "*shukran laka*" (thanks to you). Its original form is *hayta-ka*. It appears that she asked of him something that was not unusual in their palaces, namely that a woman enjoy her servant as a man enjoys his female slave. For this reason she did not first approach him with an enticement, but began by offering herself to him. The matter will be further clarified when we reach His saying: ﴿She said, "What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your wife…"﴾.

There are several readings of *Hayta*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Dhakwān (on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir), and Abū Jaʿfar read it with a *kasrah* on the *hāʾ* and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hīta*). Ibn Kathīr read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ* (*Haytu*). The rest read it with a *fatḥah* on the *hāʾ*, a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* (*Hayta*). The *fatḥah* and *ḍammah* are indeclinable vowels (*ḥarakatā bināʾ*).

*Maʿādh* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that is annexed to the Name of Majesty (Allāh) in the manner in which a verbal noun is annexed to its object. Its original form is "*aʿūdhu ʿawdhan billāh*," meaning "I seek refuge in God," that is, I take refuge in Him from what you are attempting. Its explanation will come when we reach His saying: ﴿He said, "God forbid that we take…"﴾ [Yūsuf: 79] in this sūrah.

*Inna* here conveys the reason for what ﴿God forbid!﴾ conveys of refusal and seeking refuge in God from it, which implies that God commanded that seeking of refuge.

The pronoun in *innahu* ("indeed he") may refer to the Name of Majesty, in which case *rabbī* means "my Creator." It may also refer to something known from the context, namely her husband, who would not be content for anyone else to touch her; he is known from customary understanding, and in that case *rabbī* means "my master" and "my owner."

This is speech that has been eloquently directed in a manner by which the words of Yūsuf (peace be upon him) are reported; either because Yūsuf (peace be upon him) used such a construction in the language of the Copts, or because he gave two excuses for his refusal, and the Qur'an reports them with brevity and allusion.

[Page 252]

Whichever is the case, the statement is an explanation of his refusal and an allusion to her for betraying her pledge.

In this statement there is a great lesson in chastity and piety, and the infallibility of the prophets before prophethood from the major sins.

The mention of the description of the Lord under both possibilities indicates the obligation of obeying Him and being thankful for the blessing of creation with respect to God, and for the blessing of upbringing with respect to his noble master.

He confirmed this by describing it with the clause ﴿He has given me the best residence﴾, meaning: He made my final state good, since He rescued me from destruction, or He honored my care. The explanation of *al-mathwā* (residence) has been given just above.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾ is a second reason for the refusal. The pronoun that is made the subject of *inna* is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), which conveys the importance of the clause made its predicate, because it is a comprehensive admonition. It also indicates that answering her solicitation is wrongdoing, because in it there is the wronging of both of them: himself, by committing a sin of a kind on which the religions agree that it is a major sin; and his master, who trusted him with his household and trusted her with herself, since he took her as a wife and kept her chaste.

*Al-hamm* is resolve to act. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿and they plotted what they could not attain﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74] in Sūrat Barāʾah. The resolve of hers is emphasized with *qad* and the oath-*lām* to convey that she resolved firmly and in earnest.

The clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ begins a fresh, independent statement. The intended meaning is that she was serious in what she sought from him, not testing him. The purpose of mentioning her desire for him is to prepare for the mention of the absence of his desire for her, in order to explain the difference between their two states in religion, since he was protected from sin.

The clause ﴿and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ is coordinated with the whole clause ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾. It is not coordinated with the clause *hammat* ("she desired"), which is the answer to the oath implied by the *lām*.

[Page 253]

Because the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ is followed by the clause introduced by *lawlā* ("had it not been"), which is exclusively about Yūsuf's (peace be upon him) own state and not about the state of the ʿAzīz's wife, it is evident that there is no connection between the two clauses. Hence the second clause is independent, since the condition of *lawlā* pertains to the state of the subject in it. The sense is: "And had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her." The answer was placed before its condition for emphasis. He did not attach the answer to the *lām* that frequently accompanies the answer to *lawlā*, because it is not obligatory, and because, since it was placed before *lawlā*, it was disliked to attach it to the *lām* before the mention of the conditional particle. Therefore it is good to pause at His saying ﴿And she certainly desired him﴾ so that the meaning of a new beginning with the clause ﴿and he would have desired her﴾ appears clearly. By this it becomes evident that no desire for the ʿAzīz's wife ever touched Yūsuf (peace be upon him), because God protected him from desiring sin by what He showed him of the proof.

Abū Ḥātim said: "I used to read the strange words of the Qur'an to Abū ʿUbaydah, and when I came to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾ and so on, Abū ʿUbaydah said: 'This is in the order of anteriority and posteriority (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*), that is, the placing of the answer before the condition and the postponing of the condition; as if he said: "And she certainly desired him, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her."'"

al-Ṭabarī criticized this interpretation, on the grounds that the answer of *lawlā* does not precede it. What repels this criticism is that when Abū ʿUbaydah said that, we know that he did not see a prohibition on placing the answer of *lawlā* first. Moreover, he may make what is mentioned before *lawlā* an indication of the answer, with the answer being omitted due to what precedes *lawlā* indicating it. There is no escape from this under any reading, since *lawlā* and its condition restrict his saying "and he would have desired her" under all interpretations, so whatever answer is supposed is supposed under all interpretations.

A group said: Yūsuf desired to yield to her in what she invited him to, then he drew back and refrained from it when he saw the proof of his Lord. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Ibn Abī Mulaykah, and Tha'lab. The explanation of this is that he turned away from what he desired by God's protection or His infallibility; and desiring an evil deed while refraining from carrying it out is not a major sin, so it does not contradict the infallibility of the prophets from major sins before prophethood, according to those who hold that they were infallible from them before prophethood, which is the view of the majority.

[Page 254]

There is a difference of opinion on this, and for this reason Ibn ʿAbbās permitted this concerning Yūsuf. A group said: Yūsuf desired and began to prepare for it, then he saw a proof that turned him away from it, so he desisted. This is the view of al-Suddī, and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās. It returns to what we have explained in the previous view.

The author of *al-Kashshāf* erred in attaching these reports to those he calls *al-Ḥashwiyyah* and *al-Mujabbirah*, by which he means the Ashʿarites. He averted his gaze from the names of those to whom these interpretations are attributed, "He threw his own disease at me and slipped away." He also did not marvel at the consensus of all on the attempt of Yūsuf's brothers (peace be upon him) to kill him, and killing is more grave.

The seeing (*al-ruʾyah*) here is cognitive (*ʿilmiyyah*), because the proof (*burhān*) is among the meanings that are not seen by the eye.

*Al-burhān* is the argument. This proof is included in it: its turning him away from desire for her. Had it not been for that, the state of human nature would not have been free from desiring to comply with her in that situation, because of the abundance of motives for desire arising from her beauty, her eagerness for him, the delight of such men in obeying her, nearness to her, and the impulses of youth that make it appealing. Thus God's proof was the barrier between him and desire for her, and nothing else.

The commentators differed about what this proof is. Some of them indicate that it is a theoretical argument that made this act abhorrent to him. It was said: it is divine revelation. It was said: divine protection. It was said: visions that appeared to him.

The indication in His saying ﴿Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾ refers to something understood from what precedes it, which is implied by His saying ﴿he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, namely the seeing of the proof. That is: We showed him that seeing in this manner so that We might turn away from him evil.

*Al-ṣarf* is the transfer of a thing from one place to another. Here it is used metaphorically for protection from a thing's arriving at the place where it would normally arrive. The turning away is used to express infallibility from something that is about to befall him.

[Page 255]

The expression of infallibility by "turning away" indicates that the causes of the occurrence of evil and immorality were present, but God turned them away from him.

*Al-sūʾ* is the ugly thing, and it is the betrayal of one who entrusted him. *Al-faḥshāʾ* is the disobedience, and it is adultery. *Al-sūʾ* and *al-faḥshāʾ* were mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] in Sūrat al-Baqarah. The meaning of "He turned both away from him" is that He turned away his involvement with them.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Sūrat Yūsuf, verses 23–29 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿Indeed he is among Our sincere servants﴾ gives the reason for the wisdom of diverting him from evil and indecency, a diversion that went beyond the normal course of things, so that God's choosing of him would not be diminished in this severe test to the self.

Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar and Khalaf read *al-mukhlaṣīn* with a *fatḥah* on the *lām*, meaning those whom God has made sincere and chosen. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read it with a *kasrah* on the *lām*, meaning those who make their religion sincerely for God. The sense of the causal clause is one under both readings.

*Al-istibāq* (racing one another) is a *iftiʿāl* form from *al-sabq* (precedence). It was mentioned just before, and here it indicates that each of them was forcing himself to race, that is, each was trying to be the first to the door.

*Al-bāb* (the door) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. Its original form was *wa-istabaqā ilā al-bāb* ("and they raced to the door"), like ﴿Mūsā chose from his people seventy men﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 155], meaning "from his people." Or the verb *istabaqā* is taken to include the meaning of *ibtadarā* (hastened).

The definite article in *al-bāb* is the definite article of the category, since there were several closed doors. Yūsuf, peace be upon him, fled from her solicitation toward the door, wishing to open it and go out, while she wished to get ahead of him to the door to prevent him from opening it.
