**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 12, verses 33–34:**

﴿He said: "My Lord, the prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me. And unless You turn away from me their plotting, I would incline toward them and be among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿So his Lord answered him and turned away from him their plotting. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

This is a *isti'naf bayani* (an explanatory resumptive clause, one that anticipates a question in the listener's mind). The narrative just related is a situation of great severity, so the listener would naturally ask about Yusuf's state (peace be upon him) when faced with the words of the wife of the 'Aziz.

This statement is a private supplication (*munajah*) to his Lord, who is their witness, so the apparent meaning is that he said this within himself. It is also possible that he uttered it aloud in their presence, in order to make them despair of his doing what she commanded.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read *al-sijnu* with a kasra on the *sin*. Ya'qub alone read it with a fatha on the *sin*, understanding it as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: "Indeed, imprisonment is dearer to me." He preferred imprisonment, with its pain, hardship and constriction of the soul, over what they invited him to, namely enjoying the beautiful and precious woman with the pleasure that this entails. Yet his aversion to committing what is forbidden outweighed for him the endurance of imprisonment. When he knew that there was no escape from one of the two matters, imprisonment became beloved to him insofar as it would save him from falling into what is forbidden. This love arises from the agreement of the mind, like the love of the brave warrior for war.

Thus the report that imprisonment is dearer to him than enjoying the woman is used to create contentment with imprisonment for the sake of God's good pleasure (exalted is He) and distance from what He has forbidden, since there is no benefit in informing One who knows what is in the soul. Therefore the superlative (*ism al-tafdil*) is taken in its literal sense, and there is no need to interpret it as a negation of comparison.

[Page 266 continues]

He expressed what the woman proposed with the relative form (*al-mawsuliyyah*), because of what the relative clause implies: that what is sought is a state which is likely to lead to compliance. For when people are united in requesting something, this tends to prepare the one requested to do it. So he showed that their unanimous request of him did not blunt the sharpness of his resolve to refuse, even though it was the command of the woman that was being carried out. He made this a preface to his request for protection (*'ismah*) from falling into the snare of their plotting. Thus he moved from mentioning the contentment (of the woman) with imprisonment, as her threat, to asking for protection from her plotting.

He attributed the verb ﴿yad'unani﴾ to the feminine plural *nun* (*nun al-niswah*). The *waw* in it is then a root letter, not the *waw* of the masculine plural, and the *nun* is not the *nun* of the nominative, since the verb is then *mabni* (indeclinable) because of its connection to the feminine plural *nun*. Its form is *yaf'alna*. The verb is attributed to the plural pronoun of women, although the one who invited him was a single woman. This is either because that invitation stems from the desires of the category of women, and so it follows the pattern of the plural pronoun in ﴿kaydahunna﴾, or because the women whom the wife of the 'Aziz had gathered, when they heard her words, united in blaming Yusuf (peace be upon him), urging him to respond to the one who invited him, and warning him against her threat of imprisonment. By the same pattern, the discussion of the plural pronoun in ﴿kaydahunna﴾ is that it refers to the plotting of the category of women, like the saying of the 'Aziz: ﴿Indeed, your plotting is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28], meaning the plotting of these women.

The clause ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plotting﴾ is a statement (*khabar*) used to express apprehension and expectation, as a turning to God and a maintaining of proper conduct toward his Lord, by disavowing power and strength, and by fear of the fluctuation of the heart and of the temptation toward the forbidden pleasure. The statement is therefore used as a supplication. For this reason, the clause ﴿So his Lord answered him﴾ is derived from it.

The meaning of *asbu* is "I incline." *Al-sabw* is inclination toward what is loved.

*Al-jahiliyyun* are those foolish in their judgment (*sufaha' al-ahlam*), so ignorance here is the opposite of forbearance (*hilm*). As for the statement that the intensive form in ﴿and be among the ignorant﴾ is stronger than "and be ignorant," it is like the statement regarding ﴿and he will surely be among the humbled﴾ [Yusuf: 32].

[Page 267]

The conjunction of the clause ﴿So he answered﴾ with the *fa'* of sequence (*fa' al-ta'qib*) indicates that God hastened the answer to his supplication, which was contained in his words: ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plotting﴾. *Istajaba* is an intensive form of *ajaba*, as was mentioned earlier in the words ﴿So he sought protection﴾ [Yusuf: 32].

Turning away their plotting from him means turning away its effect: He made him steadfast in chastity, so he was not deceived by her plotting, nor by the plotting of her female companions, even in the most constricted moments.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is in the position of a cause (*'illah*) for the verb ﴿istajaba﴾ conjoined with the *fa'* of sequence. That is: He answered his supplication without delay, because He is swift to respond and knows the sincere intentions. *Al-sam'* (hearing) here is used for answering the request, as one says: "God hears whoever praises Him." Its emphasis by the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) is to affirm this meaning.

For when people are united in requesting something, this tends to prepare the one requested to do it. So he showed that their unanimous request of him did not blunt the sharpness of his resolve to refuse, even though it was the command of the woman that was being carried out. He made this a preface to his request for protection (*'ismah*) from falling into the snare of their plotting. Thus he moved from mentioning the contentment (of the woman) with imprisonment, as her threat, to asking for protection from her plotting.

He attributed the verb ﴿yad'unani﴾ to the feminine plural *nun* (*nun al-niswah*). The *waw* in it is then a root letter, not the *waw* of the masculine plural, and the *nun* is not the *nun* of the nominative, since the verb is then *mabni* (indeclinable) because of its connection to the feminine plural *nun*. Its form is *yaf'alna*. The verb is attributed to the plural pronoun of women, although the one who invited him was a single woman. This is either because that invitation stems from the desires of the category of women, and so it follows the pattern of the plural pronoun in ﴿kaydahunna﴾, or because the women whom the wife of the 'Aziz had gathered, when they heard her words, united in blaming Yusuf (peace be upon him), urging him to respond to the one who invited him, and warning him against her threat of imprisonment. By the same pattern, the discussion of the plural pronoun in ﴿kaydahunna﴾ is that it refers to the plotting of the category of women, like the saying of the 'Aziz: ﴿Indeed, your plotting is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28], meaning the plotting of these women.

The clause ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plotting﴾ is a statement (*khabar*) used to express apprehension and expectation, as a turning to God and a maintaining of proper conduct toward his Lord, by disavowing power and strength, and by fear of the fluctuation of the heart and of the temptation toward the forbidden pleasure. The statement is therefore used as a supplication. For this reason, the clause ﴿So his Lord answered him﴾ is derived from it.

The meaning of *asbu* is "I incline." *Al-sabw* is inclination toward what is loved.

*Al-jahiliyyun* are those foolish in their judgment (*sufaha' al-ahlam*), so ignorance here is the opposite of forbearance (*hilm*). As for the statement that the intensive form in ﴿and be among the ignorant﴾ is stronger than "and be ignorant," it is like the statement regarding ﴿and he will surely be among the humbled﴾ [Yusuf: 32].

[Page 267]

The conjunction of the clause ﴿So he answered﴾ with the *fa'* of sequence (*fa' al-ta'qib*) indicates that God hastened the answer to his supplication, which was contained in his words: ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plotting﴾. *Istajaba* is an intensive form of *ajaba*, as was mentioned earlier in the words ﴿So he sought protection﴾ [Yusuf: 32].

Turning away their plotting from him means turning away its effect: He made him steadfast in chastity, so he was not deceived by her plotting, nor by the plotting of her female companions, even in the most constricted moments.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is in the position of a cause (*'illah*) for the verb ﴿istajaba﴾ conjoined with the *fa'* of sequence. That is: He answered his supplication without delay, because He is swift to respond and knows the sincere intentions. *Al-sam'* (hearing) here is used for answering the request, as one says: "God hears whoever praises Him." Its emphasis by the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) is to affirm this meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 35:

﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.﴾

Thumma here denotes sequence in rank (al-tartib al-rutbi), as is its usual function when conjoining sentences, for what occurred to them was more astonishing after his innocence had been established. What occurred to them was to imprison Yusuf (peace be upon him) when the rumour about the wife of al-'Aziz concerning him spread. This happened right after the women dispersed, because she feared that if they left, the rumour would spread concerning her and concerning the innocence of Yusuf (peace be upon him). So she sought to cover that up by imprisoning Yusuf (peace be upon him), so that he would appear in the guise of the wrongdoers who intended evil with the wife of al-'Aziz, and she aimed by this to make him submit to her. Perhaps she wanted to give people the impression that his solicitation of her had taken place on the day of that gathering, and to make them think that the women were witnesses against Yusuf (peace be upon him).

The pronoun in lahum refers to the group of al-'Aziz's people, from advisers and commanders.

The clause ﴿la-yasjununnahu﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and it suspends the verb badā from acting on what follows it because of the oath particle, since what follows the oath particle is a new statement. In this there is evidence for the omitted object, for the correct view is that suspension (ta'liq) is not restricted to verbs of thinking; this is the position of Yunus ibn Habib, because the cause of suspension is the presence of a particle that has the initial position in the sentence. This verse is evidence for it.

The estimate is: "What indicates this oath occurred to them", that is, the resolve to imprison him occurred to them.

In al-Mughni, at the end of the discussion of clauses that have a place in i'rab, he mentions the disagreement over whether the agent (al-fa'il) and the deputy agent (na'ib al-fa'il) can be a clause. Hisham and Tha'lab permitted it without restriction, while al-Farra' and a group permitted it when the verb is of the heart and a suspending element is present, and they interpreted the verse accordingly; this is attributed to Sibawayh. It returns to the meaning of suspension, and suspension is more fitting to the meaning.

Al-hin: a period of indeterminate duration. If ﴿hatta hin﴾ is part of their speech, the meaning is that they ordered his imprisonment without a fixed term. If it is part of the narration, the Qur'an has left vague the period up to which they permitted his imprisonment, since the purpose of the story does not depend on it.

Al-ayat: indications of the truthfulness of Yusuf (peace be upon him) and the falsehood of the wife of al-'Aziz.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 36:

﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men. One of them said, "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine." And the other said, "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread upon my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good."﴾ All the readers agreed on the kasra of the sin in "al-sijn" here, meaning the house in which one is imprisoned; because entering (dukhul) is not appropriately connected except to a place, not to a verbal noun (masdar).

These two young men were the cupbearer of the king and his baker. The king became angry with them and ordered them imprisoned. It was said: they were accused of poisoning the king in his drink and his food.

The clause ﴿qala ahaduhuma﴾ ("one of them said") is the beginning of a dialogue, as the verb of saying indicates.

Interpreting dreams was among the arts of their scholars, so God strengthened Yusuf, peace be upon him, through it among them.

These two young men perceived in Yusuf, peace be upon him, perfection of intellect and understanding, so they thought that he was good at interpreting dreams, though they had not known this about him before. They hit upon the correct judgment, and therefore they said ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good﴾, meaning: those who do good in interpretation, or those who do good in understanding.

Ihsan (excellence) is perfection (itqan). It is said: "He does not ihsan the recitation," meaning he does not perfect it. It is a custom of prisoners to recount the dreams they see, due to their lack of news, which are the means of conversation and dialogue, and because they seek omens regarding what may bring them good tidings of deliverance in the future. The science of dream interpretation was among the sciences practised by the priests of the Egyptians, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, quoting the king of Egypt: ﴿Explain to me my dream, if you are able to interpret dreams﴾ [Yusuf: 43], as will come later.

Al-'asr (pressing): applying pressure with the hand, or with a stone or the like, upon a moist thing in order to extract what is in it of liquid, oil or water. Al-'asir (juice): what is extracted from the pressed thing; it is named after its place, i.e. pressed from such-and-such.

Al-khubz (bread): the name for a piece of wheat or barley flour or the like, kneaded with water and placed near the fire until it is cooked for eating; it is also called raghif.

The pronoun in ﴿bi-ta'wilihi﴾ refers to what was mentioned, or to what was seen, considered as a genus.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we see you﴾ is a justification for the negation of what is implied by ﴿Inform us﴾.

"He said: 'No food will come to you as provision except that I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion (millah) of a people who do not believe in Allah and who, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers. And I have followed the religion of my forefathers: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon mankind, but most people do not give thanks.'"

The sentence "He said, no food will come to you" is a reply to their words, and it is therefore recounted in the manner of the recounting of dialogue sentences.

By this reply he intended to presume their turning towards him and their continued conversation with him, since they were awaiting his interpretation of the dream. Into this he weaves the call to them to true faith, together with the promise that he will interpret their dreams for them without long delay. He made for this a known time for them, which is the time of the bringing of the prisoners' food, since there are no events in the prison by which they could mark time. Moreover, the closing of the doors and the enclosing walls prevent them from seeing the sun, so they have no events other than the circumstances of their state, such as food, sleep, or waking from it.

It appears that the period until the food arrived at that time was not long, as indicated by his saying "before it comes to you," in that he hastens to give them the interpretation of their dreams and does not delay in this.

The description of the food by the clause "which you are provided with" is an explicit specification that it is food of a known time, not an awaited food that might be sent to them in an unpredictable manner.

The reality of provision (rizq) is that by which benefit is obtained, and it is applied to food, as in His saying: ﴿She found with her provision﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 37], meaning food, and His saying in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿or from what Allah has provided you﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], and His saying: ﴿They will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62]. It is also applied to customary expenditure, as in His saying: ﴿and provide for them therein and clothe them﴾ [al-Nisa': 5]. From here it is applied to a fixed grant; it is said: "the family of so-and-so were among the mercenary soldiers (murtaziqah al-jund), and the provision of the soldiers is such-and-such each day."

The pronoun in (bi-ta'wilihi) refers to what the first (bi-ta'wilihi) pronoun referred to, namely the vision or the dream. It should not refer to food, since it is not appropriate to apply the term ta'wil to the reporting of the names of kinds of food, contrary to what the majority of the exegetes (jumhur al-mufassirin) have taken.

The exception in His saying "except that I will inform you of its interpretation" is an exception from several states that suit the purpose, namely the state of informing about the interpretation of the dream and the state of its absence. That is, the customary food will not come except in a state in which I have already informed you of the interpretation of your dream, and not in a state of its absence. The restriction derived from the exception is therefore relative (idafi).

The clause of the state is stripped of the conjunction "wa" and "qad" even though it is in the past tense, being sufficient with the linking of the exception, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they do not cross a valley except that it is written for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 121].

The clause ﴿That is from what my Lord has taught me﴾ is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because his promise of interpreting the dream in a near time arouses the wonder of the askers about the strength of his knowledge and about the means by which this knowledge was obtained. So he answers that it is from what Allah taught him, as a way of reaching their call to belief in one God. The Copts were polytheists who held to the plurality of gods.

His saying "from what my Lord has taught me" is an indication that He taught him other sciences, namely the sciences of the Law, wisdom, economy and trustworthiness, as He said: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the earth; indeed, I am a guardian, knowing﴾ [Yusuf: 55].

He added to the explanatory resumption the clause ﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah﴾, because the report that Allah taught him the interpretation and other sciences raises the question of the means by which this knowledge was obtained. So he informed them that the reason for Allah's care for him was that he stood alone in that place in the oneness of Allah and left the religion of the people of the city. Allah therefore willed to choose him to guide them. It is permissible that the clause be a causal explanation.

The millah is the religion; it has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿a upright religion, the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ [al-An'am: 161] in Surat al-An'am.

By the people who do not believe in Allah he intended what includes the Canaanites among whom he grew up and the Copts among whom he was reared, as indicated by His saying: ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40]. Or he intended the Canaanites specifically, who were those among whom he grew up, as an allusion to the Copts who resembled them in associating partners with Allah. By this he intended not to confront them with harsh reproach, so as to lure in the bird of their aversion from his admonition.

The addition of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) in His saying "they are disbelievers" is intended to specify a group among them with this trait, namely the Canaanites, because they used to deny resurrection, like the disbelievers of the Arabs. By this he intended to exclude the Copts, for although the Copts were polytheists, they affirmed the resurrection of souls and recompense.

The tark (leaving) is the non-taking of a thing while being able to take it. By it he indicated that he did not follow the millah of the Copts despite dwelling among them and his master being devout in it.

He mentioned his forefathers as a teaching of their virtue, and as a manifestation of the precedence of righteousness in him, and that he is descended in a chain from his forefathers. He had understood this from the beginning of his upbringing, then he was strengthened by what his Lord taught him, so that he obtained through this both the nobility of lineage and the nobility of self-achievement. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ), when asked about the most noble of people, said: "Yusuf, son of Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, a prophet, son of a prophet, son of a prophet, son of a prophet." Such a chain in prophethood was not gathered for anyone other than Yusuf (peace be upon him), if by prophethood is meant its most perfect form, which is messengership, or if the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him) were not prophets according to the view of a group of scholars.

Ibn 'Ashur's words about the "pure" sense: he intended following the millah of his forefathers in its fundamentals before he was given prophethood, if what was revealed to him included an addition beyond what was revealed to his forefathers, such as the interpretation of dreams and economy; or that his prophethood was by revelation like what was revealed to his forefathers, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has ordained for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Nuh...﴾ [al-Shura: 13] up to His saying: ﴿Establish the religion and do not be divided therein﴾ [al-Shura: 13].

Mentioning the righteous predecessors in matters of truth increases the proof of truth in firmness, and mentioning their opposites in falsehood is intended to show the absence of proof in them by their mere status, as in His later saying: ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named, you and your fathers﴾ [Yusuf: 40].

The clause ﴿It was not for us to associate anything with Allah﴾ is in the force of an explanation of what the clause ﴿and I followed the religion of my forefathers﴾ implied, namely that monotheism had become like a disposition for them by which their forefathers were known among the nations, and he made them known to themselves by it in this opportunity. The force of the negation in the form of denial is not hidden: it indicates the emphatic negation of the attribute from the one described, as already mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should give him the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 79] in Surat Ali 'Imran, and at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, Exalted are You, it is not for me to say what I have no right to﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116] at the end of Surat al-'Uqud.

The "min" in His saying "min shay'" is extra, for the emphasis of the negation, and it is placed upon what is intended by the negation.

The clause ﴿That is from the bounty of Allah upon us﴾ is an addition to the resumption and explanation, aiming to encourage following the religion of monotheism by stating that it is a bounty.

His saying "and upon mankind" means those who follow them, and this is the intended object of the encouragement in the clause.

The istidrak (qualification) comes with His saying "but most people do not give thanks" to make clear that the condition of those addressed in their associating is the condition of one who denies the blessing of Allah, because sending guides is a blessing in which people should reflect, so that they know that what they are called to is good and a rescue for them from degradation in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, and because turning away from examining the proofs of the truthfulness of the messengers is disbelief in the blessing of reason and reflection.

**Page 275**

This is a resumptive (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that resumes the discourse) opening the address to the two young men by way of a call, which draws their attention to what he says in order to emphasise it.

He referred to them by the description "companions of the prison" rather than by their names. This is either because he did not know their names, since they had entered the prison with him at that very hour, before the companionship between them and him had lengthened, or to signal the bond that arose between them, namely the bond of sharing the same affliction, which creates intimacy in loneliness. Agreement in circumstances is a bond that takes the place of kinship, or even surpasses it.

The readers agreed on the kasra on the *sin* of **السِّجْنِ** here, with the meaning of the building in which those who are punished are imprisoned, because a companion (*sahib*) is only attributed to a prison in the sense of a place.

The attribution here is by implicit reckoning of the particle of location, like *makr al-layl* ("the cunning of the night"), meaning: "O two companions in the prison."

By the speech with which he addressed them he intended to make them acknowledge the falsehood of their religion, so the interrogative is a rhetorical question seeking affirmation. He arranged the argument for them in a rhetorical manner close to the understanding of the common people, for he posited for them one God, singular in divinity, as is the case of his own creed which he had informed them of. He then posited for them many scattered gods, each of whom disposes only of specific kinds of existing things under his authority, and does not overstep into what falls within the domain of another's authority. This is the case of the creed of the Copts.

Then he posited for them a comparison between the two states taken together: the state of the God who is alone in divinity, and the scattered states of the many gods, in order to bring them, by this, to be persuaded that the state of the one alone in divinity is greater and more self-sufficient, so that they would return from believing in a plurality of gods. The purpose of this argument is not to affirm the existence of the two states in divinity, nor the comparison between the holders of these two states, because those addressed do not believe in the existence of the one God.

This holds if the word **خَيْرٌ** (*khayr*, "better") is taken in its common, apparent sense, which is preference between things that share a quality. It is also possible that **خَيْرٌ** is used in the sense of what is good according to reason, that is, preponderance and acceptability. The meaning would then be: is the belief in the existence of scattered lords more preponderant, or the belief that there exists only one God? This is so as to draw down by it the bird of their reflection and reasoning until the corruption of the belief in a plurality of gods becomes clear to them, for it becomes evident to them that scattered lords cannot be free from corruption and disorder in their governance. This is indicated by the description of "scattered" in relation to plurality, and the description of "the Subduer" (*al-Qahhar*) in relation to unity.

The religion of the Copts in all the periods that history has preserved and that monuments have attested was a religion of polytheism (*shirk*), that is, a plurality of gods. The Chaldeans and the Assyrians, who made the gods symbols of the stars and planets, are in better condition than the Sabians.

So to God belongs the eloquence of the Qur'an, for it expressed their plurality by scattering, when it said ﴿Are scattered lords better, or God, the One, the Subduer?﴾

The meaning of restricting them to being names is a restriction of relative (*qasr idafi*, restriction relative to a specific counterpart), that they are names without named realities, so that in existence they have nothing but their names.

Its purpose is to refute their fathers, blocking the avenues of argument for the legitimacy of those gods on the ground that they were worshipped by their fathers, and also as an *idmaj* (embedding) to suggest an excuse to them, so that it would be easier for them to abandon the worship of many gods.

This is a resumptive (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that resumes the discourse) opening the address to the two young men by way of a call, which draws their attention to what he says in order to emphasise it.

He referred to them by the description "companions of the prison" rather than by their names. This is either because he did not know their names, since they had entered the prison with him at that very hour, before the companionship between them and him had lengthened, or to signal the bond that arose between them, namely the bond of sharing the same affliction, which creates intimacy in loneliness. Agreement in circumstances is a bond that takes the place of kinship, or even surpasses it.

The readers agreed on the kasra on the *sin* of **السِّجْنِ** here, with the meaning of the building in which those who are punished are imprisoned, because a companion (*sahib*) is only attributed to a prison in the sense of a place.

The attribution here is by implicit reckoning of the particle of location, like *makr al-layl* ("the cunning of the night"), meaning: "O two companions in the prison."

By the speech with which he addressed them he intended to make them acknowledge the falsehood of their religion, so the interrogative is a rhetorical question seeking affirmation. He arranged the argument for them in a rhetorical manner close to the understanding of the common people, for he posited for them one God, singular in divinity, as is the case of his own creed which he had informed them of. He then posited for them many scattered gods, each of whom disposes only of specific kinds of existing things under his authority, and does not overstep into what falls within the domain of another's authority. This is the case of the creed of the Copts.

Then he posited for them a comparison between the two states taken together: the state of the God who is alone in divinity, and the scattered states of the many gods, in order to bring them, by this, to be persuaded that the state of the one alone in divinity is greater and more self-sufficient, so that they would return from believing in a plurality of gods. The purpose of this argument is not to affirm the existence of the two states in divinity, nor the comparison between the holders of these two states, because those addressed do not believe in the existence of the one God.

This holds if the word **خَيْرٌ** (*khayr*, "better") is taken in its common, apparent sense, which is preference between things that share a quality. The meaning would then be: is the belief in the existence of scattered lords more preponderant, or the belief that there exists only one God? This is so as to draw down by it the bird of their reflection and reasoning until the corruption of the belief in a plurality of gods becomes clear to them, for it becomes evident to them that scattered lords cannot be free from corruption and disorder in their governance. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 41:

﴿O my two fellow prisoners! As for one of you, he will give his lord wine to drink; but as for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decided about which you both inquire.﴾

He opened his address to them with the vocative, showing concern for the interpretation (ta'wil) he was about to convey to them. He also addressed them by the description ﴿the two companions of the prison﴾.

Then, if the speech reported from Yusuf (peace be upon him) in the verse was uttered in the arrangement in which it is composed in the verse, which is the apparent meaning, then the gathering of the interpretation into a single concise statement (ijmal) is because the interpretation of one of the two visions contains something that would distress its owner. He intended for him to receive what distresses him only after a brief reflection, so that it would not startle him at the beginning of the speech. For after reflection he would know that the one who gives his lord wine to drink is the one who saw himself pressing wine, and that the one from whose head birds eat is the one who saw birds eating bread from upon his head.

Page 278

And if the arrangement of the verse is other than what came from Yusuf (peace be upon him), then there is in the verse a concision (ijaz) in relating Yusuf's speech. It would have been a specific speech in which each of the two youths was mentioned, by saying: "As for you, such-and-such; and as for you, such-and-such." So it was related in the verse in meaning.

The clause ﴿The matter has been decided about which you both inquire﴾ confirms what the vision indicated, namely that its interpretation is what he informed them of. For they both seek a ruling (istifta', i.e., asking for a legal opinion) on what the vision indicates about what will happen concerning their imprisonment, since that is their greatest concern. So "the matter" refers to the interpretation of their visions.

Istifta' is the verbal noun of istaftā, meaning to ask for an ifta' (a legal opinion or ruling). It is the giving of information that removes a problem, or guidance toward removing a perplexity. Its verb afta is always used with a hamza, and no unaugmented form of it has been heard. This indicates that its hamza is originally added to convey a meaning. They said the derivation of afta is from fata, meaning a young man, as if the one who gives a ruling strengthens the other's course with his explanation, so that by the strength of his explanation he becomes fatiyy, meaning strong. The noun for the report issued by the mufti (the one who gives the ruling) is fatwa, pronounced with fa' vowelled by fatha or by damma with a waw, as a shortened form, and with damma on the fa' with a ya', as a shortened form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 42:

﴿And he said to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved, "Mention me before your lord." But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord, so he remained in prison for several years.﴾

Yusuf (peace be upon him) said to the one he thought would be saved of the two young men, namely the cupbearer. The word "thought" (zann) here is used in the sense close to certainty, because he had no doubt about the accuracy of his interpretation of the dream. By "mention me" he meant mention my case and my injustice, i.e., "mention me to your lord," that is, your master. By "his lord" he meant the king of Egypt.

The pronouns in (fa-ansahu) and (rabbahu) may refer back to "the one," meaning: Satan caused the one who was saved to forget to mention him to his lord, so the second "mention" is the first "mention." It is also possible that the two pronouns refer to what the pronoun in (wa qala) refers to, i.e., Yusuf (peace be upon him): Satan caused him to forget the mention of God, so the second "mention" is other than the first. Probably both possibilities are intended, and this is from the wonderful brevity (ijaz). For Yusuf's forgetting to ask God to inspire the king to remember his affair was from Satan's casting into his wish, and that was a divine cause for the cupbearer's forgetting to remind the king. It was also a divine rebuke to Yusuf (peace be upon him) for his preoccupation with seeking help from people instead of seeking help from his Lord for his deliverance.

Perhaps in presenting this speech according to this interpretation there is a gentleness in the report about Yusuf (peace be upon him), because a statement directed at hidden meanings is gentler than an explicit one.

Al-bid' (plural: bid'): from three to nine.

What the Qur'an relates about the state of their imprisonment indicates that the prison was not regulated by a register recording the names of the prisoners, the reasons for their imprisonment, and the term to which each was sentenced, nor was there among the jailers or among their superiors anyone who oversaw the causes of imprisonment, inspected the affairs of the prisoners, and reported to the king on a day of the week or of the year. This is part of negligence and laxity regarding people's rights, which Islam has abolished, for it is part of the Shari'ah that the judge should first examine, each day, the affairs of the prisoners.

[Page 280]

This is the conjunction of one part of the story with another part of it, completing the description of Joseph's (peace be upon him) release from prison.

The definite article in *al-malik* (the king) is anaphoric (*li-l-'ahd*, referring to a known individual), meaning the king of Egypt. The Qur'an calls him *malik* here and does not call him Pharaoh (*Fir'awn*) because this king was not one of the Pharaohs, the native Coptic kings of Egypt. He was a king of Egypt during the period when Egypt was ruled by the Hyksos (*al-Hiksos*), who were the Amalekites and are among the Canaanites or the Arabs. Greek historians refer to them as the "Shepherd Kings" (*mulük al-Ru'ah*), that is, the nomads. They ruled Egypt from about 1900 to 1525 BCE. Their era fell between the Thirteenth Dynasty and the Eighteenth Dynasty of the Coptic kings, since the Coptic dynasties still retained rule in Upper Egypt, in the city of Thebes (*Tiba*), as was mentioned earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the one who bought him said﴾ [Yusuf: 21]. Their king in that period was weak, because sovereignty belonged to the kings of Lower Egypt. Historians estimate that the king of Lower Egypt at the time of Joseph (peace be upon him) was during the Seventeenth Dynasty.

Therefore, the Qur'an's reference to him as *al-malik* rather than Pharaoh, although the title Pharaoh was used for the king of Egypt at the time of Moses (peace be upon him), is one of the subtle aspects of the scientific miraculousness (*i'jaz 'ilmi*) of the Qur'an. The Torah erred when it referred to the king of Egypt at the time of Joseph (peace be upon him) as Pharaoh, though he was not Pharaoh, because his people did not speak Coptic. Their language was Canaanite, close to Aramaic and Arabic. Thus, the time of Joseph (peace be upon him) falls at the end of the period of the rule of the Shepherd Kings, though there is considerable disagreement on this.

His words *simān* (fat, plural) are the plural of *samīnah* and *samīn*, like *kirām*, and they describe *baqarāt* (cows).

*ʿIjāf* is the plural of *ʿajfāʾ* (lean). The analogical plural of *ʿajfāʾ* would be *ʿujf*, but here it is formed on the pattern *fiʿāl* for the sake of *muzāwaja* (stylistic pairing with its counterpart), since it is paired with *simān*. As the poet said:

*Hattāk akhbiyatin wa-llāj abawiyah* (Rending tents and entering doorways).

The analogical plural of *abwāb* (doors) would be *abwāb*, but he formed it on *akhbiyah* (tents).

*Al-ʿajfāʾ* is the one characterized by *ʿaraf* (emaciation), which is extreme leanness.

*Wa-sabʿa sunbulāt* (and seven ears of grain) is conjoined to *sabʿa baqarāt* (seven cows). The word *sunbulah* (ear of grain) was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿like a grain that grows seven ears﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261] in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-malaʾ* means the notables of the people. It was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿The chiefs of his people said﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 60] in Surat al-Aʿraf.

*Al-iftāʾ* means giving a ruling (*fatwā*). It was discussed just previously at His words: ﴿The matter about which you both inquire has been decided﴾ [Yusuf: 41].

The preposition *fī* (in) here expresses figurative containment (*al-ẓarfiyyah al-majāziyyah*), which has the sense of association (*mulābasah*). That is, "Give me a ruling that is connected to my dream as clarification is connected to the ambiguous."

The placement of *li-l-ruʾyā* before its governing verb *taʿburūn* (you interpret) is for the sake of observing the rhyme (*al-fāṣilah*), along with the emphasis on the dream in the act of interpretation. The definite article in *li-l-ruʾyā* is the definite of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*).

The *lām* in *li-l-ruʾyā* is the *lām* of reinforcement, because the governing verb is weak in acting when it is placed after its object. It is said: *ʿabara al-ruʾyā* (he interpreted the dream), on the pattern of *naṣara*. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshāf*: "*ʿAbarat al-ruʾyā*" with the lightened form is what the established usage relies upon. I have seen that they deny *ʿabbarat* with the doubled *bāʾ* and *al-taʿbīr*. I have come across a verse that al-Mubarrad quoted in his book *al-Kāmil* from one of the Bedouins:

*Ra'aytu ru'yāya thumma ʿabartuhā* ∗∗∗ *wa-kuntu li-l-aḥlāmi ʿabbārā*
(I saw my dream, then I interpreted it, / and I was an interpreter of dreams.)

The meaning is: he explained what it indicates, and interpreted its signs and symbols.

Interpreting dreams was one of the things they occupied themselves with. Their priests (*kahanah*) regarded it as one of their sciences and had rules for decoding the symbols of what a sleeper sees. Papyrus scrolls containing rules and principles for interpreting dreams have been found among Coptic antiquities. The fact that the two companions of the prison sought Joseph's (peace be upon him) interpretation of their dreams indicates that this was widespread among them. The king's request of his court (*malaʾ*) to interpret his dream indicates that this court included people thought to have knowledge of dream interpretation, and the king's court could not be free of soothsayers whose profession is dream interpretation.

[Page 282]

In the Torah: "Then he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men, and he related to them his dream, but there was no one who could interpret it for him." It was something sought from the priests because it belongs to the unseen. The prophetic biography (*al-sīrah al-nabawiyyah*) reports that Kisra (Khosrow) sent to Sutayh the soothsayer to interpret a dream for him at the time of the birth of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is counted among the prophetic precursors (*irhāṣāt nabawiyyah*, signs preceding prophethood). Kisra was seized with alarm, so he dispatched ʿAbd al-Masih to him.

The definite article in His words *li-l-ruʾyā* is the definite of anaphora (*taʿrīf al-ʿahd*), and the known referent is the dream which he used to relate to them. In the method of repeating an indefinite noun as a definite noun with the article, the second is the same as the first. The meaning is: "If you are able to interpret this dream."

*Al-aḍghāth* is the plural of *ḍighth* (with a kasra on the dotted *ḍād*), which is what is gathered into a single bundle from mixed plants and sticks of wood. Its being added to *al-aḥlām* (dreams) is according to the presumed *lām* (of the relation), that is, "bundles for dreams."

*Al-aḥlām* is the plural of *ḥulm* (with two dammas), which is what a sleeper sees in his sleep. The implied sense is: "This dream is a bundle of dreams." That dream was compared to bundles in its confusion and the lack of distinction among its contents when its interpretation became obscure for them.

The definite article in it is also anaphoric, that is, "We are not those who know the interpretation of these dreams of yours." The plural *aḥlām* was used in view of the multiplicity of visible things in that dream, so it is a number of visions.

The *bāʾ* in *bi-taʾwīl al-aḥlām* (with the interpretation of dreams) is for emphasizing the connection of the verb to its object. It is of the type of the *bāʾ* of adherence (*bāʾ al-ilṣāq*), like the *bāʾ* in ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 6], because they denied the ability to interpret this dream. Placing this object before the qualifying verb that governs it is like placing the prepositional phrase in His words: ﴿if you are able to interpret the dream﴾.

[Page 283]

When the difficulty of interpreting this dream became apparent, the king's cupbearer remembered what had happened to him with Joseph (peace be upon him), so he said: ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾.

The beginning of his speech with the pronoun and making it the subject, with a verbal predicate, serves to draw the king's astonishment that the cupbearer should be the one informing them of the interpretation of a dream which had puzzled the scholars of the royal court. It also conveys the strengthening of the judgment, which is his informing them of its interpretation, because placing the subject before a verbal predicate in an affirmative context conveys emphasis. Ascribing the informing to him is a rational figurative expression (*majāz ʿaqlī*), since he is the cause of the informing, and for this reason he said: ﴿so send me﴾. This contains something that stirs the king to permit him to go wherever he wishes to bring the news of the interpretation, since it is not permissible for someone like him to leave the king's assembly without permission. He was certain that he would find Joseph (peace be upon him) in prison, because he said ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ without hesitation. Perhaps the reason for his certainty that Joseph (peace be upon him) remained in prison is that it was a prison for the elite, so whatever happened there, such as release or death, would reach the king and his circle.

*Ittakara* (remembered) with the unpointed *dāl* was originally *idhtakara*, which is a form of *iftiʿāl* from *dhikr*. The *tāʾ* of *iftiʿāl* was changed to *dāl* because of its heaviness and the closeness of their points of articulation. Then the *dhāl* was changed so that it could be assimilated into the *dāl*, since the *dāl* is lighter than the *dhāl*. This is the most eloquent of the substitutions in *ittakara*. It is the reading of the Prophet (ﷺ) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is there anyone who remembers?﴾ [al-Qamar: 15], as in the authentic collection.

The meaning of ﴿after a period﴾ is after a time had passed during which he had forgotten Joseph's (peace be upon him) instruction.

*Ummah* here is used for a long period. The original usage of *ummah* for a long period is that it is a time in which a generation passes away, and a generation is called an *ummah*, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Aʾl ʿImrān: 110] according to the view of those who understood it as referring to the Companions.

Its use in this verse is hyperbole for the length of the cupbearer's forgetting. In the Torah, the period of his forgetting was two years.

The plural pronouns of address in *unabbi'ukum* (I will inform you) and *fa-arsilūn* (so send me) are addressed to the king as a sign of respect, like His words: ﴿He said: My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 99].

The placement of *li-l-ruʾyā* before its governing verb *taʿburūn* (you interpret) is for the sake of observing the rhyme (*al-fāṣilah*), along with the emphasis on the dream in the act of interpretation. The definite article in *li-l-ruʾyā* is the definite of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*).

The *lām* in *li-l-ruʾyā* is the *lām* of reinforcement, because the governing verb is weak in acting when it is placed after its object. It is said: *ʿabara al-ruʾyā* (he interpreted the dream), on the pattern of *naṣara*. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshāf*: "*ʿAbarat al-ruʾyā*" with the lightened form is what the established usage relies upon. I have seen that they deny *ʿabbarat* with the doubled *bāʾ* and *al-taʿbīr*. I have come across a verse that al-Mubarrad quoted in his book *al-Kāmil* from one of the Bedouins:

*Ra'aytu ru'yāya thumma ʿabartuhā* ∗∗∗ *wa-kuntu li-l-aḥlāmi ʿabbārā*
(I saw my dream, then I interpreted it, / and I was an interpreter of dreams.)

The meaning is: he explained what it indicates, and interpreted its signs and symbols.

Interpreting dreams was one of the things they occupied themselves with. Their priests (*kahanah*) regarded it as one of their sciences and had rules for decoding the symbols of what a sleeper sees. Papyrus scrolls containing rules and principles for interpreting dreams have been found among Coptic antiquities. The fact that the two companions of the prison sought Joseph's (peace be upon him) interpretation of their dreams indicates that this was widespread among them. The king's request of his court (*malaʾ*) to interpret his dream indicates that this court included people thought to have knowledge of dream interpretation, and the king's court could not be free of soothsayers whose profession is dream interpretation.

[Page 282]

In the Torah: "Then he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men, and he related to them his dream, but there was no one who could interpret it for him." It was something sought from the priests because it belongs to the unseen. The prophetic biography (*al-sīrah al-nabawiyyah*) reports that Kisra (Khosrow) sent to Sutayh the soothsayer to interpret a dream for him at the time of the birth of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is counted among the prophetic precursors (*irhāṣāt nabawiyyah*, signs preceding prophethood). Kisra was seized with alarm, so he dispatched ʿAbd al-Masih to him.

The definite article in His words *li-l-ruʾyā* is the definite of anaphora (*taʿrīf al-ʿahd*), and the known referent is the dream which he used to relate to them. In the method of repeating an indefinite noun as a definite noun with the article, the second is the same as the first. The meaning is: "If you are able to interpret this dream."

*Al-aḍghāth* is the plural of *ḍighth* (with a kasra on the dotted *ḍād*), which is what is gathered into a single bundle from mixed plants and sticks of wood. Its being added to *al-aḥlām* (dreams) is according to the presumed *lām* (of the relation), that is, "bundles for dreams."

*Al-aḥlām* is the plural of *ḥulm* (with two dammas), which is what a sleeper sees in his sleep. The implied sense is: "This dream is a bundle of dreams." That dream was compared to bundles in its confusion and the lack of distinction among its contents when its interpretation became obscure for them.

The definite article in it is also anaphoric, that is, "We are not those who know the interpretation of these dreams of yours." The plural *aḥlām* was used in view of the multiplicity of visible things in that dream, so it is a number of visions.

The *bāʾ* in *bi-taʾwīl al-aḥlām* (with the interpretation of dreams) is for emphasizing the connection of the verb to its object. It is of the type of the *bāʾ* of adherence (*bāʾ al-ilṣāq*), like the *bāʾ* in ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 6], because they denied the ability to interpret this dream. Placing this object before the qualifying verb that governs it is like placing the prepositional phrase in His words: ﴿if you are able to interpret the dream﴾.

[Page 283]

When the difficulty of interpreting this dream became apparent, the king's cupbearer remembered what had happened to him with Joseph (peace be upon him), so he said: ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾.

The beginning of his speech with the pronoun and making it the subject, with a verbal predicate, serves to draw the king's astonishment that the cupbearer should be the one informing them of the interpretation of a dream which had puzzled the scholars of the royal court. It also conveys the strengthening of the judgment, which is his informing them of its interpretation, because placing the subject before a verbal predicate in an affirmative context conveys emphasis. Ascribing the informing to him is a rational figurative expression (*majāz ʿaqlī*), since he is the cause of the informing, and for this reason he said: ﴿so send me﴾. This contains something that stirs the king to permit him to go wherever he wishes to bring the news of the interpretation, since it is not permissible for someone like him to leave the king's assembly without permission. He was certain that he would find Joseph (peace be upon him) in prison, because he said ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ without hesitation. Perhaps the reason for his certainty that Joseph (peace be upon him) remained in prison is that it was a prison for the elite, so whatever happened there, such as release or death, would reach the king and his circle.

*Ittakara* (remembered) with the unpointed *dāl* was originally *idhtakara*, which is a form of *iftiʿāl* from *dhikr*. The *tāʾ* of *iftiʿāl* was changed to *dāl* because of its heaviness and the closeness of their points of articulation. Then the *dhāl* was changed so that it could be assimilated into the *dāl*, since the *dāl* is lighter than the *dhāl*. This is the most eloquent of the substitutions in *ittakara*. It is the reading of the Prophet (ﷺ) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is there anyone who remembers?﴾ [al-Qamar: 15], as in the authentic collection.

The meaning of ﴿after a period﴾ is after a time had passed during which he had forgotten Joseph's (peace be upon him) instruction.

*Ummah* here is used for a long period. The original usage of *ummah* for a long period is that it is a time in which a generation passes away, and a generation is called an *ummah*, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Aʾl ʿImrān: 110] according to the view of those who understood it as referring to the Companions.

Its use in this verse is hyperbole for the length of the cupbearer's forgetting. In the Torah, the period of his forgetting was two years.

The plural pronouns of address in *unabbi'ukum* (I will inform you) and *fa-arsilūn* (so send me) are addressed to the king as a sign of respect, like His words: ﴿He said: My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 99].

[Page 284]

He did not name for them the person to whom he was sent, because he intended to surprise them with the news about Joseph (peace be upon him) after the interpretation had been achieved, so that it would have a greater effect, since someone like him is not expected to be among the prisoners.

[Page 280]

This is the conjunction of one part of the story with another part of it, completing the description of Joseph's (peace be upon him) release from prison.

The definite article in *al-malik* (the king) is anaphoric (*li-l-'ahd*, referring to a known individual), meaning the king of Egypt. The Qur'an calls him *malik* here and does not call him Pharaoh (*Fir'awn*) because this king was not one of the Pharaohs, the native Coptic kings of Egypt. He was a king of Egypt during the period when Egypt was ruled by the Hyksos (*al-Hiksos*), who were the Amalekites and are among the Canaanites or the Arabs. Greek historians refer to them as the "Shepherd Kings" (*mulük al-Ru'ah*), that is, the nomads. They ruled Egypt from about 1900 to 1525 BCE. Their era fell between the Thirteenth Dynasty and the Eighteenth Dynasty of the Coptic kings, since the Coptic dynasties still retained rule in Upper Egypt, in the city of Thebes (*Tiba*), as was mentioned earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the one who bought him said﴾ [Yusuf: 21]. Their king in that period was weak, because sovereignty belonged to the kings of Lower Egypt. Historians estimate that the king of Lower Egypt at the time of Joseph (peace be upon him) was during the Seventeenth Dynasty.

Therefore, the Qur'an's reference to him as *al-malik* rather than Pharaoh, although the title Pharaoh was used for the king of Egypt at the time of Moses (peace be upon him), is one of the subtle aspects of the scientific miraculousness (*i'jaz 'ilmi*) of the Qur'an. The Torah erred when it referred to the king of Egypt at the time of Joseph (peace be upon him) as Pharaoh, though he was not Pharaoh, because his people did not speak Coptic. Their language was Canaanite, close to Aramaic and Arabic. Thus, the time of Joseph (peace be upon him) falls at the end of the period of the rule of the Shepherd Kings, though there is considerable disagreement on this.

His words *simān* (fat, plural) are the plural of *samīnah* and *samīn*, like *kirām*, and they describe *baqarāt* (cows).

*ʿIjāf* is the plural of *ʿajfāʾ* (lean). The analogical plural of *ʿajfāʾ* would be *ʿujf*, but here it is formed on the pattern *fiʿāl* for the sake of *muzāwaja* (stylistic pairing with its counterpart), since it is paired with *simān*. As the poet said:

*Hattāk akhbiyatin wa-llāj abawiyah* (Rending tents and entering doorways).

The analogical plural of *abwāb* (doors) would be *abwāb*, but he formed it on *akhbiyah* (tents).

*Al-ʿajfāʾ* is the one characterized by *ʿaraf* (emaciation), which is extreme leanness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 46:

﴿Yusuf, O man of truth (al-siddiq), give us your interpretation concerning seven fat cows which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others dry, that I may return to the people, that they may know.﴾

The address by vocative indicates an unstated speech in the discourse, and that it is the speech of the one who was saved and recalled (the matter) after a period of time. The mention of his being sent, his going, and his arrival has been omitted from the narrative, since it serves no purpose in the story. This is one of the marvels of concision (al-iljaz).

Al-siddiq (the truthful one, the man of truth): its origin is an intensive adjective (sifat mubalaghah) derived from al-sidq (truthfulness), as was discussed earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿وأُمُّهُ صِدِّيقَةٌ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 75] in Surat al-'Uqud. The use of the description al-siddiq has come to be used as a title encompassing the meanings of perfection and uprightness of conduct in obedience to Allah, may He be exalted, because those meanings are not gathered except in one whose truthfulness in fulfilling the covenant of religion is strong.

The best I have seen on this meaning is the statement of al-Raghib al-Isfahani in Mufradat al-Qur'an, who said: "The siddiqun are those just below the prophets." This is what the Qur'an's usage in many verses testifies to, such as His saying: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ أنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنَ النَّبِيِّينَ والصِّدِّيقِينَ﴾ [al-Nisa': 69], and His saying: ﴿وأُمُّهُ صِدِّيقَةٌ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 75]. Among this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave Abu Bakr the title al-Siddiq in his saying in the hadith of the trembling of Mount Uhud: "Be still, Uhud, for upon you are a Prophet, a siddiq, and two martyrs." For this reason the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), including 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah ennoble his face), agreed that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) is the most excellent of this Ummah after the Prophet (ﷺ). Allah has combined this description with the attribute of prophethood in His saying: ﴿واذْكُرْ في الكِتابِ إدْرِيسَ إنَّهُ كانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 56] in Surat Maryam.

Al-siddiq may also be used for the root of this attribute, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ ورُسُلِهِ أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الصِّدِّيقُونَ﴾ [al-Hadid: 19], according to one of the two interpretations concerning it.

So this one who asked Yusuf (peace be upon him) about the king's dream described Yusuf (peace be upon him) in his speech with a meaning that the description al-siddiq indicates in the Arabic language. He described him with it on the basis of experience and trial that he acquired from associating with Yusuf (peace be upon him) in prison.

We combine what we have mentioned here with what was earlier discussed at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿وأُمُّهُ صِدِّيقَةٌ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 75] in Surat al-'Uqud, and with His saying: ﴿مَعَ الَّذِينَ أنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنَ النَّبِيِّينَ والصِّدِّيقِينَ﴾ [al-Nisa': 69] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The repetition of the expressions reported from the king exactly as they were is an indication that he conveyed the question as he received it, and that is the completion of the trustworthiness of the transmitter.

Al-nas (the people) was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿ومِنَ النّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ آمَنّا بِاللَّهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The intended meaning of al-nas here is some of them, as in His saying: ﴿الَّذِينَ قالَ لَهُمُ النّاسُ إنَّ النّاسَ قَدْ جَمَعُوا لَكُمْ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173]. Al-nas here are the king and the people of his council, because the interpretation of that dream concerns them all, so that the king may know the interpretation of his vision and the people of his council may know that what they were unable to interpret has been taught to one who is more knowledgeable than them. This is the reason for His saying: ﴿لَعَلَّهم يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("that they may know"), with the object of (ya'lamun) omitted, because each person knows what their knowledge benefits them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 47–49:

Page 286
﴿He said, "You will sow for seven years consecutively. So what you reap, leave it in its ears, except for a little of which you eat. Then there will come after that seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored up for them, except for a little of what you have preserved. Then there will come after that a year in which the people will be given rain and in which they will press [juice]."﴾

He interpreted the dream in all that it indicated. The cows refer to years of cultivation, because the cow is kept for the purpose of producing [crops]. The fatness is a symbol of abundance, and the leanness is a symbol of drought. The ears of grain are a symbol of food: the green ears are a symbol of food from which benefit is gained, and their being seven is a symbol of benefiting from it during the seven years. Thus each ear is a symbol of a year's food, and so they would subsist on it, fresh, during those years.

The dry ears are a symbol of what is stored, and their being seven is a symbol of storing it for seven years, because the lean cows ate the fat cows. The interpretation of that is that the years of drought consumed what the years of abundance had produced.

His saying "you will sow" (tazra'una) is a report about what will be their action, because sowing was their custom; so mentioning it is a preface to the speech that follows, and for this reason he qualified it with "da'aban" (consecutively).

Al-da'b (da'ab): custom and continuity upon it. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿as the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 11] in Surat Al 'Imran. It is in the accusative as a state (hal) of the pronoun in "tazra'una", i.e., "as your custom." He combined his interpretation with a sublime guidance regarding the conditions of provisioning and storage for the benefit of the community. This dream, whose wisdom was that the king's vision was a kindness from God toward the community that sheltered Joseph (peace be upon him), and a revelation that God inspired to Joseph (peace be upon him) through the medium of the king's dream, just as He inspired Solomon (peace be upon him) through the medium of birds. Perhaps the king had prepared himself for righteousness and faith.

Page 287
What Joseph (peace be upon him) indicated to the king regarding storage was a preparation for the legislation of storing provisions for supply, just as fulfilling measure and weight was the beginning of the call of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him). He pointed to leaving what exceeded their sustenance in its ears, so that it would be safer for it from the weevil that afflicts grain when piled upon one another; when it is in its ear, the weevil is repelled from it. He also advised them to reduce what they eat in the years of plenty, so as to store what exceeds that for a time of hardship, and so he said ﴿except for a little of which you eat﴾.

Al-shidad (hard): an attribute of the years of drought, because drought occurs in them; so he described them with hardness by way of rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli).

He used "consume" (ya'kulna) in the sense of destroying, like that in His saying ﴿And do not consume their wealth along with your wealth﴾ [al-Nisa: 2]. Attributing it in this sense to the years is a rational metaphor, because they are the time in which destruction occurs.

Al-ihsan: preserving and storing, i.e., placing in a fortress (hisn), which is a buried pit. The meaning: in those barren years, what has been stored for them will be consumed, except for a little of it that remains in the granaries. This is an exhortation to store abundantly.

As for His saying ﴿Then there will come after that a year in which the people will be given rain﴾, it is good news and a bringing back of the hope of joy after the discouraging speech, and it is a necessary consequence of the end of the period of hardship, and one of God's, the Exalted's, customs in the occurrence of ease after hardship.

Yughath means they will be given rain (al-ghayth), which is rain. Al-'asr: pressing grapes into wine. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿he presses wine﴾.

The dry ears are a symbol of what is stored, and their being seven is a symbol of storing it for seven years, because the lean cows ate the fat cows. The interpretation of that is that the years of drought consumed what the years of abundance had produced.

His saying "you will sow" (tazra'una) is a report about what will be their action, because sowing was their custom; so mentioning it is a preface to the speech that follows, and for this reason he qualified it with "da'aban" (consecutively).

Al-da'b (da'ab): custom and continuity upon it. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿as the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 11] in Surat Al 'Imran. It is in the accusative as a state (hal) of the pronoun in "tazra'una", i.e., "as your custom." He combined his interpretation with a sublime guidance regarding the conditions of provisioning and storage for the benefit of the community. This dream, whose wisdom was that the king's vision was a kindness from God toward the community that sheltered Joseph (peace be upon him), and a revelation that God inspired to Joseph (peace be upon him) through the medium of the king's dream, just as He inspired Solomon (peace be upon him) through the medium of birds. Perhaps the king had prepared himself for righteousness and faith.

Page 287
What Joseph (peace be upon him) indicated to the king regarding storage was a preparation for the legislation of storing provisions for supply, just as fulfilling measure and weight was the beginning of the call of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him). He pointed to leaving what exceeded their sustenance in its ears, so that it would be safer for it from the weevil that afflicts grain when piled upon one another; when it is in its ear, the weevil is repelled from it. He also advised them to reduce what they eat in the years of plenty, so as to store what exceeds that for a time of hardship, and so he said ﴿except for a little of which you eat﴾.

Al-shidad (hard): an attribute of the years of drought, because drought occurs in them; so he described them with hardness by way of rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli).

He used "consume" (ya'kulna) in the sense of destroying, like that in His saying ﴿And do not consume their wealth along with your wealth﴾ [al-Nisa: 2]. Attributing it in this sense to the years is a rational metaphor, because they are the time in which destruction occurs.

Al-ihsan: preserving and storing, i.e., placing in a fortress (hisn), which is a buried pit. The meaning: in those barren years, what has been stored for them will be consumed, except for a little of it that remains in the granaries. This is an exhortation to store abundantly.

As for His saying ﴿Then there will come after that a year in which the people will be given rain﴾, it is good news and a bringing back of the hope of joy after the discouraging speech, and it is a necessary consequence of the end of the period of hardship, and one of God's, the Exalted's, customs in the occurrence of ease after hardship.

Yughath means they will be given rain (al-ghayth), which is rain. Al-'asr: pressing grapes into wine. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿he presses wine﴾.
