Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 50:

Page 288
﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what happened with the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾
The king said: "Bring him to me," after the cupbearer had conveyed to him the account of the interpretation. The address was to the chiefs (al-mala'), so that they would send someone who could assist in bringing him. For this reason it is followed by ﴿when the messenger came to him﴾. The implied sense is: they sent a messenger from among them. The pronouns of the absent third person in His words "to him" (bihi) and "came to him" (jaa'ahu) refer to Yusuf, peace be upon him. The hidden pronoun in "he said" (qala) refers to him as well.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, refused to leave the prison before his innocence was established regarding what he had been accused of in the house of the 'Aziz. This is because that matter had certainly reached the king, so that his release would not be as one who was merely a mediator (shafi') in the interpretation that required his release from prison, leaving the story of his accusation spreading among the people, whereby the envious could later use it to diminish his standing before the king at some point. Clearing one's honour from false accusations is a legitimate objective (maqsad shar'i), and so that his presence before the king would be esteemed, viewed by an eye that sees no flaw in him.

He made the path to establishing his innocence begin with a question about the matter, so that the account would be recalled from its beginning. The meaning of "ask him" (fas'alhu) is: convey to him a question on my behalf. This is a great wisdom worthy of being emulated. It involves a wrongly imprisoned person seeking that he not remain in prison until his innocence from the cause for which he was jailed becomes clear, and it returns to adorning oneself with patience until victory appears.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If I had remained as long as Yusuf remained in prison, I would have answered the summoner." That is, the summoner of the king, who is the messenger in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿when the messenger came to him﴾, meaning, when I had returned to the king. This is one of the signs and lessons to which His words, Exalted is He, point: ﴿Indeed, in Yusuf and his brothers are signs for those who ask﴾ [Yusuf: 7].

Page 289
The question is used for alerting rather than seeking understanding, because the questioner already knows the matter asked about; the questioner only wishes to urge the one questioned to convey knowledge of the report. Close to this is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [An-Naba': 1].

The question was directed about the women who cut their hands, rather than about the wife of the 'Aziz, to facilitate uncovering the matter, because mentioning her together with her husband's standing before the king might have turned the king away from investigating, out of consideration for the 'Aziz. Also, the story of the reclining couch had spread among the women, and the affair of Yusuf, peace be upon him, had become famous on that account, as was mentioned earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then it appeared to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him﴾ [Yusuf: 35]. And also because the women were witnesses to the wife of the 'Aziz's admission that she had sought to seduce Yusuf, peace be upon him, against himself. Therefore, asking about those women was indeed the height of wisdom in investigation and the utmost brevity in address.

The clause ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot﴾ is from the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It serves as a concluding affirmation (tadhyil) and an allusion that the sought-after uncovering will reveal his innocence and the manifestation of the plotting of the plotters against him, out of trust in God, his Lord, that He is his helper.

The attribution of "plot" (kayd) to the pronoun of the women is for the closest connection, since the plotting was done by some of them, namely the wife of the 'Aziz in her purpose in gathering the women; it was attributed to the pronoun of their group deliberately, for a specific ambiguity that clarifies the matter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 51:

﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?" They said, "Far be Allah from imperfection! We know of him no evil." The wife of the chief said, "Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is of the truthful."﴾

The clause ﴿He said, "What was your affair?"﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), because the preceding sentences raise a question in the listener's mind about what the king did when he was informed of Joseph's proposal, despite his intense longing to have him brought into his presence. That is, the king said to the women:

The occurrence of this after the clause ﴿Return to your lord﴾ [Yusuf: 50] to its end indicates an omitted statement, whose estimate is: So he returned and informed the king, and the king summoned the women whom the wife of the chief had gathered when she prepared a banquet for them. Then he said to them, ﴿What was your affair?﴾ to its end.

The seeking (murawadah) is attributed to the pronoun of the women because it was committed by some of them without specification, or because the rumor that spread in the city was mixed up, thinking that the seeking took place in the gathering of the banquet.

Al-khatb (الخَطْبُ) means an important matter, whether a state or an event. It was said that it is called khatb because it requires that a person address his companion with questioning about it. It was also said that it is derived from al-khutbah (الخُطْبَة), i.e., one delivers a speech about it, and a sermon is only given about a great matter; so its origin is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle, meaning "a matter about which one speaks."

The clause (qulna) is separated because it is the narration of an answer to the king's speech. That is, the women, other than the wife of the chief, said, as shown by His saying afterwards ﴿The wife of the chief said﴾.

﴿Hasha lillah﴾ is an intensification in negation and exoneration. The intended meaning is disavowal of what was attributed to them of seeking. Its explanation has been given earlier, along with the differences of the readers regarding it.

The clause ﴿We know of him no evil﴾ explains the general negation contained in ﴿Hasha lillah﴾. It encompasses the negation of their seeking him and of his seeking them, because both states are among the states of evil.

The negation of their knowledge of that is a metonymy (kinayah) for the negation of their calling him to evil and of his calling them to it; because if that had occurred, it would have been known to them. Moreover, they did not add to their testimony beyond what relates to the king's question, so they did not mention the confession of the wife of the chief in their gathering that she had sought him from himself, and he had refrained, [out of fear of her] or out of affection for her; so they confined themselves to answering what they were asked.

This indicates an omitted statement, namely that the wife of the chief was among the women whom the king had summoned. The words of Joseph, peace be upon him, ﴿What is the matter with the women who cut their hands?﴾ [Yusuf: 50] did not include her, because she had not cut her hand with them; but the king's speech included her when he said ﴿When you sought to seduce Joseph from himself﴾, for the seeking came only from the wife of the chief and not from the women to whom she had prepared a banquet. So in the speech there is concision by omission.

The clause ﴿The wife of the chief said﴾ is separated because it is the narration of an answer to the king's question.

Al-an (الآنَ) is an adverb of present time. It was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ [al-Anfal: 66] in Surah al-Anfal.

Hasahsa (حَصْحَصَ) means became firm and settled.

Al-haqq (الحَقُّ) is the innocence of Joseph, peace be upon him, from what the wife of the chief had accused him of. It was established at that time because it had been a subject of talk, speculation and doubt, and that was removed by her confession of what had occurred.

The use of the past tense, although it was established only through her confession which had not yet preceded, is because it was very recent; so it brings the time of the present close to the past.

It is also possible that what is meant is the establishment of the truth by the women's words ﴿We know of him no evil﴾, so the past tense is in its literal sense. The fronting of the time noun indicates restriction, i.e., "now and not before it," indicating that the time before that was a false time, namely the time of the accusation against Joseph, peace be upon him, of seeking. The restriction is then one of specification, since the king did not know which of the two times was the time of truth: was it the time of the women's acknowledgment of Joseph's purity, peace be upon him, or the time when the wife of the chief accused him of seeking?

The fronting of the subject over the verbal predicate in the clause ﴿I sought him﴾ serves restriction, to refute that the women had sought him. This is a confession from her against herself and a testimony to the innocence of another; and she increased by emphasizing its truth with "inna" and the lam.

The phrase ﴿of the truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 27] follows its parallels, as has been mentioned before, among them His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: I will not follow your desires; I would then have gone astray, and I would not be of the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 56] in Surah al-An'am.

[p. 293]

﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the scheme of the treacherous.﴾

The apparent structure of the discourse indicates that this sentence is part of the speech of the wife of the ruler (al-'Aziz). The lesser number of exegetes took it this way. Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to a group of the people of ta'wil (interpretation), it is ascribed to al-Jubba'i, and al-Mawardi preferred it. It stands in the position of a cause (for what is stated in the statement) ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾ [Yusuf: 51] and what follows it of acknowledgment of the innocence of Yusuf, peace be upon him, regarding what she had accused him of. So the demonstrative ﴿that﴾ refers to the acknowledgment derived from the statement ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾ [Yusuf: 51]. That is: that acknowledgment is so that Yusuf, peace be upon him, may know that I did not betray him.

The lam in ﴿liya'lama﴾ is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the verb after it is in the subjunctive, governed by an implied "an" (that), so it is in the sense of a verbal noun, and it is the predicate of the demonstrative.

The ba' in ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ is for accompaniment or for time/place (zarfiyyah), meaning "in his absence," that is, I did not accuse him of what would harm him in his absence. The phrase in the prepositional construction is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the accusative pronoun.

Khiyanah (betrayal) here is accusing him of attempting evil with her falsely, since lying is the opposite of trustworthiness in speech regarding the truth.

The definite article in al-ghayb is the definite article of the genus. She praised herself for not betraying him in the most emphatic way, when she negated betrayal in his absence, and absence is a state in which he is prevented from defending himself. The state of absence is more conducive to greater betrayal than the state of presence, because a present person may notice the intention of the traitor and repel his betrayal with proof.

﴿And that Allah does not guide the scheme of the treacherous﴾ is coordinated with ﴿liya'lama﴾ and is a second cause for her declaring the truth openly. That is: and because Allah does not guide the scheme of the treacherous. The predicate is used to convey its necessary implication, which is that the speaker knows the content of the statement, because the cause of her acknowledgment is her knowledge that ﴿Allah does not guide the scheme of the treacherous﴾.

The meaning of ﴿does not guide the scheme of the treacherous﴾ is that He does not let it take effect or make it succeed. Guidance, which is directing to the path that leads to the destination, is used for facilitating arrival, and its negation is used for the negation of that facilitation. That is: the practice of Allah in the cosmos is that the arts of falsehood, even if their beginnings flourish, do not persist long before they vanish, ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes﴾ [al-Anbiya: 18].

As for al-kayd (scheming), it has been discussed earlier.

[Page 5]

﴿And I do not declare myself innocent. Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except for those upon whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The apparent order of the discourse indicates that this is part of the speech of the wife of the Chief (al-'Aziz). She continued in the rest of her confession and said, ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾. This is like a precaution against what her statement ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾ [Yusuf: 52] might imply, namely that declaring her own soul free of this grave sin is a claim that her soul is innocent in a general way. So she said, ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾, meaning: I do not declare myself free of attempting this sin, because the soul commands to evil and it has commanded me to evil, but it did not happen.

The wa' in the sentence is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah, introducing a new clause), and the sentence is a fresh beginning.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil﴾ gives the reason (ta'lil) for the sentence ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾, meaning: I do not claim that my soul is free from committing sin, because souls often command to evil.

The exception in ﴿except for those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾ is an exception from the general time (istithna' min 'umum al-azman), meaning the times when evil occurs, on the basis that the soul's command to it moves one to commit it at all times, except the time when God shows mercy to His servant, meaning His mercy by providing for him what turns him away from committing evil, or by placing a barrier between him and committing evil, as He made Yusuf, peace be upon him, refusing her invitation to what she called him to a barrier between her and becoming entangled in this sin. This is a kindness from God toward both of them.

For this reason she followed it with the sentence ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, as a praise of God, that He is exceedingly forgiving to whoever sins, and exceedingly merciful to His servant when He wishes to turn him away from sin.

[Page 6]

This implies that her people believed in God and forbade what is forbidden. That does not contradict their being polytheists, for the polytheists among the Arabs also believed in God. God the Exalted said, ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God"﴾ [Luqman: 25], and they knew righteousness and sin.

In the confession of the wife of the Chief in the presence of the king there is a lesson on the virtue of confessing the truth, and on clearing the innocent of what has been attached to him, and on fear of God's punishment of traitors.

It has also been said that this statement is the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him, connected to his saying ﴿Return to your lord and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands﴾ [Yusuf: 50], and so on.

His saying ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Yusuf?"﴾ [Yusuf: 51], up to his saying ﴿and that God does not guide the plot of the traitors﴾ [Yusuf: 52], is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) within the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Mujahid, Qatadah, Abu Salih, Ibn Jurayj, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr explained it this way, and al-Tabari restricted himself to it. In al-Kashshaf he said: "The meaning is sufficient evidence leading to its being taken as the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Similar to it is his saying ﴿The eminent ones of the people of Pharaoh said, 'Indeed, this is a knowing magician'﴾ [al-A'raf: 109], ﴿who wants to drive you out of your land﴾ [al-A'raf: 110], then he said ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ [al-A'raf: 110], and that is from the speech of Pharaoh, addressing them and consulting them." End of quotation.

He means that the meaning of this sentence is more fitting to be the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him, because it is characteristic of him to come from a heart full of knowledge.

On this reading, the third-person pronoun in his saying ﴿I did not betray him﴾ [Yusuf: 52] refers to something known from the context of the matter, namely the Chief (al-'Aziz), meaning: I did not betray my master in his honor during his absence.

And the meaning of ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾ and so on, like what has preceded, is intended as humility, meaning: I do not say this as a claim that my soul is free from committing sins, except during the period in which God's mercy has rendered the soul sufficient, by granting it success so that I refrain from evil. That is, I did not do what I was accused of, and I am not infallible.

[Page 7]

﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself." So when he had spoken with him, he said, "Indeed, today you are with us established and trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾

The *sīn* and *tā'* in "*astakhlisuhu*" (I will take him exclusively) are for emphasis, like those in *istajāba* (he responded) and *istā'ara* (he hired). The meaning is "I will make him sincerely mine," that is, specially mine, with no one sharing him with me. This is a *kināyah* (allusion, a figure of speech by which a meaning is conveyed indirectly) for the intensity of his closeness to the king and his working closely with him. The king's choice of Yusuf (peace be upon him) for this closeness was based on what had become evident of his wisdom and knowledge, his patience in bearing hardships, and his good character and integrity. All of this made his selection necessary.

The clause "*falammā kallamahu*" (so when he had spoken with him) is built upon an omitted clause that is indicated by "*wa-qāla al-malik ītūnī bihi*" (the king said, bring him to me). The implied meaning is: so they brought him to him, that is, Yusuf (peace be upon him), and he came before him and spoke with him, and when he had spoken with him.

The object pronoun in "*kallamahu*" refers back to the king. Thus the speaker is Yusuf (peace be upon him), who spoke to the king with words that pleased him because of their wisdom and courtesy. For this reason, the clause "*qāla innaka al-yawma ladaynā makīnun amīn*" (he said, indeed today you are with us established and trustworthy) is the response to "*lammā*" (when), and the one who speaks is undoubtedly the king.

*Makīn*: an adjective of quality (*ṣifah mushabbahah*) from *makuna*, with the *kāf* pronounced with a *ḍammah*, when someone attains a high status (*makānah*), namely a great rank. It is derived from *makān* (place).

*Amīn*: an intensive form (*fa'īl*) in the sense of a passive participle (*maf'ūl*), meaning one who is entrusted with something, that is, one who is trusted in safeguarding it.

That this statement follows his speaking with the king indicates that Yusuf (peace be upon him) spoke to the king with the speech of a wise and courteous man. When the king saw the excellence of his speech, the eloquence of his words, and the soundness of his judgment, he regarded him as worthy of his trust and of being brought close to him.

[Page 8]

This is a phrase of appointment that encompasses all the qualities a ruler (*walī al-amr*) needs. Standing in a high position requires knowledge and ability, for through knowledge one can recognize what is good and aim toward it, and through ability one can carry out whatever good becomes apparent. Trustworthiness requires wisdom and justice: through wisdom one chooses right actions and avoids baseless pitfalls, and through justice one delivers rights to their rightful owners. This praise of Yusuf (peace be upon him) and this commendation of him are an implicit indication that the king wished to seek his help in the affairs of his kingdom, and to have him propose what he hoped would bring good. Therefore Yusuf (peace be upon him) answered him with "*ijʿalnī ʿalā khazāʾin al-arḍ*" (appoint me over the treasuries of the land).

The clause "*qāla ijʿalnī ʿalā khazāʾin al-arḍ*" (he said, appoint me over the treasuries of the land) is a report of his answer to the king's speech, and for this reason it is presented in the manner of dialogues.

Here "*ʿalā*" (over) denotes figurative elevation, which means authority and control. The meaning is: appoint me to have authority over the treasuries of the land.

*Khazāʾin* is the plural of *khizānah* (with a *kasrah* on the *khāʾ*), meaning the storehouse in which grains and wealth are stored. The definite article in "*al-arḍ*" (the land) is the definite of previous reference (*taʿrīf al-ʿahd*), meaning the land known to them, that is, the land of Egypt. What is meant by "*khazāʾin al-arḍ*" is treasuries that already existed, namely treasuries of wealth. For no ruler is without a number of established treasuries for the calamities of his lands, not the treasuries that were added later for storing provisions in preparation for the years referred to in His words, "*mimmā tuḥṣinūn*" (of what you store) [Yusuf: 48].

Yusuf's (peace be upon him) proposal of this was a preparation of himself to take charge of the community's welfare, following the custom of people of virtue and perfection, who are delighted to work for the public good. For this reason he did not ask for wealth for himself, nor for any worldly goods, but asked that the king appoint him over the treasuries of the kingdom, so that he might protect the wealth, distribute it justly, and treat the community kindly in gathering it and delivering it to its places.

[Page 9]

He justified his request with his words, "*innī ḥafīẓun ʿalīm*" (indeed I am a knowing guardian). The particle *inna* at the beginning of the clause makes it a justification of what precedes it. He knew that he possessed two qualities, both of which are difficult to find in people, indeed both together: guarding what is entrusted to him, and knowing how to manage what he takes charge of. This was so that the king would know that his high standing with him and his entrusting him had fallen upon their proper place and person, and that he deserved them because he possessed the qualities that fulfill their obligations. These are the quality of guarding, which secures trust, and the quality of knowledge, which secures standing. In this there is an explanation of his excellence so that people may be guided to follow him. This belongs to the category of *ḥisbah* (seeking reward, offering oneself for a good cause).

I say: this is an elegant comparison, since both were *ṣiddīq* (truthful, a title of high sincerity).

or if someone unfit for appointment takes it. Likewise, if someone whose appointment is not permitted has taken it, and there is no way to remove him except by the request of qualified people.

﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself." So when he had spoken with him, he said, "Indeed, today you are with us established and trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾

The meaning is "I will make him sincerely mine," that is, specially mine, with no one sharing him with me. This is a *kināyah* (allusion, a figure of speech by which a meaning is conveyed indirectly) for the intensity of his closeness to the king and his working closely with him. The king's choice of Yusuf (peace be upon him) for this closeness was based on what had become evident of his wisdom and knowledge, his patience in bearing hardships, and his good character and integrity. All of this made his selection necessary.

The clause "*falammā kallamahu*" (so when he had spoken with him) is built upon an omitted clause that is indicated by "*wa-qāla al-malik ītūnī bihi*" (the king said, bring him to me). The implied meaning is: so they brought him to him, that is, Yusuf (peace be upon him), and he came before him and spoke with him, and when he had spoken with him.

The object pronoun in "*kallamahu*" refers back to the king. Thus the speaker is Yusuf (peace be upon him), who spoke to the king with words that pleased him because of their wisdom and courtesy. For this reason, the clause "*qāla innaka al-yawma ladaynā makīnun amīn*" (he said, indeed today you are with us established and trustworthy) is the response to "*lammā*" (when), and the one who speaks is undoubtedly the king.

*Makīn*: an adjective of quality (*ṣifah mushabbahah*) from *makuna*, with the *kāf* pronounced with a *ḍammah*, when someone attains a high status (*makānah*), namely a great rank. It is derived from *makān* (place).

*Amīn*: an intensive form (*fa'īl*) in the sense of a passive participle (*maf'ūl*), meaning one who is entrusted with something, that is, one who is trusted in safeguarding it.

That this statement follows his speaking with the king indicates that Yusuf (peace be upon him) spoke to the king with the speech of a wise and courteous man. When the king saw the excellence of his speech, the eloquence of his words, and the soundness of his judgment, he regarded him as worthy of his trust and of being brought close to him.

[Page 8]

This is a phrase of appointment that encompasses all the qualities a ruler (*walī al-amr*) needs. Standing in a high position requires knowledge and ability, for through knowledge one can recognize what is good and aim toward it, and through ability one can carry out whatever good becomes apparent. Trustworthiness requires wisdom and justice: through wisdom one chooses right actions and avoids baseless pitfalls, and through justice one delivers rights to their rightful owners. This praise of Yusuf (peace be upon him) and this commendation of him are an implicit indication that the king wished to seek his help in the affairs of his kingdom, and to have him propose what he hoped would bring good. The clause "*qāla ijʿalnī ʿalā khazāʾin al-arḍ*" (he said, appoint me over the treasuries of the land) is a report of his answer to the king's speech, and for this reason it is presented in the manner of dialogues.

Here "*ʿalā*" (over) denotes figurative elevation, which means authority and control. The meaning is: appoint me to have authority over the treasuries of the land.

*Khazāʾin* is the plural of *khizānah* (with a *kasrah* on the *khāʾ*), meaning the storehouse in which grains and wealth are stored. The definite article in "*al-arḍ*" (the land) is the definite of previous reference (*taʿrīf al-ʿahd*), meaning the land known to them, that is, the land of Egypt. What is meant by "*khazāʾin al-arḍ*" is treasuries that already existed, namely treasuries of wealth. For this reason he did not ask for wealth for himself, nor for any worldly goods, but asked that the king appoint him over the treasuries of the kingdom, so that he might protect the wealth, distribute it justly, and treat the community kindly in gathering it and delivering it to its places.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 12, verses 56–57:**

﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle in it wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and were mindful of God.﴾ The tafsir (exegesis) of the verse ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾ has already been given shortly before. Al-tabawwu' means taking a place for settling (al-bawʾ), i.e., returning to it, so the meaning of tabawwu' is descending and residing. It has occurred before in His saying, ﴿that you two settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾ (Yunus: 87) in Surah Yunus. His saying, ﴿he settles in it wherever he wills﴾, is a kinaya (metonymy) for his disposal over the entire kingdom of Egypt, so that when he settles in one place of the kingdom, had he willed to settle elsewhere, he would have done so. Thus the clause yatabawwa'u (he settles) may be a hal (circumstantial clause) relating to Joseph, and it may be a bayan (explanatory elaboration) of the clause ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read ﴿wherever he wills﴾ with the ya' of the third person, while Ibn Kathir read ﴿wherever We will﴾ (Al-Zumar: 74) with the nun of majesty, meaning wherever God wills, i.e., wherever We command him or inspire him. The meaning is one, because he wills only what God has willed.

[Page 11]

The clause ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾ to its end is a tadhyil (concluding statement that reinforces and generalizes the preceding meaning), on account of its generality covering the specific mercy that befell Joseph, peace be upon him, in his circumstances in this world, and the positions of goodness he had, for which what he was given of blessings and elevated station was a recompense in this world, because God does not waste the reward of the good-doers. His reward in the Hereafter is better for him than that, and for everyone who believed and was mindful of God.

The expression regarding belief is in the past tense, and regarding God-consciousness (taqwa) in the present tense, because belief is the firm commitment of the heart, so it is attained in a single instance, whereas God-consciousness is renewed with the renewal of the causes of commands and prohibitions and the variation of deeds and times.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verses 58–60:

﴿And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.﴾ ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said: "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?"﴾ ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ The Qur'an omitted the final outcome of the matter of the wife of the ruler (imra'at al-'Aziz), the arrival of years of abundance and storing (al-khisb wa al-idkhar), and then the onset of years of drought (al-qahT), because all of that has little bearing on the purpose for which the surah was revealed, which is to show what the prophets encounter from their own kin and how the outcome becomes victory and the good end for them. Moreover, its occurrence is known. For this reason the narrative moved on to what it contains regarding the fate of the brothers of Joseph, peace be upon him, in their need of his favor; and to God's gathering him together with his brother whom he loves, then with his two parents; then to the manifestations of his pardon toward his brothers and his maintaining of kinship ties with them; because all of that has an effect in recognizing his virtues.

The coming of the brothers of Joseph, peace be upon him, to Egypt for provisions occurred when drought struck the land of Egypt and the lands bordering it from the regions of Palestine, the dwelling place of the family of Joseph, peace be upon him. Their coming was in the third year of the years of drought. The brothers came, apart from Benjamin because of his youth, and they all journeyed for provisions, perhaps because the supply of food was measured according to the number of those seeking provision. Also, so that they would be a group that highway robbers would not covet. Those who came were ten. It is known that they came as seekers of provisions from the earlier statement ﴿He said: "Set me over the storehouses of the land"﴾ [Yusuf: 55] and from his later statement ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure?﴾.

Their entering upon him indicates that he was supervising the sale of food by his own presence and permitting it in his council, out of concern that the staple foods be wasted, since in them is the life of the community.

Joseph, peace be upon him, recognized his brothers after years had passed since their separation, owing to the strength of his insight (firasa) and the acuity of his intellect, which were beyond theirs.

The clause ﴿and they did not recognize him﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the clause "fa-'arafahum" (so he recognized them). The report about them was given in a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) to indicate that their not recognizing him is a fixed and established matter in them. The report about his recognizing them was given in a verbal sentence (al-jumla al-fi'liyya), which conveys renewal, to indicate that his recognition of them occurred at the moment of seeing them, without deliberate scrutiny or reflection. The object of "munkirun" (not recognizing), which is the pronoun referring to Joseph, peace be upon him, was joined by the emphatic lam (lam al-taqwiya), and it was not said "wa hum munkirun" (and they are unrecognizing), in order to add emphasis to their ignorance of his identity.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase with the emphatic lam in "lahu munkirun" serves the rhyme (al-ri'aya 'ala al-fasila) and to highlight the connection of their denial to him, drawing attention to the fact that this is by the doing of God Most High; for otherwise Joseph's features are not of the kind that one would forget or fail to recognize.

Al-jihaz, with the jim vowelled either with a fatha or a kasra, is what the traveler needs; its primary sense is the loads he travels with. Al-tajhiz is giving the jihaz.

His saying ﴿Bring me a brother of yours﴾ implies that there had been prior talk among them about their having a brother from their father who had not come with them; otherwise, Joseph's informing them of this would have made them aware that he speaks to them knowing who they are, and he did not wish to disclose this to them. In the Torah it is stated that Joseph, peace be upon him, contrived for this by giving them the impression that he accused them of being spies for the enemy, or that they cleared themselves of this, so they informed him of their place among their people, of their father, and of the number of their household. When they mentioned this to him, he made it appear that he would take one of them as a pledge with him until they returned and brought their youngest brother, so that they would confirm their statement regarding what they had told him. For this reason he said ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me.﴾

And "min abikum" (from your father) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) modifying "akhin lakum," meaning his brotherhood is from the side of your father. This is from the concept of restriction (mafhum al-iqtisar), which indicates that no other is intended, i.e., from your father and not from your mother, meaning he is not a full brother.

The shift from saying "bring me your brother, from your father" to the indefinite form is because the intent is to relate what Joseph, peace be upon him, included in his speech of showing that he does not know their brother except through their mention of him before him. So he departed from the idafa, which implies definiteness, to indefiniteness, for the sake of feigning ignorance of him.

﴿Nor shall you come near me﴾ means: do not return to Egypt; and he knew that they would not leave their brother as a pledge.

His saying ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts﴾ is an encouragement for them to return to him, and he knew that they were compelled to return to him because the provisions they had obtained were insufficient for a family of many people like them, as indicated by their later statement ﴿That is a small measure﴾ [Yusuf: 65].

His saying ﴿the best of hosts﴾ indicates that he would lodge those seeking provision as his guests, because of the large number of those coming to Egypt for provisions. Al-munzil means the host. This clause is a metaphor (kinaya) for the promise that he would give them full measure and honor their hospitality if they brought their brother. The word "kayl" in both places is intended as the verbal noun. So the meaning of ﴿there will be no measure for you with me﴾ is: no measuring will be done for you, a metaphor for preventing them from buying food.

It is known that they came as seekers of provisions from the earlier statement ﴿He said: "Set me over the storehouses of the land"﴾ [Yusuf: 55] and from his later statement ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure?﴾.

Their entering upon him indicates that he was supervising the sale of food by his own presence and permitting it in his council, out of concern that the staple foods be wasted, since in them is the life of the community.

Joseph, peace be upon him, recognized his brothers after years had passed since their separation, owing to the strength of his insight (firasa) and the acuity of his intellect, which were beyond theirs.

The clause ﴿and they did not recognize him﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the clause "fa-'arafahum" (so he recognized them). The report about them was given in a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) to indicate that their not recognizing him is a fixed and established matter in them. The report about his recognizing them was given in a verbal sentence (al-jumla al-fi'liyya), which conveys renewal, to indicate that his recognition of them occurred at the moment of seeing them, without deliberate scrutiny or reflection. The object of "munkirun" (not recognizing), which is the pronoun referring to Joseph, peace be upon him, was joined by the emphatic lam (lam al-taqwiya), and it was not said "wa hum munkirun" (and they are unrecognizing), in order to add emphasis to their ignorance of his identity.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase with the emphatic lam in "lahu munkirun" serves the rhyme (al-ri'aya 'ala al-fasila) and to highlight the connection of their denial to him, drawing attention to the fact that this is by the doing of God Most High; for otherwise Joseph's features are not of the kind that one would forget or fail to recognize.

Al-jihaz, with the jim vowelled either with a fatha or a kasra, is what the traveler needs; its primary sense is the loads he travels with. Al-tajhiz is giving the jihaz.

His saying ﴿Bring me a brother of yours﴾ implies that there had been prior talk among them about their having a brother from their father who had not come with them; otherwise, Joseph's informing them of this would have made them aware that he speaks to them knowing who they are, and he did not wish to disclose this to them. In the Torah it is stated that Joseph, peace be upon him, contrived for this by giving them the impression that he accused them of being spies for the enemy, or that they cleared themselves of this, so they informed him of their place among their people, of their father, and of the number of their household. When they mentioned this to him, he made it appear that he would take one of them as a pledge with him until they returned and brought their youngest brother, so that they would confirm their statement regarding what they had told him. For this reason he said ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me.﴾

And "min abikum" (from your father) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) modifying "akhin lakum," meaning his brotherhood is from the side of your father. This is from the concept of restriction (mafhum al-iqtisar), which indicates that no other is intended, i.e., from your father and not from your mother, meaning he is not a full brother.

The shift from saying "bring me your brother, from your father" to the indefinite form is because the intent is to relate what Joseph, peace be upon him, included in his speech of showing that he does not know their brother except through their mention of him before him. So he departed from the idafa, which implies definiteness, to indefiniteness, for the sake of feigning ignorance of him.

﴿Nor shall you come near me﴾ means: do not return to Egypt; and he knew that they would not leave their brother as a pledge.

His saying ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts﴾ is an encouragement for them to return to him, and he knew that they were compelled to return to him because the provisions they had obtained were insufficient for a family of many people like them, as indicated by their later statement ﴿That is a small measure﴾ [Yusuf: 65].

His saying ﴿the best of hosts﴾ indicates that he would lodge those seeking provision as his guests, because of the large number of those coming to Egypt for provisions. Al-munzil means the host. This clause is a metaphor (kinaya) for the promise that he would give them full measure and honor their hospitality if they brought their brother. The word "kayl" in both places is intended as the verbal noun. So the meaning of ﴿there will be no measure for you with me﴾ is: no measuring will be done for you, a metaphor for preventing them from buying food.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 61:

Page 14
﴿They said, "We will try to get him from his father, and indeed we will do it."﴾

It is a promise that they will exert their utmost effort in bringing their brother, and an indication that this is difficult. So the meaning of ﴿we will try to get him from his father﴾ is: we will endeavour that he not withhold him, and this was already mentioned at His words, exalted is He, ﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself﴾ [Yusuf: 23].

The clause ﴿and indeed we will do it﴾ is coordinated with the promise, confirming the fulfilment of what was promised: they will do what he commanded them. They emphasised this with the nominal sentence and the particle of emphasis.

And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their families, that they may come back."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 62:

The majority of readers recited "لِفِتْيَتِهِ" (li-fityatihi), on the pattern *fi'lah*, as the broken plural of *fata* (young man), like *akh* (brother) and *ikhwah*.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim, and Khalaf recited "لِفِتْيانِهِ" (li-fityanihi), on the pattern *ikhwan*. The first is a form denoting a small number, and the second a form denoting a large number, and each of them is used for the other. The number of the young men does not differ.

A *fata* is one who is in the beginning of youth, and its feminine is *fatah*. It is also applied to a servant as a term of endearment, because they used to belittle youth in service, and they mostly employed slaves.

The *biḍāʿah* (merchandise) is wealth or goods prepared for trade. What is meant here is the silver coins with which they had bought the food, as in the Torah (al-Tawrah).

His saying, ﴿so that they may recognize it﴾, means hoping that they would know that it was the very merchandise they had paid, either because it was minted with the coinage of their land, or by recognizing the bundles in which it had been tied, as in the Torah. That is, they would know that it had been placed there intentionally as a gift from the Governor of Egypt.

[Page 15]

The *rihal* (saddlebags) is the plural of *rahl*, which is what is placed on a camel of the rider's belongings, and for this reason the camel is called *rahilah*.

The *inqilab* means returning. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿if you turn back on your heels﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 144], in the surah of Ali ʿImran.

The clause ﴿so that they may come back﴾ is the answer to the imperative in His saying, ﴿Put their merchandise into their saddlebags﴾, because when he ordered them to return, he sensed, through the effectiveness of his judgment, that they might not have merchandise with which to buy provisions, since he saw signs of hardship upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 12, verses 63–64:

﴿When they returned to their father, they said: "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send our brother with us, that we may measure (grain). Indeed, we will surely guard him."﴾ ﴿He said: "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted you with his brother before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

The meaning of ﴿measure has been withheld from us﴾ is: access to measuring (grain) has been barred between us and it in the future. Their return with provisions, which is expressed by "the supplies" (al-jihāz), implies that the withholding of measure would occur in the future. The phrase (mun'a minnā, "withheld from us") also indicates this, since they made the measuring something whose beginning was prohibited from them, because (min) is a particle of beginning.

Al-kayl (measuring) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that can carry the sense of either the agent or the object. Here it has the sense of being attributed to the agent, meaning "we will not measure," so what is prohibited is the beginning of measuring from them. Since they did not have in their hands anything to be measured, the measuring must be interpreted as seeking it, that is, "that was withheld from us, because there is no benefit in it, for we will not be granted it except when we fulfil what we promised concerning bringing our brother." For this reason, the clause ﴿so send our brother with us﴾ is correctly made a consequence of it. The sentence therefore becomes: "We have been prevented from seeking measure unless our brother comes with us." Hence it is determined that they related the story to their father in detail, and the Qur'an abbreviated it because the intended meaning was clear. The meaning is: "If you send him with us, we will travel for measuring and seek him." Applying the word "withheld" to this meaning is figurative (majāz), because they had been warned of deprivation, so their request became something prohibited to them, since seeking it would be futile.

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of reciters) read (nakhtal) with the first-person plural nūn of the speaker who is included. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf read it with a yā' (third-person prefix) in place of the nūn, referring it to (akhānā, "our brother"), meaning: "he will measure with us."

The clause ﴿and indeed we will surely guard him﴾ is conjoined to the clause (fa-arsil, "so send"). They emphasised his protection by using a nominal sentence, which indicates constancy, and by the particle of emphasis.

Their father's reply is an ambiguous statement which may mean: "I entrust him to you as I entrusted you with his brother," or it may mean: "What did your entrusting me with his brother before achieve, that I should entrust him to you?"

The interrogative is one of denial, containing the sense of negation. Thus it questions the reason for the emphasis in their words ﴿and indeed we will surely guard him﴾. The purpose of the sentence, under both possibilities, is the consequence stated in his words (﴿but Allah is the best guardian﴾), that is, "Allah is better at guarding than you are. If Allah protects him, he will be safe; if He does not protect him, he will not be safe, just as his brother was not safe before, when I entrusted him to you."

They were convinced by his answer and understood from it that he would send their brother with them, and for this reason they did not question him further about the matter.

(ḥifẓan, "guarding") is an accusative noun of specification (tamyīz) according to the reading of the majority. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Ḥafṣ read (ḥāfiẓan, "guarding") as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring to the name of Allah, and it is a necessary (lāzima) circumstantial state.

[Page 16]
