Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 65:

Page 17
﴿When they opened their goods, they found their merchandise had been returned to them. They said: "O our father, what more could we want? This is our merchandise, returned to us. We will bring provisions for our family, guard our brother, and gain an extra camel-load. That is an easy measure."﴾ The root meaning of matā' (goods) is what one enjoys of commodities and garments. It was mentioned earlier at His words, exalted is He, ﴿If you were heedless of your arms and your goods﴾ [al-Nisa': 102] in Surat al-Nisa'. Here it is applied to the sacks and loads of goods, by the figure of naming a thing after what it contains.

The sentence "They said: O our father" is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), answering the listener's expectation to know what they said when the discovery of their merchandise in their goods surprised them, since it was a striking surprise. For this subtle reason it was not joined with the particle fa'.

The (ma) in His words "what more could we want" may be an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari), treating the addressee as one who seeks from them the attainment of some aim, so they deny that they have any further aim: that is, "what do we seek after this?" It may also be a negating (ma) and the meaning is the same, since the denying interrogative carries the sense of negation.

The sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ explains the sentence ﴿what more could we want﴾ on both possibilities. They knew it had been returned to them by the indication of its being placed in the sack after the food was placed, whereas they had handed it to the measurers, or by the indication of what they witnessed from Yusuf, peace be upon him, of kindness toward them and the promise of good if they came with their brother, when he said: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?﴾ [Yusuf: 59].

The sentence ﴿and we will bring provisions for our family﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, because it has the sense of: "this is the price of what we need of provisions, which has come back to us, and with it we will bring provisions to our family," that is, we will go to them with provisions.

Al-mir'ah (provisions), with a kasra on the mim followed by a silent ya', is the food that is brought in.

Page 18
The sentence ﴿and guard our brother﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿and bring provisions for our family﴾, because procuring provisions requires travel to fetch them, and they had asked their father that their brother be a companion for them in the aforementioned journey. Thus the connection between the sentence ﴿and bring provisions for our family﴾ and the sentence ﴿and guard our brother﴾ is established on this basis, and they mentioned this to reassure a concern in him.

The sentence ﴿and gain an extra camel-load﴾ is an addition emphasizing their eagerness for the safety of their brother, because in his safety there is a benefit for them through the gain of an extra camel-load, since Yusuf, peace be upon him, would not give the one seeking provisions more than one camel-load of food, so if their brother were with them he would give them a camel-load for each brother. By this the connection between this sentence and the one before it becomes apparent.

These sentences are arranged in a wonderfully ordered sequence, since some of them arise from others.

The indication in ﴿That is an easy measure﴾ refers to the food that was in their goods. The application of "measure" to it is the application of the verbal noun to the object, by the indication of the demonstrative.

It is said that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said to them: "Perhaps they forgot the merchandise. So when you come to them, inform them that you found it in your baggage."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 66:

﴿He said: "I will never send him with you until you give me a binding oath by Allah that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are encompassed (by some calamity)." So when they gave him their binding oath, he said: "Allah is Witness over what we say."﴾

It is well known that "ita'" (giving) and "i'ta'" (bestowing) and what is meant by them in the making of an oath, so that the one to whom the oath is sworn may be reassured of the sincerity of the one who swears.

In the hadith of the Gathering (on the Day of Resurrection): "He will give Allah pledges and binding covenants that he will not ask Him for anything else" (fa-yu'ti Allaha min 'uhudin wa mawathiqa an la yas'alahu ghayrahu). Likewise, the verb "akhadh" (taking) is used for the one to whom the oath is sworn receiving it, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they took from you a solemn covenant﴾ [al-Nisa': 21], and ﴿Has not Allah already taken from you a binding oath?﴾ [Yusuf: 80].

Perhaps the reason for using the verb "i'ta'" is that in earlier times the one swearing would give the one to whom the oath was sworn something as a reminder of the oath, such as his whip or his ring, or that they would place with the holder of the right a guarantee that would be a pledge in his keeping. Surety (hamalah) was a method of securing commitments, so the oath was likened to surety, and giving and taking were attributed to it by way of metaphor (al-makniyyah). The opposite of this is well known in the nullification of a commitment, as one says: "He rejected his oath to him" (radda 'alayhi hilfahu).

"Al-mawthiq" originally is a mimi verbal noun of "al-tawthiq" (securing), and here it is used for the object, that by which security is obtained, meaning the oath.

"Min Allah" is an attribute of "mawthiqan," and "min" denotes origin, i.e., a binding oath proceeding from Allah the Exalted. The meaning of this is that they make Allah a witness over them regarding what they promised, by swearing by Allah, so that Allah's witnessing over them becomes, in this respect, like a binding commitment proceeding from Allah the Exalted. This is by their saying: "For you is the covenant of Allah" or "the pledge of Allah" or something similar, and in this way the covenant and pledge are attributed to the Name of Majesty, as if the one swearing had entrusted to Allah that by which security is given to the one to whom the oath is sworn.

The clause ﴿la-ta'tunnanni bihi﴾ ("you will surely bring him to me") is the answer to an omitted oath indicated by "mawthiqan." It is a reported statement of words that his sons were to be made to utter, reported in meaning according to the manner of reporting speech, because had they spoken the oath they would have said: "We will surely bring him to you." When he reported it, he composed the report with the clause that is their speech and with the pronouns suited to his own speech, addressing them directly.

Of this type is the saying of the Exalted concerning 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117], whereas what Allah commanded him was: "Say to them: Worship your Lord and their Lord."

The meaning of ﴿yuhata bikum﴾ is "an encompasser encompasses you." Ihata means seizing with destruction or capture, or something beyond their power. Its origin is the encircling of an army in battle, and it is used metaphorically for the state in which one cannot prevail. It has already been discussed at the words of the Exalted ﴿and they thought that they were encompassed﴾ [Yunus: 22].

The exception in ﴿illa an yuhata bikum﴾ is an exception from a general category of circumstances. The verbal noun formed from "an" with the verb is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is like a report by a verbal noun, so its interpretation is: "unless encompassed by you."

His saying ﴿wallahu 'ala ma naqulu wakil﴾ [al-Qasas: 28] is a reminder to them that Allah is a watcher over what passed between them. This is a confirmation of the oath.

"Al-wakil" is a form (fa'il) in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., one to whom affairs are entrusted. It has been discussed at ﴿they said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] in Surat Al 'Imran.

[Page 21]

*Wa-qala ya baniyya* ("And he said, 'O my sons'") is joined by coordination (*'atf*) to the clause ﴿Allah is Witness over what we say﴾ [Yusuf: 66].

The repetition of the verb *qala* ("he said") indicates that the two statements were made at different times, even though both were consequences of their giving him their covenant. This is because he was reassured about their care for his son and the benefit of their journey to obtain grain became clear to him. So his saying ﴿O my sons, do not enter from one gate﴾ was issued at the time they were preparing to depart. The purpose of relating this statement is the lesson contained in his words ﴿but I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾, and so on.

*Al-abwab* ("the gates") means the gates of the city. The mention of "the gate" has preceded just now. Memphis (*Mannafis*) was among the greatest cities of the world, and so it had many gates. He forbade them to enter it through one gate only out of fear that their number would attract the eyes of the city's people and its guards. Their appearance, being the appearance of strangers to the people of the city, could make them suspect that they were spies or thieves. Thus they might be imprisoned, or their movements might be watched, which would be harmful to them and would prevent them from reaching Yusuf (peace be upon him) quickly and from having their needs fulfilled. It has been said regarding wisdom: "Seek help in fulfilling your needs by keeping them secret."

Since the task of stationing guards and watchers is normally at the city gates, he limited his warning to entering through one gate, without warning them against walking in one street of the city's streets. He trusted that they knew the city's streets, so he did not fear their getting lost there. He also knew that Binyamin would be in the company of one of his brothers so that he would not get lost in the city.

By *al-mutafarriqah* ("dispersed") he meant *al-muta'addidah* ("multiple"), because he set it opposite to "one." The reason for deviating from "multiple" to "dispersed" is to point to the cause of the command, which is concealing the fact that they were one group.

The clause ﴿but I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾ is a parenthetical insertion at the end of the speech, meaning: "and I cannot avail you anything by this my advice." *Min Allah* ("from Allah") is connected to *ughni* ("I avail"), meaning: what I have commanded you is not able to avail by an availing that originates from Allah. Rather, it is good manners and standing at what Allah has commanded. If it coincides with what He has decreed, two benefits are achieved. If it contradicts what He has decreed, the benefit of obeying His commands is achieved, along with the soul being at peace from having neglected nothing.

The construction of ﴿but I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾ was explained previously at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever Allah intends for him fitnah, you cannot avail him anything from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], in Surat al-'Uqud.

By this he intended to teach them to rely on Allah's success and gentle favour, while taking the usual apparent means, out of good manners toward the One who established the causes and determines the subtleties, in observing both states. For we cannot know what Allah intends in actions. So it is upon us to recognize them by their signs, and this is achieved only by striving for them.

This is the secret of the question of *qadar* (divine decree), as indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Act, for each is made easy for that for which he was created," and in the report: "When Allah wills a matter, He makes its causes easy."

[Page 22]

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it while he is a believer, those – their striving will be appreciated﴾ [al-Isra': 19]. That is because the nature of causes is that their effects occur in their presence. But this may fail through the opposition of other causes contrary to those causes occurring at the same time, or because a single cause may be a cause of contrary things in different respects, so the one who takes the cause misses the intended effect. Were it not for the order of causes and their observance, human society would become unregulated and chaotic.

*Al-ighna'* ("availing") here is derived from *al-ghana'* – with a fatha on the ghayn and a long vowel – which means sufficiency, competence, and fulfilling what is important. Its origin is synonymous with *al-ghina'* – with a kasra on the ghayn and short vowel – and both together are the opposite of poverty. The use of *al-ghana'* with fatha and long vowel for sufficiency and competence became frequent as a metonymic figure (*majaz mursal*, a figure of speech in which a term is used for a related meaning). This is because whoever suffices and is sufficient has removed from himself the need for another to suffice him, and has removed from the one he suffices the need as well. This figurative usage became widespread until it dominated this verb. Therefore, in speech it became common to restrict *al-ghana'* – with fatha and long vowel – to this meaning, and to restrict *al-ghina'* – with kasra and short vowel – to the meaning of the opposite of poverty and the like, until the long-vowelled *al-ghana'* is hardly heard in the sense of the opposite of poverty. This is a fine distinction, one of the subtle points of their usage in the inflections of synonyms. As for what occurs in the words of Ibn Barri, that *al-ghana'* is a verbal noun arising from the verb *aghna* (with a hamza), with the augmenting element deleted, which gives the false impression that it has no simple (unaugmented) verb form, he only meant that the use of the verb *ghaniya* in this figurative sense has been abandoned and become obsolete, not that it has no simple verb form at all.

Accordingly, the meaning of the verb *aghna* in this usage is the meaning of intransitive verbs, and the hamza did not make it transitive. Perhaps its hamza indicates becoming possessed of sufficiency. For this reason its proper use is not to govern a direct object, but in most cases to be synonymous with an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*, cognate accusative), as in the words of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

*Ughni ghanā'a al-dhāhibīna ua'uddu li-l-hadathāni 'addā*

("I serve the service of those who have gone, and I am counted for calamities, counted one by one.")

[Page 23]

They say: *aghna fulanun 'an fulanin* ("so-and-so availed so-and-so"), meaning he sufficed in his place, and stood in his stead. They use it with an object, which is an unusual construction, since the particle *'an* in it expresses substitution, which is figurative passing over (*al-mujawazah al-majaziyyah*). The thing that is the substitute for another thing is said to pass over it, because it occupies its place during its absence, as if it passed over it. They called this passing over "substitution" and said that *'an* comes to express substitution just as *bi* (the particle "in exchange for") does. So the meaning of ﴿I cannot avail you﴾ is: "I cannot substitute for you," i.e., "I cannot suffice as a substitute for your own sufficiency."

*Min shay'* ("anything") takes the place of *shay'an* ("anything" in the accusative). *Min* is added to emphasize the generality of *shay'* in the context of negation. It is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Their intercession will not avail me anything﴾ [Ya-Sin: 23], meaning "of harm." The author of al-Kashshaf permitted in similar cases that *shay'an* be an absolute object, meaning "some amount of availing," which is the apparent meaning. He said regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and fear a day when no soul will compensate for another soul at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], "i.e., a little of compensation," like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they will not be wronged at all﴾ [Maryam: 60]. However, he also permitted that *shay'an* be a direct object, and this is not correct except according to the meaning of extension through omission and transitivity, i.e., by removing the governing preposition.

The clause ﴿The decision is only for Allah﴾ is in the position of giving the reason for the content of ﴿but I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾. *Al-hukm* ("the decision") here means disposal and determination. The meaning of restriction is that nothing is accomplished except what Allah wills, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah accomplishes His purpose﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. It is not for the servant to contend with Allah's will in reality. Rather, his duty is to seek matters through their causes, because Allah commanded that. The clause ﴿And enter from separate gates, but I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾ combines these two meanings.

The clause ﴿In Him I have put my trust, and in Him let the trusting put their trust﴾ is in the position of elucidation of the clause ﴿but I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾, to make clear to them that his instruction to take the means, together with the reminder to rely on Allah, is the meaning of *tawakkul* (trust in God, reliance), which many people misunderstand, either by limiting it or by denying it. For this reason he used the clause ﴿and in Him let the trusting put their trust﴾ as a command to them

[Page 24]

and to others, in the sense that it is the duty of those present and absent, and that this station is not restricted to the sincere truthful (*al-siddiqun*) but is the duty of every believer whose faith is complete and who does not mix his faith with the errors of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance).

[Page 25]

﴿When they entered from the gate their father had commanded, it did not avail them anything against God. It was only a need within the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled. And he was truly a possessor of knowledge, because of what We had taught him, but most people do not know.﴾ This is a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah), and the waw is a parenthetical waw (waw i'tirad).

The word ﴿ḥaythu﴾ (from where) indicates a direction, meaning: when they entered from the directions their father had commanded them to enter by. The clause that follows ﴿ḥaythu﴾ is what specifies the intended direction.

The clause ﴿When they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾ dispenses with many clauses that are implied, namely: they set out and entered from where their father had commanded them; and when they entered from where he had commanded them, they were safe from what he feared for them. Their entering from where he had commanded would not have availed them anything against God, had God decreed that they be overtaken, so the speech is concise (ijaz). The meaning of ﴿it did not avail them anything against God﴾ is that it would not have turned away God's decree from them, were it not that God had decreed their safety.

The exception in His words ﴿except a need﴾ is disjunctive (munqati', an exception not of the same kind), because the need that was in the soul of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, is not a part of the thing negated, namely that it avails them against God. So the sense is: "but a need within the soul of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, which he fulfilled."

Al-qada' (fulfilment) means execution (al-infadh), and the meaning of ﴿qadaha﴾ (he fulfilled it) is that he carried it out. It is said: "He fulfilled a need for himself" when he carried out what he had resolved in his soul. That is, it was counsel to his sons, which he delivered to them and did not withhold from them, so that his heart would be reassured that he had left nothing he thought beneficial to them without conveying it to them.

Al-hajah (need) is the matter that is desired. It is called a need because one is in need of it, so it is a case of naming by the verbal noun (ism al-masdar). The need that was in the soul of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, was his eagerness to alert them to the dangers that confront people like them on such a journey if they enter by one gate, and his teaching them to take the means (al-asbab) together with reliance upon God (tawakkul).

The clause ﴿And he was truly a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾ is parenthetical between the clause ﴿When they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾ etc., and the clause ﴿but most people do not know﴾.

It is a praise of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, for knowledge and planning, and that the counsel he gave them is part of the knowledge God granted him, which is from the knowledge of prophethood (nubuwwah).

His words ﴿but most people do not know﴾ are a corrective (istidrak) that arises from the clause ﴿When they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾ etc. The meaning is that God commanded Ya'qub, peace be upon him, to take the means of precaution and counsel, while knowing that this would not avail them anything against a destiny God had decreed for them, for the will of God, exalted is He, is hidden from people, and He had commanded the pursuit of the customary means. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew this, but most people do not know to seek both matters, so they neglect one of them. Some neglect knowing that apparent means do not repel a matter God has decreed and knows will occur, and others neglect the means while not knowing that God wills in some circumstances that they have no effect.

His words ﴿And he was truly a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾ indicate explicitly that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, acted upon what God had taught him. His words ﴿but most people do not know﴾ indicate by implication that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, was among the few people who knew how to observe both matters, so that the praise of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, is established by deriving it from the speech twice: once explicitly and once by the corrective.

The meaning is that most people are in ignorance about placing these realities in their proper positions, and they are not free of neglecting one of the two. This meaning is explained by the saying of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, when he commanded the Muslims to turn back from 'Amwas when news reached him of the spread of the plague (ta'un) there, and Abu 'Ubaydah said to him: "Are you fleeing from the decree of God?" Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "If anyone other than you had said it, O Abu 'Ubaydah! Are we not fleeing from the decree of God to the decree of God?..." up to the end of the report.

The placement of the clause ﴿When they entered upon Yusuf﴾ is like the placement of the clause ﴿When they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾ [Yusuf: 68], in terms of elliptical brevity (ījāz al-ḥadhf, concision through omission).

Al-īwāʾ (the verb āwā) means to bring back. It was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿Those, their refuge is the Fire﴾ [Yunus: 8], in Surat Yunus.

Here al-īwāʾ is used figuratively to mean bringing near and drawing close, as if he were bringing him back to a shelter. He brought him near only so that he could speak to him privately with His saying ﴿Indeed I am your brother﴾.

The clause ﴿He said: Indeed I am your brother﴾ is a substitute by inclusion (badal ishtimāl, apposition of inclusion) for the clause ﴿He took his brother to himself﴾. He addressed him with a brief, eloquent expression, since it informed him that he was the brother whom he had thought the wolf had devoured. He confirmed the news with inna (indeed), with the nominal sentence, and with the restriction conveyed by the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl, the pronoun of separation), namely the word (anā, I). The meaning is that I am restricted to being your brother and am not a stranger to you. This is a qaṣr qalb (restriction that corrects a mistaken belief), because he believed that the one speaking to him had no kinship with him.

He built upon this news with ﴿So do not be distressed by what they used to do﴾. Al-ibtiʾās (being distressed) is the reflexive form of al-ibʾās, meaning to make someone wretched, i.e., to become one who is in distress.

Al-bu's is grief and turbidity. A parallel of this construction was discussed in the story of Nuh, peace be upon him, in Surat Hud. The two pronouns in (kānū) and (yaʿlamūn) refer to their brothers by contextual indication. By this he meant what his brother Binyamin was experiencing of grief over the loss of his full brother and the harshness and jealousy of their brothers toward him.

The prohibition against ibtiʾās requires refraining from it. That is, remove grief from yourself and replace it with joy.

The verb of being in the past tense indicates that what is meant is what they did in the past. Phrasing (yaʿlamūn) in the present form indicates that these were repeated acts of harm. In this there is a preparation of his brother's soul to receive the incident of the drinking cup calmly, so that he would not fear that he was under suspicion from Yusuf, peace be upon him.

[p. 27]

﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking-cup (*al-siqāyah*) in his brother's saddlebag. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are surely thieves!"﴾ ﴿They turned to them and said, "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We are missing the king's measure (*ṣuwā‘*), and for whoever brings it, there is a camel-load [of grain], and I vouch for it."﴾ ﴿They said, "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves."﴾ ﴿They said, "What then is its penalty, if you are lying?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Its penalty is: whoever is found with it in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty. Thus do We requite the wrongdoers."﴾

The discussion of the similar phrase ﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾ has already occurred in the verses before this. The attribution of "he placed (*ja‘ala*) the cup" to the person of Joseph is a rational metaphor (*majāz ‘aqlī*): he was the one who gave the order to place it, while those who actually placed it were the servants entrusted with measuring.

The *siqāyah* is a large vessel from which water and wine are poured. The *ṣuwā‘* is a dialectal variant of *ṣā‘*, a measuring vessel estimated at the weight of a *ritl* and a quarter or a third. They used to drink wine by measure: each drinker would measure out for himself what he was accustomed to, such that it would not intoxicate him, and they would make the wine vessels of various measures, so the drinker would say to the cupbearer: "a *ritl*, or a *ṣā‘*, or something like that." Therefore, calling this vessel a *siqāyah* and calling it a *ṣuwā‘* is consistent with that practice. In the Torah it is called a *ṭās* (basin), and it is described as being of silver.

The definiteness of *al-siqāyah* is the definiteness of mental reference (*al-‘ahd al-dhihnī*), meaning a well-known cup, of the sort that is never absent from the assembly of a great man.

The attribution of the *ṣuwā‘* to "the king" serves to honour it and to magnify the seriousness of its theft in a literal sense, since all affairs of the state belong to the king. It is also possible that "the king" was applied to Joseph, peace be upon him, as a mark of honour.

*Ta’dhīn* means a repeated call. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Then a crier called out among them﴾ [al-A‘rāf: 44] in Surah al-A‘rāf.

*Al-‘ayr* is a term for the baggage-train of camels and donkeys, together with what is loaded on them and the riders with them; it is a term for the collective of these three. The theft is attributed to all of them, in keeping with the usual practice of holding a group accountable for the crime of one of its members.

The feminine form of the demonstrative *ayyatuhā* is used because *al-‘ayr* is taken to mean the group, since the riders are the more important part.

The clause ﴿They said﴾ is a response to the caller's address to them, ﴿You are surely thieves﴾; hence the clause is detached (*fuṣilat*), since it stands in the manner of dialogue, as has recurred more than once.

The pronoun in ﴿They said﴾ refers back to the caravan.

The clause ﴿They turned to them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relating to the pronoun in ﴿They said﴾. The pronoun in ﴿turned﴾ refers to Joseph's attendants, and the pronoun in ﴿to them﴾ refers to what the pronoun in ﴿They said﴾ refers to; that is, Joseph's attendants had turned toward them.

They set a reward (*ju‘l*) for whoever brings the cup. The one who said ﴿and I vouch for it﴾ was one of those who had turned toward them, and he was their eldest. *Al-za‘īm* means the guarantor.

The jurists have made this verse a basis for the legitimacy of the *ju‘l* (reward) and of *kafālah* (surety). This requires consideration, because Joseph, peace be upon him, was not at that time a bearer of a law (*sharʿ*), so that one might take as evidence the principle that "the law of those before us is law for us" when it is related by the speech of God or of His Messenger. Even if it is supposed that Joseph, peace be upon him, was then a prophet, it is not established that he was a messenger with a law, since it is not established that he was sent to the people of Pharaoh, and Joseph, peace be upon him, had no followers in Egypt before the arrival of his father, his brothers and their families. Hence this is a weak basis.

The *tā’* in ﴿By God (*tallāhi*)﴾ is, according to the preferred view, a particle of oath. It is specific to being prefixed to the name of God, the Exalted, and to the word *Rabb* (Lord). It is also specific to an oath about something remarkable. It will come at His saying ﴿And by God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 57] in Surah al-Anbiyā’.

Their saying ﴿You know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves﴾: they affirmed this with an oath, because they had previously come to Egypt once and had been accused of espionage, and then their innocence became clear by the fact that they told Joseph, peace be upon him, the truth about the condition of their father and their brother, as they described it to him. Thus "the land" here refers to the known land, which is Egypt.

As for their innocence of theft, it is by what they reported when they arrived, of finding their merchandise in their saddlebags, and perhaps it had been placed in their saddlebags by mistake.

Moreover, they negated from themselves the attribute of theft more emphatically than they negated corruption from themselves, by denying that they were thieves, rather than saying, "We did not come to steal." This is because theft is a quality that brings disgrace, whereas the corruption they denied, namely espionage, is something an enemy aims at against his enemy, so it is not a disgrace, although in the enemy's view it is an aggression.

The statement of the young men ﴿What is its penalty, if you are lying?﴾ is an act of arbitration (*taḥkīm*), because they could not do otherwise than specify a penalty by which they would be held accountable. This is the arbitration of a man concerning his own offence.

The meaning of ﴿What is its penalty﴾ is: what is its punishment. The pronoun in ﴿its penalty﴾ refers to the *ṣuwā‘*, with an omitted genitive construction indicated by the context; that is, "what is the penalty of its thief, or of his theft?"

The meaning of ﴿if you are lying﴾ is: if your lying is made clear by the presence of the cup in your saddlebags.

As for His saying ﴿Its penalty is: whoever is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty﴾: the first *jazā’uhu* (its penalty) is the subject (*mubtada’*). The word *man* (whoever) may be conditional, in which case it is a second subject, and the clause ﴿is found in his saddlebag﴾ is the conditional clause, and the clause ﴿he himself is its penalty﴾ is the response of the condition, with the *fā’* marking the response; the compound of the condition and its response is the predicate of the first subject. Or *man* may be a relative pronoun, the second subject, and the clause ﴿is found in his saddlebag﴾ the relative clause. The meaning is that whoever in whose saddlebag the cup is found, he is the penalty for the theft; that is, his very person is the penalty for theft, meaning that his person becomes a recompense for this crime, namely that he becomes a slave to the owner of the cup, so that the meaning of the penalty is fulfilled by another person. This is known from the context, since the intent is not the destruction of the thief's person, because the penalty for theft does not reach the level of capital punishment.

Thus the clause ﴿he himself is its penalty﴾ is a verbal emphasis (*ta’kīd lafẓī*) of the clause ﴿its penalty is whoever is found in his saddlebag﴾, to establish the ruling and to prevent escape from it. The *fā’* is for consequence, the consequence of emphasis upon what is emphasised. Joseph's brothers passed this judgment upon themselves, agreed to it, and so what they had committed themselves to was binding upon them.

It appears that this was a well-known ruling among the nations, that a thief be enslaved. This is close to the enslavement of the vanquished in battle. Perhaps it was a known ruling in Egypt, as will come shortly at His saying ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ [Yūsuf: 76].

The clause ﴿Thus do We requite the wrongdoers﴾ is the remainder of the speech of Joseph's brothers, peace be upon him; that is, "thus is the judgment of our people regarding the penalty of the wrongdoing thief for his theft." Or they meant that it is the judgment of the brothers concerning whoever among them is found to have the cup in his saddlebag; that is, he is deserving of being requited thus.

The demonstrative *kadhālika* (thus) refers to the penalty derived from *najzī* (We requite), meaning: We requite the wrongdoers with a penalty like that penalty, which is "whoever is found in his saddlebag."

The *tā’* in ﴿By God (*tallāhi*)﴾ is, according to the preferred view, a particle of oath. It is specific to being prefixed to the name of God, the Exalted, and to the word *Rabb* (Lord). It is also specific to an oath about something remarkable. It will come at His saying ﴿And by God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 57] in Surah al-Anbiyā’.

Their saying ﴿You know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves﴾: they affirmed this with an oath, because they had previously come to Egypt once and had been accused of espionage, and then their innocence became clear by the fact that they told Joseph, peace be upon him, the truth about the condition of their father and their brother, as they described it to him. Thus "the land" here refers to the known land, which is Egypt.

As for their innocence of theft, it is by what they reported when they arrived, of finding their merchandise in their saddlebags, and perhaps it had been placed in their saddlebags by mistake.

Moreover, they negated from themselves the attribute of theft more emphatically than they negated corruption from themselves, by denying that they were thieves, rather than saying, "We did not come to steal." This is because theft is a quality that brings disgrace, whereas the corruption they denied, namely espionage, is something an enemy aims at against his enemy, so it is not a disgrace, although in the enemy's view it is an aggression.

The statement of the young men ﴿What is its penalty, if you are lying?﴾ is an act of arbitration (*taḥkīm*), because they could not do otherwise than specify a penalty by which they would be held accountable. This is the arbitration of a man concerning his own offence.

The meaning of ﴿What is its penalty﴾ is: what is its punishment. The pronoun in ﴿its penalty﴾ refers to the *ṣuwā‘*, with an omitted genitive construction indicated by the context; that is, "what is the penalty of its thief, or of his theft?"

The meaning of ﴿if you are lying﴾ is: if your lying is made clear by the presence of the cup in your saddlebags.

As for His saying ﴿Its penalty is: whoever is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty﴾: the first *jazā’uhu* (its penalty) is the subject (*mubtada’*). The word *man* (whoever) may be conditional, in which case it is a second subject, and the clause ﴿is found in his saddlebag﴾ is the conditional clause, and the clause ﴿he himself is its penalty﴾ is the response of the condition, with the *fā’* marking the response; the compound of the condition and its response is the predicate of the first subject. Or *man* may be a relative pronoun, the second subject, and the clause ﴿is found in his saddlebag﴾ the relative clause. The meaning is that whoever in whose saddlebag the cup is found, he is the penalty for the theft; that is, his very person is the penalty for theft, meaning that his person becomes a recompense for this crime, namely that he becomes a slave to the owner of the cup, so that the meaning of the penalty is fulfilled by another person. This is known from the context, since the intent is not the destruction of the thief's person, because the penalty for theft does not reach the level of capital punishment.

Thus the clause ﴿he himself is its penalty﴾ is a verbal emphasis (*ta’kīd lafẓī*) of the clause ﴿its penalty is whoever is found in his saddlebag﴾, to establish the ruling and to prevent escape from it. The *fā’* is for consequence, the consequence of emphasis upon what is emphasised. Joseph's brothers passed this judgment upon themselves, agreed to it, and so what they had committed themselves to was binding upon them.

It appears that this was a well-known ruling among the nations, that a thief be enslaved. This is close to the enslavement of the vanquished in battle. Perhaps it was a known ruling in Egypt, as will come shortly at His saying ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ [Yūsuf: 76].

The clause ﴿Thus do We requite the wrongdoers﴾ is the remainder of the speech of Joseph's brothers, peace be upon him; that is, "thus is the judgment of our people regarding the penalty of the wrongdoing thief for his theft." Or they meant that it is the judgment of the brothers concerning whoever among them is found to have the cup in his saddlebag; that is, he is deserving of being requited thus.

The demonstrative *kadhālika* (thus) refers to the penalty derived from *najzī* (We requite), meaning: We requite the wrongdoers with a penalty like that penalty, which is "whoever is found in his saddlebag."

*Badaʾa* means *amara* (he ordered). Yusuf, peace be upon him, ordered that the search begin with the bags of the rest of his brothers before the bag of his full brother.

*Awʿiya* is the plural of *wiʿaʾ*, meaning a container (*al-ẓarf*). It is derived from *al-waʿy*, which means preservation (*al-ḥifẓ*). Beginning with the bags of others than his brother was meant to remove any suspicion that the one in whose bag it was found was the intended target from the outset. The feminine pronoun in *istakhrajahā* (he brought it out) refers to the drinking-cup (*al-siqāya*). This feminine form is a fine stylistic touch, since the reality was that it was a drinking-cup that had been made into a measuring vessel (*ṣuwāʿ*). It is like returning the last part of a sentence to its beginning (*radd al-ʿajuz ʿalā al-ṣadr*), a figure in which the end of a phrase echoes its start.

The discussion of ﴿So it was that We devised for Yusuf﴾ is the same as the discussion of ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾.

*Al-kayd* is an act by which one reaches a hidden aim through an outward appearance. Here *al-kayd* means the inspiration given to Yusuf, peace be upon him, for this well-crafted stratagem: placing the cup and searching the bags, and inspiring his brothers to that firm judgment.

The act of *kayd* is attributed to God because He is the one who inspires it, so He is its cause. The *kayd* is described as being for Yusuf, peace be upon him, because it was for his benefit.

The clause ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, except that God should will﴾ explains the *kayd* in terms of everything in it: the placing of the cup and the brothers' ruling against themselves, in a way that suits Yusuf's desire, peace be upon him, to keep his brother with him. Were it not for this, the law of the Copts would not have authorised that. It has been said that their law for the punishment of a thief was that the stolen property be taken from him, he be beaten, and he be made to pay twice the value of what was stolen, or twice its price. Mujahid said that ﴿in the king's law﴾ means in his ruling, which is the enslavement of the thief. This is what the apparent meaning of the verse requires, given His words, ﴿he could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾, meaning that without the stratagem of placing the cup in his brother's baggage, he could not have done so. Perhaps this was a ruling common among many nations. Do you not see their saying, ﴿whoever is found in his bag, he himself is its recompense﴾, as was mentioned earlier? That is, the king of Egypt was just, so no one was taken in his lands without right. Similar to this was the Roman law concerning the enslavement of a debtor. Therefore it is established that what is meant by *al-dīn* (the law) is the legal code, not absolute authority.

The meaning of the *lām* of denial (*lām al-juḥūd*, the negating *lām*) here is the negation that, in reality, there was any cause that would have authorised Yusuf, peace be upon him, to take his brother into his keeping.

The exception (*istithnāʾ*) is from the generality of the causes of taking his brother, which are negated. In the sentence there is an omitted preposition before the verbal *an* (that), namely the preposition of causation (*bāʾ al-sababiyya*), which is indicated by the negation of taking. That is, its causes. The sense is: except by means of God's willing, that is, that He inspire the depiction of his situation and permit Yusuf, peace be upon him, to act, in view of the many benefits for Yusuf and his brothers, both in the present and in the future for them and their descendants.

The clause ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ is a concluding appendage (*tadhyīl*) to the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, taking his brother, because in it there is the raising of Yusuf's rank, peace be upon him, at present, through the wise plan from the time of his private conversation with his brother until the drinking-cup was brought out from his baggage. It also raises the rank of his brother at present, by joining him to Yusuf, peace be upon him, in a comfortable and perfect life, receiving wisdom from him. It raises the ranks of his brothers and father in the future, by means of the raising of Yusuf's rank, peace be upon him, and his compassion towards them. So "degrees" is used figuratively for the strength of nobility, through the metaphor of the perceptible for the intelligible (*istiʿārat al-maḥsūs lil-maʿqūl*, a metaphor in which a sensible thing is borrowed to express an abstract one). This was mentioned earlier in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and men have a degree over them﴾ in Surat al-Baqara, and His words ﴿for them are degrees with their Lord﴾ in Surat al-Anfal.

[Page 33]

The clause ﴿and over every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾ is a second concluding appendage to the clause ﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf﴾, the verse as a whole.

In it there is evidence for the variation of people in knowledge, which indicates that the knowledge of the One who created their knowledge is not confined in its extent, and that He is above every limit of human knowledge.

The "above" (*al-fawqiyya*) is a figurative use for the nobility of a state, because nobility is likened to elevation.

He expressed the genus of the one who excels in knowledge by the attribute *ʿalīm* (one who knows), in view of its relation to the one who is above him, until it reaches the Absolute Knower, glory be to Him.

The apparent sense of the indefiniteness of *ʿalīm* is that it is meant to denote the genus, so it encompasses every described as possessing strength in knowledge, up to the point of ending at the knowledge of God, Exalted is He. The generality of this ruling with respect to created beings is unproblematic, but this generality must be restricted with respect to God, Exalted is He, by the evidence of reason, since there is no one who knows above God.

The indefiniteness may also be taken to indicate unity, so that what is meant is one Knower, and the indefiniteness is then for unity and magnification, namely God, Exalted is He, and so it needs no restriction.

The recitation of the majority (*al-Jumhūr*) is ﴿degrees whom We will﴾ with the noun *darajāt* in construct with *man nashāʾ* (whom We will). Ḥamza, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf recited it with tanwīn (nunation) on *darajātin*, taking it as a specifying accusative (*tamyīz*, an accusative noun clarifying the sense of a verb) for the action of *narfaʿu* (We raise), with its object being *man nashāʾ* (whom We will).

[Page 34]

﴿They said, "If he steals, then a brother of his has stolen before. But Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, 'You are worse in position, and God knows best what you describe.'"﴾ When they were confounded by the discovery of the drinking cup in their brother's baggage, what confounded people experience overtook them, and they made excuses for their claim of innocence from theft, when they said (﴿We were not thieves﴾ [Yusuf: 73]). They offered as an excuse that their brother had inherited the trait of theft from someone other than their father. They claimed that his brother, whose loss had been publicized, had stolen before. The servants of Joseph, peace be upon him, knew that the accused was a brother from another mother. Thus this is an excuse made by allusion to the side of the mother of the two brothers, who was the wife of their father, namely Rachel, daughter of Laban, the maternal uncle of Jacob, peace be upon him.

Jacob, peace be upon him, had four wives: Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and Leah, daughter of Laban and sister of Rachel, who was the mother of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun; Bilhah, the maidservant of Rachel, who was the mother of Dan and Naphtali; and Zilpah, also a maidservant of Rachel, who was the mother of Gad and Asher.

They said, "a brother of his has stolen before" (﴿a brother of his has stolen before﴾) only as a lie and a denial of the disgrace from themselves. Joseph, peace be upon him, had no earlier theft on that day. The brothers of Joseph, peace be upon him, were not prophets. There is a great difference between theft and lying when no harm results from it.

This speech was made in the hearing of Joseph, peace be upon him, in his judgment session.

His saying (﴿Joseph kept it hidden﴾) may permit the apparent pronoun to refer to the whole statement (﴿They said, "If he steals, then a brother of his has stolen before"﴾), by interpreting that statement as a saying in the sense of an utterance, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He (﴿It is a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]), after His saying (﴿My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99]). The meaning of (﴿kept it hidden within himself﴾) would then be that he bore it and did not show anger at it, and turned away from rebuking and punishing them, even though it was an accusation against him and a lie. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and Abu Hayyan incline toward this interpretation.

His saying (﴿He said, "You are worse in position"﴾) would then be a resumptive sentence reporting what Joseph, peace be upon him, openly answered them, in the manner of reporting a dialogue. It is a statement that does not imply the confirmation of what they attributed to the brother of their brother. That is: you are worse in your present condition, because your theft is witnessed, whereas the theft of your brother's brother is merely a claim. The verb (he said) favors this interpretation.

It is also possible that the pronoun of absence in (kept it hidden) refers to what follows it, namely His saying (﴿He said, "You are worse in position"﴾). Al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari explained it this way, meaning: he said within himself. This resembles the pronoun of the matter and the story (dhamir al-sha'n wa al-qissa), but its feminine form is due to interpreting it as a statement or a word. The clause (﴿He said, "You are worse in position"﴾) is then an explanation of the pronoun in (kept it hidden).

Concealment, on this interpretation, is used in its literal sense, which is hiding speech so that no listener hears it.

The clause (﴿and did not reveal it to them﴾) is said to be an emphasis of the clause (﴿Joseph kept it hidden﴾), and it is the nature of emphasis that it not be joined by a conjunction. The reason it is joined is the difference it contains from the preceding clause, through the added restriction (to them), which implies that he revealed to his brother that they were lying. It is also possible that what is meant is that he did not show them anger or punishment, as mentioned before, as an exaggeration of suppressing his rage. In that case the speech contains an implied suitable noun, meaning: he did not show its effect.

(Sharr) is an elative (ism al-tafdil), and its original form is ashharr. (Makanan) is a specification (tamyiz) for the relation of the superlative.

The word "place" (makan) is applied to a state by way of metaphor, and the state is theft. The application of place and standing (makana) to a state is common. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted is He (﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your standing"﴾ [al-An'am: 135]) at the end of Surat al-An'am. This is the comparison of attributing a quality to residing in a place. The meaning is that when they justified their brother's theft by saying that his brother had stolen before, then if a previous theft by one brother prepared the other brother for theft, they, with two brothers who had preceded them in theft, were more deserving of being thieves than the one whose brother had preceded him alone. The speech is also open to being understood as meaning: you are worse in condition than your brother here and the one before him, since those two are innocent of what you accused them of, while you are guilty against them both, for you cast the first of them into the well, and you supported the charge of theft against the second.

Then he followed it with the clause (﴿And God knows best what you describe﴾), which is a comprehensive statement. That is, God knows best your truthfulness in what you have described, or your lying. The intended meaning is that He knows their lie, so the meaning is: He knows best the condition of what you describe.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 12, verses 78–79:

﴿They said, "O ʿAzīz, indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are among the good-doers."﴾ ﴿He said, "God forbid that we should take anyone but him with whom we found our property. Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers."﴾

They addressed him with the description ʿAzīz, either because every head of an important office is called by a term synonymous with ʿAzīz, so that Yūsuf, peace be upon him, was ʿAzīz, just as the chief of police is called ʿAzīz, as mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿the wife of the ʿAzīz﴾; or because the office of the ʿAzīz who had purchased him had been added to him, so that he combined the authorities and they petitioned him concerning the taking of their brother.

They described their father with three attributes that call for compassion towards him: the tenderness of fatherhood, the state of old age, and his deserving to have his heart consoled, either because he was the elder of his people, or because he had reached the utmost limit of old age. The descriptions are thus presented to urge the release of the son, not for the sake of the basic information, since they had already informed Yūsuf, peace be upon him, of the news of their father.

By "the great one" (al-kabīr) is meant either the elder of his tribe, whose harm would grieve them all, and it is the custom of rulers to win over tribes; or it is an emphasis on (shaykhan), meaning that he had reached the extreme of old age in years. For this reason they made it a consequence of that, saying (﴿so take one of us in his place﴾), since he was the youngest of the brothers, and the youngest is closer to the father's tenderness towards him.

The clause (﴿indeed, we see you are among the good-doers﴾) is a causal clause explaining the granting of the request, not the request itself. The implied meaning is: "Do not reject our petition, for we see you are among the good-doers, and one such as you does not do what would grieve an aged father."

The word al-makān (place) originally means the location of being, i.e., that in which a body settles. Here it is used metaphorically to mean a substitute (ʿiwaḍ), because the substitute is placed by the one who takes it in the place of the thing it replaces, as in the ḥadīth: "This is in place of your argument" («هَذِهِ مَكانُ حُجَّتِكَ»).

(Maʿādh) is a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī) meaning refuge, which is seeking shelter in a place for protection. It was mentioned shortly before, in His saying, ﴿He said, "God forbid! Indeed, He is my Lord, who has made my residence good."﴾ [Yūsuf: 23].

This verbal noun is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, i.e., a cognate object) standing in place of its omitted verb. The implied meaning: "I seek refuge in God with a seeking." When the verb was omitted, the noun marked with the transitive preposition (bāʾ) was attached to the verbal noun by way of annexation (iḍāfa), so it was said (maʿādha Allāh), just as they said (subḥāna Allāh), as a substitute for (usabbiḥu Allāh). The thing sought refuge from is the verbal noun formed from (that we take anyone but him with whom we found our property), and the meaning is: the refraining from that; i.e., we seek God's protection that He preserve us from taking one who has no right to be taken, that is, that He preserve us from wrongdoing. This is because taking the one in whose possession the property was found became a right against him by his own judgment, since judgment has the force of the law. As for taking another, it is not permissible, for no one may enslave himself without a judgment. For this reason the refusal of that was justified by the statement that doing so would be wrongdoing.

The evidence for the causal justification is two things: the placement of (inna, indeed) at the beginning of the clause, and the bringing of the conditional particle (idhan, then), while the pronouns in (nazakhudha, we take), (wajadnā, we found), (matāʿanā, our property), (innā, indeed we) and (la-ẓālimūn, wrongdoers) are intended to refer to the speaker alone without a partner. It is possible that this is the use of the plural pronoun for majesty, relating his speech in the language in which he spoke, since he was a great man of the city. It is also possible that the first-person plural pronoun was used by him out of humility, likening himself to one who has a partner in the action; this is a usage found in speech. Among it is His saying, quoting al-Khiḍr, peace be upon him: ﴿We feared that he would overburden them with rebellion and disbelief, so we wished that their Lord would replace them…﴾, the verse from Sūrat al-Kahf.

As for why Yūsuf, peace be upon him, did not disclose his condition to them and command them then to bring their father: either because he feared that if he left them to their own choice they would plot against Binyāmīn, claiming that they were all returning to their father, and then once they were alone with Binyāmīn they would destroy him on the road; or because there was hostility between the Copts and the Canaanites during that period, and he feared that if he brought his kin to Egypt, suspicions of evil from the king of Egypt would fall upon him and upon them. So he waited until he found an opportunity for that. The king had shown him kindness, so it was not part of fidelity to him to do what he disliked or to cause him to think ill. Thus he awaited the king's death or the effort to win his approval in that way. Or he wished to learn from his brother, during the period of being alone with him, the circumstances of their father and family, so that he might see how to bring them or some of them. We will mention this at His saying, ﴿He said, "Do you know what you did to Yūsuf?"﴾ [Yūsuf: 89].

*Istay'asu* means *ya'asu* (they despaired). The *sin* and *ta'* add emphasis, as in ﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾ [Yusuf: 34] and *is'a'sama* (he abstained). Their despair "of him" means despair of his release of their brother, so this is an attribution of the judgment to the essence (*min ta'liq al-hukm bil-dhat*). What is meant is some of its circumstances, as the context indicates, for the sake of emphasis.

The majority of readers recite ﴿*istay'asu*﴾ with a *ta'* (tā' fawqiyya) after the *sin*, then a *ya'* (yā' taḥtiyya), then a *hamza* after the *ya'*, according to the original morphological form. Al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, is reported with a variant (*bi-khulf*) reciting it with an *alif* after the *ta'*, then a *ya'*, based on metathesis of place (*al-qalb fi al-makan*) followed by substitution of the *hamza*.

*Khalasu* means "withdrew and separated." Its root meaning is purity, being free from mixtures. Thus he would not believe what you report about taking Benjamin for the theft of the cup. He would not accept for himself to remain a stranger were it not for fear of his father, and his full brothers would not accept that they should plot against him as they plot against someone who is not a full brother.

This is either for the purpose of gently addressing their father in attributing theft to his son, or because they knew from their brother's trustworthiness what made doubt about the theft occur to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 83:

﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾

The sentence ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made [it] attractive"﴾ is placed in the form of a reply to the speech that their brother had taught them, by way of concision. The estimated meaning is: they returned to their father and said that speech which Ruben had taught them. Their father said: "Rather, [your souls] have made [it] attractive..." and so on.

His words here are like his words to them when they claimed that Yusuf (peace be upon him) had been eaten by the wolf; it is an accusation against them of deceiving their brother. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He thought ill of them, and his thought about them was correct in their claim concerning Yusuf (peace be upon him), but he was not certain of what he thought about the matter of Binyamin; that is, he was mistaken in his thought about them in the matter of Binyamin. His basis for this thought was his knowledge that his son does not steal, so he knew that in the claim of theft there was a plot. His thought is therefore correct in general, not in detail. As for his accusation against his sons, that they had conspired against their brother Binyamin, it is a thought based on analogy with what had previously happened concerning the matter of Yusuf (peace be upon him), for he had said to them, "Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?" And it is permissible for a prophet to be mistaken in thought regarding matters of ordinary custom, as came in the hadith about leaving the date palms unpollinated.

Perhaps he accused Ruben of having hidden himself in order to promote the claim of his brothers. The pronoun in ﴿them﴾ refers to Yusuf (peace be upon him), Binyamin and Ruben. This is a disclosure from him, since he had not despaired of the life of Yusuf (peace be upon him).

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾ is a justification for his hope from Allah: Allah is All-Knowing, so their scattered whereabouts are not hidden from Him; All-Wise, so He is able to create the means of bringing them together after their separation.

[Page 42]

﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from grief, for he was suppressing (his grief).﴾ ﴿They said, "By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become wasted or become among the perishing."﴾ ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God, and I know from God what you do not know."﴾ ﴿O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people.﴾

This is a transition to narrating the state of Ya'qub (peace be upon him) when he was alone, away from his sons, and conversing with himself. So the "turning away" (tawalli) follows the exchange. Tawalli means he departed, and it was a departure of anger.

Since turning away implies seclusion, he mentioned one of his states: the renewal of his sorrow over Joseph (peace be upon him). So he said (﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾). Al-asaf means intense grief; asif is like hazina (to grieve).

The calling of asaf is a metaphor (majaz). He treated the grief as one who understands, saying to it, "Be present, for this is the time of your presence." He attributed the grief to his own self, because this particular grief was specific to him among the particular instances of the genus of grief.

The alif is a substitute (iwad) for the ya' of the first person, since in the vocative the ya' is replaced by an alif.

The Qur'an mentioned his grief over Joseph (peace be upon him) and did not mention his grief over his two other sons, because that grief is what relates to this story. Mentioning it does not imply that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) never grieved except over Joseph, especially since the conjunction "wa" (and) does not indicate the sequential order of the clauses it joins.

[Page 43]

Likewise is the conjunction of the clause "and his eyes turned white from grief," since the whitening of his eyes would only have occurred over a long period. So each of the turning away, the grieving, and the whitening of the eyes is among his states, though they differ in time.

Ibyad al-'aynayn (the whitening of the two eyes) means weakness of sight. It is evident that the blackness of their pupils changed due to emaciation. For this reason, the expression "his eyes turned white" was used rather than "his eyes became blind."

The "min" (from) in His saying (﴿from grief﴾) is causal (sababiyya). Grief is the cause of the abundant weeping, which is the cause of the whitening of the eyes. In my view, the whitening of the eyes is a metonymy (kinaya) for loss of sight, as al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Before today, she whitened eyes of people,
in them there is aversion and refusal."

And the grief is the cause of loss of sight, as is the apparent meaning, for the successive sensation of grief upon the brain led to the disabling of the optic nerve's function. Moreover, weeping from grief is a natural matter, so its occurrence from a prophet is not strange. Or it may be that patience (tasabbur) in calamities was not part of the Israelite law, but rather it was among their customs to show grief and distress at calamities. The Torah relates the weeping of the Children of Israel over Musa (peace be upon him) for forty days, and it relates that some prophets tore their garments out of distress. Patience in calamity is a perfection to which the Islamic law has attained.

Al-kazim is an intensive form of al-kazim (one who suppresses). Al-kazm is inward restraint, meaning he suppresses his grief and does not show it among people, and he weeps in his seclusion. Or it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, meaning "grieved," like His saying "and he is maksum" (suppressed).

The clause (﴿They said, "By God..."﴾) is the dialogue of his sons with him when they heard his saying (﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾). He had said it in his seclusion, and they heard it.

The ta' is a particle of oath, and it is a substitute for the waw of oath. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf, in the chapter of al-Anbiya': the ta' carries an additional meaning, which is wonder (ta'ajjub). Ibn Hisham accepted this in Mughni al-Labib.

[Page 44]

Al-Tibi explained that what is sworn by the ta' is something rarely occurring, because the thing that causes wonder does not frequently occur. Hence the use of the ta' is rare except with the Name of God, since swearing by the Name of God is the strongest form of oath.

The answer to the oath is (﴿you will not cease remembering Joseph﴾), in view of the limit that follows it, since the intent of this oath is to express pity for him, that he is heading toward destruction because he does not forget the calamity of Joseph (peace be upon him). The intent is not to affirm that he will never cease remembering Joseph. The answer of the oath here contains a negation particle that is implied, as shown by the absence of the emphatic nun attached to it, for if it were affirmative, the emphatic nun would have to be attached. So the negation particle is omitted here.

The meaning of (tafta') is tafturu (he will slacken). It is said: fati'a (from the pattern 'alima), when one slackens regarding something. The meaning is: you will not slacken while remembering Joseph. Because the negation is tied to this verb and there is a state that follows its agent, it became similar to the defective verbs (af'al nakisa).

(Haraḍan) is a verbal noun meaning the intensity of an illness that brings one near death. It is used as a description by means of the verbal noun, meaning "until you become haradan," that is, wasted, having no awareness. Their intent is disapproval of him, to prevent him from constantly mentioning Joseph (peace be upon him) with his tongue, since mentioning him with the tongue leads to his constant presence in the mind.

In their making the limit to be haraḍ or destruction, there is an allusion (ta'rid) that he mentions a matter for which there is no hope of recovery. So he answered them that his mention of Joseph (peace be upon him) is directed to God, as a supplication that God return him to him. Thus his saying, "Alas for Joseph!" is an allusion to supplicating God to remove his grief by returning Joseph (peace be upon him) to him, because he knew that Joseph had not perished, but was in a land of strangeness, unknown. He knew this by revelation (wahy) or by true insight (firasa), which is called inspiration (ilham) among the Sufis.

So the clause (﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾) conveys the restriction of his complaint to attachment to the Name of God, meaning he complains to God, not to himself, so as not to renew the grief. Thus the complaint, with this intent, became supplication (dara'a), which is worship, since supplication is worship. And the whitening of his eyes, arising from the remembrance that arose from the complaint, [Page 45] became a bodily effect arising from worship, like the swelling of the feet of the Prophet (ﷺ) from standing in night prayer.

Al-bathth is intense concern, which is thinking about a troubling matter. Al-huzn is grief over something lost. So between concern and grief there is partial overlap (al-'umum wa al-khusus al-wajhi), and both were united in Ya'qub (peace be upon him), because he was preoccupied with thinking about the fate of Joseph (peace be upon him) and the distress he faced in his exile, and he was grieving over his separation.

He followed his speech with His saying (﴿and I know from God what you do not know﴾) to alert them to the deficiency of their minds in grasping lofty purposes, so that they would know they are below the rank of knowing it or of blaming him. That is: I know by knowledge from God, which He taught me, that you do not know, and it is the knowledge of prophethood. A similar clause was mentioned earlier in the story of Nuh (peace be upon him) in Surat al-A'raf, so this is from the speech of the first prophecy. A similar statement is related from Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

In this there is an allusion that rejects their allusion that he hopes for the impossible, [implying] that what they consider impossible will occur.

Then he clearly told them some of what he knew, and revealed to them what establishes their lie in claiming that the wolf devoured Joseph (peace be upon him), when God permitted him that at the time the trial's end was determined. So he said (﴿O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother﴾).

The clause (﴿O my sons, go﴾) is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because in His saying (﴿and I know from God what you do not know﴾) there is something that arouses in their souls the expectation of his disclosing their lie, for the one who schemes often suspects (﴿they think every cry is against them﴾, Surat al-Munafiqun: 4).

Al-tahassus with the unpointed ha' means intense seeking and recognizing; it is more general than al-tajassus with the jim, for the latter is seeking with concealment and secrecy.

Al-rawh with a fatha on the ra' is breath, with a fatha on the fa'. It was borrowed for the removal of distress, because distress and worry are both described as ghamm (affliction), constriction of breath, and constriction of the chest. Likewise, breathing and relief (tarawwuh) are applied to the opposite of that. From this is the borrowed expression: "the dawn breathed" when the darkness of night departed.

[Page 46]

In their address to them with the description of sonship there is gentleness toward them and tenderness, so that it would more effectively move them to comply.

The clause (﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people﴾) is a causal justification for the prohibition against despair, so the position of "inna" is causal. The meaning is: do not despair of succeeding in finding Joseph (peace be upon him), citing the long duration of separation, after which reunion is ordinarily unlikely. For when God wills to relieve a distress, He prepares its causes. Whoever believes that God is all-powerful does not deem such a thing impossible, so it is incumbent upon him to take up its cause and rely upon God to facilitate it. As for the disbelieving people who disbelieve in God, they confine themselves to what is usual and typical, and they deny anything beyond it.

Al-Bazzi, by one of two transmissions from him, read (wa la ta'yasu) and (innahu la ya'yasu) with the hamza placed before the second ya', and this was discussed in His saying (﴿when they despaired of him﴾).

[Page 42]

﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from grief, for he was suppressing (his grief).﴾ ﴿They said, "By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become wasted or become among the perishing."﴾ ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God, and I know from God what you do not know."﴾ ﴿O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of God. [Page 46]
