The fa' (فاء) here is conjunctive, coordinating with an implied statement understood from the context, meaning: they set out for Egypt with the aim of securing the release of Benjamin from the 'Aziz of Egypt, and then by seeking to investigate about Yusuf (peace be upon him). So they reached Egypt, and they entered upon Yusuf, and when they entered upon him, etc. . .

The reason for their addressing Yusuf (peace be upon him) with the title al-'Aziz has already been mentioned earlier.

By "touch of adversity" they meant that affliction had reached him. The use of "touch of adversity" to mean affliction has already been mentioned at the words of the Exalted, (﴿And if Allah touches you with adversity﴾ [al-An'am: 17]) in Surat al-An'am.

Al-bidha'ah (بِضاعَة, merchandise) has already been discussed earlier. Al-muzjah (المُزْجاة) refers to that which is little and not desired, as though its owner propels it (yuzjihā), i.e., pushes it forward with difficulty so that the one to whom it is pushed will accept it. What is meant by it is wealth that is

Page 47
small, for the purpose of procuring grain; and for this reason the phrase ﴿so give us full measure﴾ is made a consequence of it. They sought charity from him as an allusion to the release of their brother, because that would be a favor from him, since (Benjamin) had become his property, as has been mentioned earlier.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable﴾ serves as a reason for their request that he be charitable to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 12, verses 89–93:

﴿He said, "Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Are you indeed Yusuf?" He said, "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers."﴾ ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were certainly sinners."﴾ ﴿He said, "No reproach upon you today. Allah will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face; he will regain his sight. And bring me your whole family.﴾

The interrogative is used for rebuke (al-tawbikh).

The particle (hal) here conveys confirmation (al-tahqiq), because it has the sense of (qad) in interrogation. So the rebuke concerns something they know with certainty regarding Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother, namely their blameworthy deeds, as the context of rebuke indicates. With regard to Yusuf (peace be upon him), this is clear. As for Binyamin, it refers to how they treated him, along with his brother Yusuf (peace be upon him), with the humiliation that is incompatible with brotherhood. For this reason, he described that time as a time of their ignorance by saying: (﴿when you were ignorant﴾).

There is also an allusion (ta'ridh) that their condition had since become righteous. This was either by revelation from Allah, if he had by then become a prophet, or by insight (al-firasa), because when he saw them eager to fulfil their father's wishes, in seeking the ransom of Binyamin when he had been seized on the charge of theft, and in seeking his release in this situation with insistence, and since he knew from them their opposition to their father regarding Binyamin, he knew that they had returned to righteousness.

[Page 48]

He revealed his identity to them only now, because knowledge of his position required bringing his father and family to live in the land under his authority, and that depended on matters which perhaps were not arranged until then. We have already pointed to this at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Allah forbid that we take anyone except him with whom we found our property"﴾ [Yusuf: 79]. Yusuf (peace be upon him) had by then become of firm standing (jadd makin) with Pharaoh.

In Chapter 45 of the Book of Genesis (Sifr al-Takwin), it is said that Yusuf (peace be upon him) said to his brothers at that time, "God has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his house, and ruler over all the land of Egypt." The apparent meaning is that the king who released Yusuf (peace be upon him) from prison and made him the 'Aziz of Egypt had died, and his successor, a son of his, was under Yusuf's (peace be upon him) influence. He became to the young king like a father and came to act as he wished. So he saw the situation as favourable for bringing his kinsfolk to the land of Egypt.

The names of the kings of Egypt in this period in which Yusuf (peace be upon him) lived are not known, because the kingdom at that time was divided into two kingdoms. One of them had kings of the Copts, who are the kings that Western historians (al-Ifranj) divide into the fifteenth, sixteenth, seventeenth and part of the eighteenth dynasties.

The second kingdom had kings from the Hyksos. They are called the Amalekites or the Shepherds, and they were Arabs.

This division lasted five hundred and eleven years, from 2214 BC to 1703 BC.

Their saying (﴿Are you indeed Yusuf?﴾) indicates that they perceived it first from his speech, then from his features, then from their understanding of their father's words to them: ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾ [Yusuf: 86], since the allusive meaning of his speech had become clear to them, and so they knew that he was speaking about himself.

[Page 49]

The emphasis of the sentence by (inna), the lam of emphasis, and the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) reflects the intensity of their certainty that he was Yusuf (peace be upon him).

The confirmatory interrogation (al-istifham al-taqriri) was applied to the emphasised sentence, because they sought his confirmation, although they already knew it.

Ibn Kathir read (innaka) without interrogation, as a declarative statement. The intended meaning is the necessary implication of a statement, namely, "we have recognised you." Do you not see that his answer with "I am Yusuf" is without emphasis, because they were already certain of that? So there remained only his confirmation of it.

His saying (﴿and this is my brother﴾) is a declarative statement used to express wonder at Allah bringing the two of them together after long separation. Thus the clause (﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾) is an explanation of what is meant by the clause (﴿and this is my brother﴾).

The clause (﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient﴾) is a reason for the clause (﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾). Yusuf (peace be upon him) feared Allah and was patient, and Binyamin was patient and did not disobey Allah, so he was among the God-fearing. Yusuf (peace be upon him) intended to teach them the means of attaining the blessings of Allah, may He be exalted, and urged them to piety and to acquiring patience, alluding to the fact that they had not feared Allah concerning him and his brother, and had not been patient in the face of their father's preference for those two over them.

This is one of the refinements of rhetoric (afanin al-khitaba): the preacher seizes the opportunity to deliver admonition, which is the moment when the listener is affected and moved and the signs of the preacher's sincerity in his admonition become evident.

The mention of (al-muhsinin, the good-doers) is the placing of an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun. The expected form would have been: "Indeed Allah does not waste their reward." He turned from this to (al-muhsinin) to indicate that this is a matter of goodness, and for generality in the ruling, so that it serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil), and so that he and his brother enter within its scope.

Furthermore, this is in the context of speaking about a blessing, and conveying admonition is permissible for prophets, since it is part of conveying the message, like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, I am the most God-fearing of you and the most knowing of Him."

[Page 50]

Al-iithar (preference) means preference in giving. The form of the oath is used with its necessary implication, namely their knowledge and certainty that what he had attained was a preference from Allah, and that they recognised his rank. The aim is not to inform him of that, because Yusuf (peace be upon him) already knows it. The meaning is preference in the world through what Allah gave him of blessings.

They acknowledged their sin when they said (﴿and we were certainly sinners﴾). The one who is khati' is the doer of a sin (khati'a), that is, a crime. So the admonition benefited them.

For this reason, he informed them that the sin had been forgiven, and thus blame was lifted from them. He said, "No reproach upon you."

Al-tathrib means rebuke and reprimand. The apparent view is that the sentence ends at his saying "upon you," because this kind of saying functions as a proverb, which is built on brevity, so one suffices with (﴿no reproach﴾), like their saying "la ba's" (no harm), and His saying, may He be exalted, (﴿There is no refuge﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11]).

The addition of (upon you) is for emphasis, like the addition of (laka) after (saqya wa ra'ya, may you be watered and pastured). Therefore the word (today) is not part of the sentence, but is connected to the verb (﴿Allah will forgive you﴾). He followed this by informing them that Allah would forgive them at that very hour, because it was an hour of repentance. So the sin is forgiven by the announcement of Allah in His earlier laws, without need for further revelation, except that the revelation was for recognising the sincerity of their repentance.

He applied the word "today" to a period of time. It was discussed earlier at His saying, may He be exalted, (﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾) at the beginning of Surah al-Ma'idah.

His saying (﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾) indicates that he gave them a shirt. Perhaps he made his shirt a sign for his father of his being alive, and perhaps that was an agreed signal between them. In the ancient social order, families had signs which they agreed upon and kept as means of recognising one another during times of strife and estrangement, since they were exposed to events of loss and separation through raids, incursions and highway robbery. These signs were clothing, words by which they recognised one another (shi'ar), and marks on the body and birthmarks.

[Page 51]

The benefit of his sending the shirt to his father was that his father would be confident of his life and existence in Egypt, and would not suspect the invitation to come as a plot from the king of Egypt, and in order to hasten joy for him.

The more evident view is that he made sending his shirt a sign of the truthfulness of his brothers regarding what they would convey to their father about Yusuf (peace be upon him) and their bringing him. Indeed, the shirts of kings and nobles were woven specially for them and similar ones were not found among people, and kings used to bestow them upon their close associates. So Yusuf (peace be upon him) made sending his shirt a sign to his father of the truthfulness of his brothers, that they had come from Yusuf (peace be upon him) with a true report.

It is far-fetched to say that the shirt was the shirt of Abraham (peace be upon him), since the shirt of Yusuf had already been brought to their father by his brothers when they came to him with false blood.

As for casting the shirt over his father's face, it was for the purpose of surprising him with good tidings, because he could not see from afar, and so he would not perceive the lifting of the shirt except from close by.

As for his becoming able to see again, this came to Yusuf (peace be upon him) by revelation, and so he gave them the good news of it from that moment. Perhaps Yusuf (peace be upon him) was informed of it at that very time.

The command to bring his father was incorporated into the announcement of his father's existence through a eloquent idmaj (a rhetorical device of incorporation, where one matter is embedded within another), when he said (﴿he will regain his sight﴾), and then said (﴿And bring me your whole family﴾), for the purpose of maintaining the ties of kinship with his relatives. The commentators said: the family of Ya'qub (peace be upon him) numbered seventy-six persons, men and women.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 12, verses 89–93:

﴿He said, "Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Are you indeed Yusuf?" He said, "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers."﴾ ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were certainly sinners."﴾ ﴿He said, "No reproach upon you today. Allah will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face; he will regain his sight. And bring me your whole family.﴾

The interrogative is used for rebuke (al-tawbikh).

The particle (hal) here conveys confirmation (al-tahqiq), because it has the sense of (qad) in interrogation. So the rebuke concerns something they know with certainty regarding Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his brother, namely their blameworthy deeds, as the context of rebuke indicates. With regard to Yusuf (peace be upon him), this is clear. As for Binyamin, it refers to how they treated him, along with his brother Yusuf (peace be upon him), with the humiliation that is incompatible with brotherhood. For this reason, he described that time as a time of their ignorance by saying: (﴿when you were ignorant﴾).

There is also an allusion (ta'ridh) that their condition had since become righteous. This was either by revelation from Allah, if he had by then become a prophet, or by insight (al-firasa), because when he saw them eager to fulfil their father's wishes, in seeking the ransom of Binyamin when he had been seized on the charge of theft, and in seeking his release in this situation with insistence, and since he knew from them their opposition to their father regarding Binyamin, he knew that they had returned to righteousness.

[Page 48]

He revealed his identity to them only now, because knowledge of his position required bringing his father and family to live in the land under his authority, and that depended on matters which perhaps were not arranged until then. We have already pointed to this at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Allah forbid that we take anyone except him with whom we found our property"﴾ [Yusuf: 79]. Yusuf (peace be upon him) had by then become of firm standing (jadd makin) with Pharaoh.

The apparent meaning is that the king who released Yusuf (peace be upon him) from prison and made him the 'Aziz of Egypt had died, and his successor, a son of his, was under Yusuf's (peace be upon him) influence. He became to the young king like a father and came to act as he wished. So he saw the situation as favourable for bringing his kinsfolk to the land of Egypt.

The names of the kings of Egypt in this period in which Yusuf (peace be upon him) lived are not known, because the kingdom at that time was divided into two kingdoms. One of them had kings of the Copts, who are the kings that Western historians (al-Ifranj) divide into the fifteenth, sixteenth, seventeenth and part of the eighteenth dynasties.

The second kingdom had kings from the Hyksos. They are called the Amalekites or the Shepherds, and they were Arabs.

This division lasted five hundred and eleven years, from 2214 BC to 1703 BC.

[Page 49]

The confirmatory interrogation (al-istifham al-taqriri) was applied to the emphasised sentence, because they sought his confirmation, although they already knew it.

Al-dalal is distance from the path that leads to the goal. The use of the locative sense is a figurative usage (majaz) of strong attribution and of being characterized by something, as when the one contained is characterized by the container. The meaning is: you are persistently engaged in seeking something outside its proper path. They meant his hope of meeting Joseph, upon him be peace, and they described that as "old" because of its long duration. The period of Joseph's absence from his father, upon them both be peace, was twenty-two years. Their address to him in this way contained some harshness, since the courtesy of his clan did not forbid such speech by their customs.

The purpose of the emphasis in this verse is to confirm this honour granted to Ya'qub, upon him be peace, since it is a breach of the normal course. For this reason, (inna) is not used in similar verses where there is no reason for emphasis.

Al-bashir is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of mufa''il, that is, "the one who gives glad tidings," like al-sami' (the hearer) in the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

It was discussed previously at His words ﴿Their Lord gives them glad tidings of mercy from Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 21] in Surat Bara'a. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 101:

Page 59
﴿My Lord, You have given me [some] of the dominion and taught me [some] of the interpretation of narrations, Creator of the heavens and the earth. You are my protector in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.﴾ He followed the mention of God's blessing upon him with turning to intimate supplication to his Lord, acknowledging the greatest blessings of this world and the supreme blessing of the Hereafter. He mentioned three blessings: two worldly, namely the blessing of authority over the land and the blessing of knowledge, and a third, otherworldly, which is the blessing of the true religion, expressed as Islam.

He made what was given to him "some" of the dominion and "some" of the interpretation, because what he was given is a part of the kind of dominion and a part of the interpretation, indicating that this, in relation to God's dominion and God's knowledge, is a small thing. Accordingly, "dominion" here means the great management resembling the management of a king, since Yusuf, peace be upon him, was the one who directed the realm by his own judgment. It is also permissible that "dominion" be understood in its literal sense, with the partitive being literal, meaning: You gave me some of the dominion, since dominion is the totality of dispositions concerning the affairs of the subjects, and Yusuf, peace be upon him, had the largest share of that. Likewise is the interpretation of narrations. The meaning of "interpretation of narrations" has already been explained at the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿And He will teach you of the interpretation of narrations﴾ [Yusuf: 6] in this surah.

"Creator of the heavens and the earth" is a vocative whose particle of address is omitted. "Fatir" means the Creator. It was already discussed at the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Shall I take other than God as a protector, Creator of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-An'am: 14] in Surat al-An'am.

"Wali" means the helper, and it was already discussed at the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Shall I take other than God as a protector?﴾ [al-An'am: 14] in Surat al-An'am.

The clause ﴿You are my protector in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is, in form, a declarative statement within a supplicatory utterance; although it is possible to take it as informative regarding the protection of this world, it is said that it is for affirming that matter for the protection of the Hereafter. So the meaning is: Be my protector in this world and the Hereafter.

Page 60

The Muslim is the one who has attained Islam, which is the complete religion, the same that God worshipped the prophets and messengers with, peace be upon them. It was already discussed at the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132] in Surat al-Baqarah.

**Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, on Surah 12, verse 102:**

﴿That is of the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you, and you were not with them when they resolved on their affair while they were scheming.﴾ This is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to the story at the end of its narration.

The demonstrative refers to the events mentioned, i.e., "that which has been mentioned." The demonstrative is used to distinguish the tidings in the most complete distinction, so that they may settle in the minds of the listeners because of the admonitions contained in them.

Al-ghayb (the unseen) is that which is hidden from the knowledge of people. Its origin is the verbal noun of *ghaba* (to be absent), and then the thing that is not witnessed was named by it. The masculine pronoun in (*nuhihi*, "We reveal it") is for the sake of agreement with the demonstrative.

[Page 61]

The pronouns in ﴿*ladayhim*, "with them"; *idh ajma'u amrahum*, "when they resolved on their affair"; *wa hum yamkurun*, "while they were scheming"﴾ refer to all who acted in this manner in this story, men and women, by way of the rule of predominance (taghlib). They include the brothers of Joseph, peace be upon him, the caravan (al-sayyara), the wife of the Minister (al-'Aziz), and her women.

The phrase ﴿ajma'u amrahum﴾ is explained by His saying: ﴿and they resolved to put him into the depths of the well﴾ [Yusuf: 15].

Al-makr (scheming) has already been discussed, and this sentence is a drawing out of the points of lesson from the story. In it there is a favour (minnah) upon the Prophet ﷺ, and an allusion to the polytheists, alerting them to the inimitability of the Qur'an from the scientific side, for the issuing of this from the unlettered Prophet ﷺ is a great sign that it is a revelation from Allah, the Exalted. For this reason it is followed by His saying: ﴿And most people, even if you should strive, will not be believers﴾ [Yusuf: 103].

In His saying ﴿*wa ma kunta ladayhim*, "and you were not with them"﴾ there was a rebuke (tawarruk) directed at the polytheists.

The clause ﴿*wa ma kunta ladayhim*﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), since it completes the expression of wonder.

The clause ﴿*wa hum yamkurun*, "while they were scheming"﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (*ajma'u*, "they resolved"), and (*yamkurun*, "they scheme") was given in the present tense (mudari') to bring the wondrous state vividly before the mind.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verses 103–104:

﴿Most of mankind will not believe, however eager you are.﴾ ﴿You ask them no wage for it; it is only a reminder to all the worlds.﴾ This is a transition from narrating this story to the lesson about the polytheists' determination to deny the truth after these clear proofs. The conjunction "wa" (and) coordinates with the sentence ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you﴾ (Yusuf: 102), in view of what it conveys: that this Qur'an is a revelation from God, and that it is worthy of calling its hearers to belief in the Prophet ﷺ. Since this was of a nature to raise hope in their faith, it was followed by informing the Prophet ﷺ that most of them do not believe.

The word "al-nas" (mankind) may be taken to refer to the whole genus of mankind, or it may mean specific people, namely the people whom the Prophet ﷺ called in Makkah and its surroundings, in which case it is a generality of customary usage ('umum 'urfi).

The sentence ﴿however eager you are﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), interposed between the particle "ma" and its predicate.

"Law" (even if/however) here is a conjunctive particle (lau wasliyya), which indicates that its condition represents the utmost of the means toward its answer. Its explanation was previously given at the words of the Most High ﴿Never will be accepted from any of them the earth full of gold, even if he offers it in ransom﴾ (Al 'Imran: 91) in Surat Al 'Imran.

The answer to "law" is ﴿Most of mankind will not believe﴾, which is placed before it, or it is the indicator of the answer.

"Al-hirs" (eagerness) is intense pursuit to obtain something and persistence in it. It was previously discussed at the words of the Most High ﴿eager for you﴾ (al-Tawbah: 128) at the end of Surat Bara'a.

The sentence ﴿You ask them no wage for it﴾ is coordinated with the sentence ﴿Most of mankind will not believe﴾ to its end, in view of what it conveys of despair regarding the belief of most of them. That is: their unbelief should not grieve you, for you do not seek that their belief be a recompense for the delivery of the message; rather, their belief is for their own benefit, as in His saying ﴿Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour upon me﴾ (al-Hujurat: 17).

The plural pronoun in His saying ﴿You ask them﴾ refers back to "mankind", that is, those to whom the Prophet ﷺ was sent.

The sentence ﴿it is only a reminder to all the worlds﴾ serves as the reason (ta'lil) for the sentence ﴿You ask them no wage for it﴾. The restriction (qasr) is relative (qasr idafi): that is, it is only a reminder to all the worlds, not for obtaining a wage for the one who conveys it.

The pronoun in "'alayhi" (for it) refers back to the Qur'an, known from His saying ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you﴾ (Yusuf: 102).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verses 105–106:

Page 63
﴿And how many a sign there is in the heavens and the earth which they pass by, yet they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah except while associating others with Him.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And most of mankind, even if you should strive, are not believers﴾ [Yusuf: 103]. That is, their aversion is not limited to the sign of the unlettered man's acquisition of knowledge through what is in the earlier scriptures alone; rather, they turn away from many signs in the heavens and the earth.

And (kaʾayyin) is a noun indicating a large but indefinite number, which is specified by a genitive tamyiz introduced by (min). It was discussed previously at His words, exalted is He, ﴿And how many a prophet fought, along with him many devoted followers﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 146], in Surat Ali ʿImran.

The word (ayah) means the sign. Here it means what indicates the oneness of Allah, exalted is He, by the indication of the mention of associating partners after it.

The meaning of ﴿they pass by it﴾ is they see it. The passing (murur) is a metaphor (majaz mursal) used as a figure of speech (kinayah) for realization and witnessing, since the literal sense of passing cannot be applied to the signs of the heavens. So the passing here is like that in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72].

The pronoun in (yamurruna) refers to mankind, from His words, exalted is He, ﴿And most of mankind, even if you should strive, are not believers﴾ [Yusuf: 103].

The clause ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (yamurruna). That is: and most of mankind do not believe except while they are associators. The intended meaning of "most of mankind" is the people of polytheism among the Arabs. This is a refutation of what they claim of acknowledging that Allah is their Creator, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ and that their belief in Allah is as nothing, because they do not believe in the existence of Allah except by associating with Him another in divinity.

The exception is from the generality of states, so the clause ﴿while they are associators﴾ is a circumstantial clause from (akthoruhum). The aim of this is to censure their condition. It is most apparent that this is of the category of affirming a matter by what resembles its opposite, in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum). The attribution of this ruling to most of them is in regard to most of their states and statements, since statements devoid of mention of a partner may issue from them. The intended meaning is not that some of them believe in Allah without associating another deity with Him.

Page 64

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 107:

﴿Do they then feel secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming covering of the punishment of Allah, or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive?﴾ This is a parenthetical statement (i'tirad) introduced as a consequence (tafri') of what the two preceding sentences indicated, namely the depiction of their terrible state, their audacity toward their Creator, and their persistence in that without giving up. Thus, in their turning away from expecting the outbreak of Allah's wrath upon them, they are secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming covering of His punishment in this world, or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly, so that it will come between them and repentance, and they will proceed to the everlasting punishment.

The interrogative (istifham) here is used for rebuke (tawbikh).

Al-ghashy and al-ghashayan: encompassing from every direction. ﴿And when a wave covers them like shade-canopies﴾ [Luqman: 32]. It was discussed in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] in Surat al-A'raf. Al-ghashiyah: the calamity that encompasses people. The Arabs make these calamities feminine, like al-tammah (the great calamity), al-sakhkhah (the deafening blast), al-dahiyah (the great calamity), al-musibah (the misfortune), al-karithah (the catastrophe), al-hadithah (the event), al-waqi'ah (the event), and al-haqqah (the inevitable reality).

Al-baghtah: the sudden onset (al-fajʼah). It was discussed in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 31], at the end of Surat al-An'am.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 12, verse 108:

﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah upon insight, I and whoever follows me. And glory be to Allah; and I am not of those who associate others with Allah.﴾ This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) marking a shift from the lesson drawn from the revelation of this story to the Prophet ﷺ, who was unlettered, as proof of the truth of his prophethood and of the truth of what he brought of monotheism, to the lesson drawn from all that this Sharia brought from Allah, Exalted is He. This is what is expressed by "the way" (al-sabil), used metaphorically to convey it to the goal, which is the eternal success, just as a road conveys a traveler to the intended place. This metaphor is recurrent in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-sabil may be feminine, as in this verse, and may also be masculine, as already mentioned under His words ﴿And if they see the way of guidance, they will not take it as a way﴾ [al-A'raf: 146] in Surah al-A'raf. The sentence is an independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) placed as a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated sentences.

The reference to the Sharia by treating the intelligible as if it were perceptible is because it has reached such clarity to the intellects that none is unaware of it except one who is not regarded as a perceiver. The ambiguity in the sentence ﴿this is my way﴾ is explained by the sentence ﴿I call to Allah upon insight﴾.

Al-basira (insight) is a form (fa'ila) in the sense of the active participle (fa'ila), and it means the clear proof. The meaning is: I call to Allah with insight, being firmly grounded in it. Describing the proof as "insight" is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli). The basir (one who sees) is the possessor of the proof, because by it he has become truly seeing. Similar to this is the description of the signs as "mubsira" (making seeing) in His words ﴿So when Our signs came to them as making seeing﴾ [al-Naml: 13], and conversely, obscurity is described as blindness, as in His words ﴿And has given me mercy from Him, but it has been made obscure to you﴾ [Hud: 28].

The pronoun (anā) is an emphatic confirmation of the concealed pronoun in (ad'u). It was brought in to beautify the conjunction with His words ﴿and whoever follows me﴾, and this beautification is obligatory in the language.

The verse indicates that the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers who have believed in him are commanded to call to faith in what they are able to. They have carried this out by means of spreading the Qur'an, the pillars of Islam, and jihad in the way of Allah. In the early period of the Muhammadan mission, calling to Islam was an obligation upon every individual (wajib 'ala al-a'yan), according to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Convey from me, even if it is one verse," meaning according to one's capacity. Then, when Islam became manifest and its call reached the ears, calling to it became an obligation upon the community as a whole (wajib 'ala al-kifaya), as indicated by His words ﴿Let there be from you a community that calls to good﴾ [Al 'Imran: 104], the verse in Surah Al 'Imran.

The clause ﴿and glory be to Allah﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿I call to Allah﴾, meaning: I call to Allah and I exalt Him. Subhana is a verbal noun (masdar) of tasbih, used in place of the verb for emphasis. The implied sense is: "and I glorify Allah with glorification," meaning I call people to His unity and obedience and I exalt Him above the deficiencies with which the polytheists associate Him, such as claiming partners, offspring, and consorts.

The clause ﴿and I am not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil) of what precedes it, because it encompasses what that contained.

[p. 67]

This is a continuation (*'atf*, conjunction) on the sentence ﴿Yet most people are not believers, even if you are eager﴾ [Yusuf: 103], etc. The meaning of these two verses is connected to what is contained in His saying, ﴿That is part of the news of the unseen, which We reveal to you﴾ [Yusuf: 102], up to His saying, ﴿It is only a reminder for all the worlds﴾, and His saying, ﴿Say: This is my way﴾ [Yusuf: 108], the verse. Those verses contained the proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he brought them,

[p. 68]

and they contained that those who associated partners with God were not affirming him, out of obstinacy and turning away from the signs of truthfulness. So the meaning is that the sending of messengers, peace be upon them, is an ancient divine practice (*sunnah ilahiyyah*). Why, then, do the polytheists make your prophethood something impossible, so that they do not believe in it despite the signs of truthfulness that accompanied it, and so they say ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra': 94]? And were the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, anything other than men from the people of the towns, to whom God revealed? So in what way were they superior to you? The polytheists thus acknowledged their being sent, spoke of their stories, and denied your prophethood.

Behind this there is another meaning of admonition: the equality of the circumstances of the messengers, peace be upon them, and what they encountered from their peoples. It is therefore a warning that the outcome will be equal for both groups.

The phrase ﴿from before you﴾ is connected to ﴿We sent﴾, so *min* (from) indicates the beginning of time periods, and the referent of "before" becomes the earlier periods, i.e., from the very first times of sending. Without the presence of *min*, "before you" would function as a descriptive modifier of the messengers, implied by the verb of sending.

*Rijal* (men) is a generic noun (*ism jins*) that has no conceptual restriction. It is used here to mean people (*unas*), as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man who remembered God in solitude, and his eyes overflowed." That is, a human being or a person. The intention is therefore not to exclude women. It was chosen here over other words because it matches the reality: God did not send women as messengers, for the wisdom that peoples accept leadership from men in their souls, since a woman is considered weak in the eyes of men, but not the reverse. Do you not see the saying of Qays ibn 'Asim when Sajah claimed prophethood:

"Our prophetess has become a female, whom we circle around,
And the prophets of the people have become males."

The specification of "men" and that they were "from the people of the towns" is not for the purpose of excluding women or the people of the desert. Rather, it is to show the similarity between those who accepted the message of earlier messengers and Muhammad (ﷺ), when they said ﴿Then let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5], and ﴿They said: Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ [al-Qasas: 48]. That is, Muhammad (ﷺ) was no novelty among the messengers, so that you should hasten to deny his message and turn away from considering his signs.

[p. 69]

Thus the restriction is relative (*qasr idafi*): the messengers, peace be upon them, before you were not angels, nor kings of great cities. There is therefore no indication in the verse negating the sending of a messenger from the people of the desert, such as Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi, or Ya'qub, peace be upon him, when he lived in the desert, as was mentioned earlier.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *yuha* with a *ta'* below... [i.e., with the letter *ya'* and with a fatha on the *ha'*], in the passive voice. Hafs read it with *nun*, as active, and the *nun* is the *nun* of majesty.

The branching of His saying ﴿Have they not traveled in the land?﴾ is upon what the sentence ﴿We did not send before you except men﴾ indicates of the model (*uswah*). That is: their peoples denied them before your people, just as your people denied you, and their outcome was punishment. ﴿Have they not traveled in the land and seen what was the end of those before them?﴾ That is, they should see the traces of the last state of their affairs: destruction and punishment. Thus your people would know that their end is by analogy with the end of those who denied the messengers before them. The pronoun in *yasiru* refers to something known from the context that indicates it, and what I am not of the polytheists.

The interrogation is denunciatory (*inkari*), for the totality of those spoken of traveled in the land and saw the end of the deniers, like 'Ad and Thamud. This branching is an interjected threat and warning.

*Kayf* (how) is an interrogative that suspends the verb of seeing from its object.

The clause ﴿and the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾ is a predicate, conjoined to the interjection, so it has its ruling. It is an interjected good news and a promise of good outcome for the messengers, peace be upon them, and for those who believed in them, and they are ﴿those who had taqwa﴾. It is an allusion to the safety of the outcome of the God-fearing in this world, and also an allusion that the abode of the Hereafter is even harsher for those before them than the outcome that was in this world. Thus there is brevity by omitting two clauses.

The construction of *dar* (abode) with *akhirah* (hereafter) is an annexation of a described noun to its descriptor, like "O women of the Muslims" in the hadith.

[p. 70]

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ with the *ta'* of address, by way of *iltifat* (shift of address), because when the obstinate ones were mentioned and their mention was repeated, they became like those present, so the address turned to them directly. The rest read it with the *ya'* of the third person, in keeping with what precedes it.

*Hatta* (until) in His saying ﴿until when the messengers despaired﴾ is initial (*ibtida'iyyah*), and it conjoins the clause ﴿when the messengers despaired﴾ to the clause ﴿We did not send before you except men whom We revealed to﴾, in the sense that it is proof against the deniers. The meaning therefore is: We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, and those to whom they were sent denied them and persisted in denial, until, when the messengers despaired... For *idha* is a temporal noun carrying the meaning of a condition, so it requires an annexation to a clause that specifies the time. The clause *istay'asa* (despaired) is annexed to *idha*, and the clause ﴿Our help came to them﴾ is the answer of *idha*, because this order in meaning is what is intended by bringing *idha* in such a structure. The "messengers" here, peace be upon them, are not the same as the "men" mentioned, so the definiteness of "the messengers" is definiteness of remembered reference, and it is among the explicit nouns in the place of the pronoun, to give the speech independence in meaning and to emphasize the clause.

The particle of limit (*hatta*) signals an omitted meaning indicated by the clause ﴿We did not send before you except men﴾ with what is intended by it of the sense of taking the earlier messengers as a model. The meaning is: their denial and aversion continued, and the fulfilment of what they warned them of, namely the punishment, was delayed, until they felt secure in safety, mocked the messengers, and the messengers, peace be upon them, despaired of their people's faith.

*Istay'asa* (despaired) is an intensified form of *ya'isa*, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿and do not despair of the mercy of God﴾ [Yusuf: 87].

It was also mentioned earlier that al-Bazzi, by a variant from him, read with the *hamza* placed before the *ya'*. These are four words in this surah in which al-Bazzi differed from his narration.

[p. 70 continued]

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Urwa, that he asked 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her: "Were they denied (*kudhdhibu*) or were they lied to (*kudhibu*)?" That is, with the light or the emphatic form? She said: "They were denied (*kudhdhibu*), that is, with the emphatic form." He said: "Then they were certain that their people had denied them, so it was not a matter of supposition." She said: "They were lied to (*kudhibu*), that is, with the light form." She said: "God forbid! The messengers, peace be upon them, did not think this about their Lord. Rather, they were the followers of those who believed and affirmed, so the affliction lengthened upon them and the help was delayed, until, when the messengers, peace be upon them, despaired of the faith of those among their people who denied them, and the messengers, peace be upon them, thought that their followers would deny them." End of quotation.

This statement of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, is her own opinion in interpretation. Her rejection that it be read as *kudhibu* in the light form is a rejection based on what appears from the return of pronouns to the nearest preceding mention, which is "the messengers." That is not definitive, and 'A'isha had not received the transmission of the reading *kudhibu* with the light form.

The branching of ﴿and We deliver whom We will﴾ upon ﴿Our help came to them﴾ is because the help of the messengers, peace be upon them, is their support by punishing those who denied them with the descent of punishment, which is *ba's* (violent punishment). So God delivers those who believed, and His might is not averted from the guilty people. *Ba's* is the punishment of the guilty, which is the help of the messengers, peace be upon them, and "the guilty people" are those who denied the messengers.

Al-Jumhur read *fanunji* with two *nun*s, a light *jim*, and a sukun on the *ya'*, as the imperfect of *anja*. And *man nasha'* (whom We will) is the object of *nunji*. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read *fanujjiya* with one *nun* with a damma, a stressed *jim* with a kasra, and a fatha on the *ya'* below, as the past of *najja* (the doubled form), built for the passive. In that case *man nasha'* is the deputy subject. The combination of the past in *nujjiya* with the present in *nasha'* is an *ihtibak* (an implicit compensatory omission), its sense being: "so whom We willed of those who were saved in earlier generations was delivered, and We will deliver whom We will of the deniers in the future."

[p. 67]

This is a continuation (*'atf*, conjunction) on the sentence ﴿Yet most people are not believers, even if you are eager﴾ [Yusuf: 103], etc. The meaning of these two verses is connected to what is contained in His saying, ﴿That is part of the news of the unseen, which We reveal to you﴾ [Yusuf: 102], up to His saying, ﴿It is only a reminder for all the worlds﴾, and His saying, ﴿Say: This is my way﴾ [Yusuf: 108], the verse. Those verses contained the proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he brought them,

[p. 68]

and they contained that those who associated partners with God were not affirming him, out of obstinacy and turning away from the signs of truthfulness. So the meaning is that the sending of messengers, peace be upon them, is an ancient divine practice (*sunnah ilahiyyah*). Why, then, do the polytheists make your prophethood something impossible, so that they do not believe in it despite the signs of truthfulness that accompanied it, and so they say ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra': 94]? And were the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, anything other than men from the people of the towns, to whom God revealed? So in what way were they superior to you? The polytheists thus acknowledged their being sent, spoke of their stories, and denied your prophethood.

Behind this there is another meaning of admonition: the equality of the circumstances of the messengers, peace be upon them, and what they encountered from their peoples. It is therefore a warning that the outcome will be equal for both groups.

The phrase ﴿from before you﴾ is connected to ﴿We sent﴾, so *min* (from) indicates the beginning of time periods, and the referent of "before" becomes the earlier periods, i.e., from the very first times of sending. Without the presence of *min*, "before you" would function as a descriptive modifier of the messengers, implied by the verb of sending.

*Rijal* (men) is a generic noun (*ism jins*) that has no conceptual restriction. It is used here to mean people (*unas*), as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man who remembered God in solitude, and his eyes overflowed." That is, a human being or a person. The intention is therefore not to exclude women. It was chosen here over other words because it matches the reality: God did not send women as messengers, for the wisdom that peoples accept leadership from men in their souls, since a woman is considered weak in the eyes of men, but not the reverse. Do you not see the saying of Qays ibn 'Asim when Sajah claimed prophethood:

"Our prophetess has become a female, whom we circle around,
And the prophets of the people have become males."

The specification of "men" and that they were "from the people of the towns" is not for the purpose of excluding women or the people of the desert. Rather, it is to show the similarity between those who accepted the message of earlier messengers and Muhammad (ﷺ), when they said ﴿Then let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5], and ﴿They said: Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ [al-Qasas: 48]. That is, Muhammad (ﷺ) was no novelty among the messengers, so that you should hasten to deny his message and turn away from considering his signs.

[p. 69]

Thus the restriction is relative (*qasr idafi*): the messengers, peace be upon them, before you were not angels, nor kings of great cities. There is therefore no indication in the verse negating the sending of a messenger from the people of the desert, such as Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi, or Ya'qub, peace be upon him, when he lived in the desert, as was mentioned earlier.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *yuha* with a *ta'* below... [i.e., with the letter *ya'* and with a fatha on the *ha'*], in the passive voice. Hafs read it with *nun*, as active, and the *nun* is the *nun* of majesty.

The branching of His saying ﴿Have they not traveled in the land?﴾ is upon what the sentence ﴿We did not send before you except men﴾ indicates of the model (*uswah*). That is: their peoples denied them before your people, just as your people denied you, and their outcome was punishment. ﴿Have they not traveled in the land and seen what was the end of those before them?﴾ That is, they should see the traces of the last state of their affairs: destruction and punishment. Thus your people would know that their end is by analogy with the end of those who denied the messengers before them. The pronoun in *yasiru* refers to something known from the context that indicates it, and what I am not of the polytheists.

The interrogation is denunciatory (*inkari*), for the totality of those spoken of traveled in the land and saw the end of the deniers, like 'Ad and Thamud. This branching is an interjected threat and warning.

*Kayf* (how) is an interrogative that suspends the verb of seeing from its object.

The clause ﴿and the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾ is a predicate, conjoined to the interjection, so it has its ruling. It is an interjected good news and a promise of good outcome for the messengers, peace be upon them, and for those who believed in them, and they are ﴿those who had taqwa﴾. It is an allusion to the safety of the outcome of the God-fearing in this world, and also an allusion that the abode of the Hereafter is even harsher for those before them than the outcome that was in this world. Thus there is brevity by omitting two clauses.

The construction of *dar* (abode) with *akhirah* (hereafter) is an annexation of a described noun to its descriptor, like "O women of the Muslims" in the hadith.

[p. 70]

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ with the *ta'* of address, by way of *iltifat* (shift of address), because when the obstinate ones were mentioned and their mention was repeated, they became like those present, so the address turned to them directly. The rest read it with the *ya'* of the third person, in keeping with what precedes it.

*Hatta* (until) in His saying ﴿until when the messengers despaired﴾ is initial (*ibtida'iyyah*), and it conjoins the clause ﴿when the messengers despaired﴾ to the clause ﴿We did not send before you except men whom We revealed to﴾, in the sense that it is proof against the deniers. The meaning therefore is: We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, and those to whom they were sent denied them and persisted in denial, until, when the messengers despaired... For *idha* is a temporal noun carrying the meaning of a condition, so it requires an annexation to a clause that specifies the time. The clause *istay'asa* (despaired) is annexed to *idha*, and the clause ﴿Our help came to them﴾ is the answer of *idha*, because this order in meaning is what is intended by bringing *idha* in such a structure. The "messengers" here, peace be upon them, are not the same as the "men" mentioned, so the definiteness of "the messengers" is definiteness of remembered reference, and it is among the explicit nouns in the place of the pronoun, to give the speech independence in meaning and to emphasize the clause.

The particle of limit (*hatta*) signals an omitted meaning indicated by the clause ﴿We did not send before you except men﴾ with what is intended by it of the sense of taking the earlier messengers as a model. The meaning is: their denial and aversion continued, and the fulfilment of what they warned them of, namely the punishment, was delayed, until they felt secure in safety, mocked the messengers, and the messengers, peace be upon them, despaired of their people's faith.

*Istay'asa* (despaired) is an intensified form of *ya'isa*, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿and do not despair of the mercy of God﴾ [Yusuf: 87].

It was also mentioned earlier that al-Bazzi, by a variant from him, read with the *hamza* placed before the *ya'*. These are four words in this surah in which al-Bazzi differed from his narration.

[p. 70 continued]

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Urwa, that he asked 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her: "Were they denied (*kudhdhibu*) or were they lied to (*kudhibu*)?" That is, with the light or the emphatic form? She said: "They were denied (*kudhdhibu*), that is, with the emphatic form." He said: "Then they were certain that their people had denied them, so it was not a matter of supposition." She said: "They were lied to (*kudhibu*), that is, with the light form." She said: "God forbid! The messengers, peace be upon them, did not think this about their Lord. Rather, they were the followers of those who believed and affirmed, so the affliction lengthened upon them and the help was delayed, until, when the messengers, peace be upon them, despaired of the faith of those among their people who denied them, and the messengers, peace be upon them, thought that their followers would deny them." End of quotation.

This statement of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, is her own opinion in interpretation. Her rejection that it be read as *kudhibu* in the light form is a rejection based on what appears from the return of pronouns to the nearest preceding mention, which is "the messengers." That is not definitive, and 'A'isha had not received the transmission of the reading *kudhibu* with the light form.

The branching of ﴿and We deliver whom We will﴾ upon ﴿Our help came to them﴾ is because the help of the messengers, peace be upon them, is their support by punishing those who denied them with the descent of punishment, which is *ba's* (violent punishment). In that case *man nasha'* is the deputy subject. The combination of the past in *nujjiya* with the present in *nasha'* is an *ihtibak* (an implicit compensatory omission), its sense being: "so whom We willed of those who were saved in earlier generations was delivered, and We will deliver whom We will of the deniers in the future."

[Page 71]

﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for people of understanding. It was not a fabricated narration, but a confirmation of what came before it, a detailed explanation of all things, and a guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ This is from *radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-ṣadr* (a rhetorical device in which the end of a passage echoes its beginning), so this verse is connected to the statement "That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you" [Yusuf: 102]. It stands to it in the position of *bayan* (explanation) for what the phrase "that is from the news of the unseen" contains of wonder (*taʿjib*), and for what the phrase "and you were not with them" contains of inference that it is a revelation from God, together with the indication of the Prophet's being unlettered (*al-ummiyya*).

It also stands in the position of *tadhyil* (a concluding statement that sums up what precedes) for the sentences that digressed (*al-mustaṭrad bihā*) for the purpose of taking lesson from the story, beginning with His saying: "And most people, though you were eager, will not be believers" [Yusuf: 103].

Thus it has three wondrous positions within the inimitable composition of the Qur'an. The emphasis of the sentence by *qad* and the *lam* is for affirmation (*tahqiq*).

*Ulu al-albab* means: possessors of intellects. It was mentioned earlier in His saying: "And fear Me, O possessors of intellects" [al-Baqara: 197], in the middle of Surat al-Baqara.

*Al-ʿIbra* is a verbal noun (*ism al-maṣdar*) of *al-iʿtibar* (taking a lesson), which is reaching knowledge of the unseen through knowledge of what is witnessed and known. *Al-ʿIbra* is also used for what the taking of lesson results in, by the usage of the verbal noun for the object (*ism al-mafʿul*), as here. The meaning of the lesson being in their stories is that it is contained in them in a figurative sense of containment, namely the containment of the indicated in the indicator. So it is settled in their stories, whether or not those who are granted the ability to take lesson take it, and whether or not some people fail to take lesson from it.

The clause "It was not a fabricated narration" up to its end is a justification (*taʿlil*) for the clause "There was certainly in their stories a lesson", meaning: because that story is a true report that conforms to reality, and is not a fabricated story. [Page 72] The reason for the justification is that taking lesson from a story is not achieved unless it is a report of a matter that actually occurred, because the consequences following from real events follow naturally; it is in their nature that their like follows their like whenever it occurs in reality. Also, because its occurrence is possible, since what exists externally does not contain the impossible or the extremely rare. This is unlike invented stories made up by imagination and lies, from which no lesson is taken, because the hearer deems their occurrence unlikely, since their like is not known. Examples are the exaggerations of fables and the tales of the jinn and the *ghul* among the Arabs, and the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar among the Persians. The hearer receives them as amusements and pleasant fantasies, and he is not prepared to take lesson from them except as a supposition and possibility, and souls do not retain such things.

This verse refers back to His saying at the beginning of the surah: "We relate to you the best of stories" [Yusuf: 3]. Just as God named it "the best of stories" at the beginning of the surah, He negated fabrication from it in this verse, as an allusion against al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his like.

*Al-iftiraʾ* (fabrication) was mentioned earlier in His saying: "But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God" [al-Ma'ida: 103], in Surat al-ʿUqud.

*Alladhi bayna yadayhi* means: the previous divine scriptures. The pronoun in *bayna yadayhi* refers to the Qur'an, of which these stories are a part.

*Al-tafsil* means: clarification. What is meant by "all things" is the many matters that relate to taking lesson from the stories.

The use of "all" for abundance has already passed in His saying: "And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it" [al-Anʿam: 25], in Surat al-Anʿam.

The guidance found in the stories is: the lessons that prompt faith and piety by witnessing the proofs that appear within the stories, that the one who disposes affairs is God Most High, and that piety is the foundation of good in this world and the Hereafter. Likewise is mercy, for in the stories of the people of virtue [Page 73] there is an indication of God's mercy toward them and His care for them. That is a mercy for the believers, because by taking lesson from them they act and refrain, so their conditions are set right and they live in tranquil peace of mind. That is a mercy from God upon them in their life, and a cause of His mercy toward them in the Hereafter, as He Most High said: "Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them with their best deeds" [al-Nahl: 97].

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Raʿd

It was named thus since the time of the early generation (*al-salaf*). This indicates that it was named so since the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), since they did not differ about its name.

It was named by attribution to *al-raʿd* (thunder) because of the mention of thunder in it, in His saying: "And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and the angels from fear of Him, and He sends the thunderbolts" [al-Raʿd: 13]. It was named after thunder because thunder is not mentioned in any surah like this surah. This surah is Meccan entirely or mostly. Thunder is mentioned in Surat al-Baqara, which was revealed in Medina. Since the verses "It is He who shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope" [al-Raʿd: 12] up to His saying "and He is severe in might" [al-Raʿd: 13] were revealed in Medina, as will come, it is established that this was revealed before Surat al-Baqara was revealed.

This surah is Meccan according to Mujahid and his narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, the narration of ʿAli ibn Abi Talha and Said ibn Jubayr from him, and it is the view of Qatada. From Abu Bishr, who said: I asked Said ibn Jubayr about His saying: "And whoever has knowledge of the Book" [al-Raʿd: 43], that is at the end of Surat al-Raʿd, "is it ʿAbdullah ibn Salam?" He said: "How, when this is a Meccan surah?" From Ibn Jurayj and Qatada in one narration from him, and from Ibn ʿAbbas as well, that it is Medinan. This is from ʿIkrima, al-Hasan al-Basri, and from ʿAta from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Suyuti and others reconciled the narrations by saying that it is Meccan except for some verses of it that were revealed in Medina, meaning His saying: "It is He who shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope" [al-Raʿd: 12] up to His saying "severe in might" [al-Raʿd: 13], and His saying: "Say: God suffices as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book" [al-Raʿd: 43].

[Page 76]

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: The apparent view is that much of it is Medinan, and everything that was revealed concerning ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabiʿa is Medinan.

I say: The verses most resembling being Medinan are His saying: "Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its edges?" [al-Raʿd: 41], as you will know, and His Most High saying: "Thus We have sent you to a community" [al-Raʿd: 30] up to "and to Him is my return". Muqatil and Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning the treaty of al-Hudaybiya, as will come when its interpretation is given.

Its meanings run in the style of the meanings of the Meccan Qur'an: the argument for monotheism, and the denunciation and threatening of the polytheists. The reasons that prompted the claim that it is Medinan are weak reports, and we will mention them in their places in this tafsir. There is no obstacle to it being Meccan. Some of its verses may have been revealed in Medina and appended to it, since this occurs in some surahs of the Qur'an. Those who said it is Meccan did not mention its position in the order of Meccan surahs, except that they mentioned it after Surat Yusuf and mentioned Surat Ibrahim after it.

Those who considered it Medinan counted it in the order of revelation after Surat al-Qital and before Surat al-Rahman, and counted it as the ninety-seventh in the order of revelation. Since Surat al-Qital was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiya or the year of the Conquest, Surat al-Raʿd would be after it.

Its verses are counted as forty-three by the Kufans, forty-four by the Medinans, and forty-five according to the Syrians.

* * *

This surah is established on the basis of affirming the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) in what was revealed to him: the oneness of God in divinity, the resurrection, and the refutation of the statements of the deniers. Therefore the recounting of their statements is repeated five times, distributed throughout the surah at its beginning and its end.

This is prepared for by the praise of the Qur'an and that it is sent down from God, and by the argument for His unique divinity through the proofs of the creation of the two worlds and their order, which indicate His sole possession of complete knowledge and power, and by including gratitude for the blessings upon people contained in that.

Then it moves on to the statements of the people of polytheism and their claims in denying the resurrection.

And their threat that what befell those like them will befall them, and the reminder of God's blessings upon people, and the affirmation that God is the one deserving worship to the exclusion of their gods, that God knows the hidden things, and that the idols know nothing and bestow no blessing.

And the threat through atmospheric events, that among them there may be a punishment for the deniers as befell the nations before them.

And the warning of the Day of Recompense.

And the reminder that this world is not a place of permanence.

And the demonstration of the polytheists' obstinacy in their demand that signs come in accordance with their proposals.

And the contrast of that with the certainty of the believers, and what God has prepared for them of good.

And that the Messenger (ﷺ) met from his people only what the messengers before him, peace be upon them, met.

And the praise of a group of the People of the Book who believe that the Qur'an is sent down from the Lord.

And the allusion to the reality of predestination (*al-qadar*) and the manifestations of erasure and affirmation (*al-mahw wal-ithbat*), and the admonitions, lessons and parables interspersed within that.
